explanation:
The oculomotor nerve is highest in the lateral wall; the maxillary nerve runs along its lower border. The abducent nerve is not in the wall — it lies inside the sinus.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET, 2015 AIIMS (nerve in superior part of lateral wall)

stem: A patient with cavernous sinus thrombosis following a facial furuncle develops diplopia. The earliest ocular movement to be lost is usually
explanation:
The abducent nerve runs *through* the sinus, lateral to the internal carotid artery, with no protection from the dural wall. It is therefore affected first, giving lateral rectus palsy.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS cavernous sinus; 2017 AIIMS tributaries

subject: Anatomy
stem: A boy is struck by a cricket ball on the side of his head about 4 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch. He is lucid for an hour, then becomes drowsy. The vessel most likely torn is
options: Anterior (frontal) branch of the middle meningeal artery
Posterior (parietal) branch of the middle meningeal artery
explanation:
The point described is the pterion. The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies deep to it, so a fracture here causes an extradural haematoma with a lucid interval.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (artery deep to pterion)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which bone does NOT take part in forming the pterion?
explanation:
The pterion is the H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of sphenoid. The zygomatic bone meets the frontal bone lower down, at the frontozygomatic suture.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (bone deep to pterion), 2023 INI-CET (sulcus deep to pterion)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A neurosurgeon makes a burr hole at the asterion. The structure deep to this point that is at greatest risk is the
options: Junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinuses
Posterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
explanation:
The asterion is where the parietal, occipital and mastoid part of the temporal bone meet. It overlies the transverse–sigmoid sinus junction, a key landmark in retrosigmoid approaches.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (asterion sutures), pterion cluster 2022–2023

subject: Anatomy
stem: A basal skull fracture passes through the jugular foramen. Which finding is NOT expected?
options: Loss of taste over the posterior third of the tongue
Deviation of the uvula towards the normal side
Weakness of shrugging the shoulder on the side of injury
Deviation of the protruded tongue towards the side of injury
explanation:
The jugular foramen transmits the IX, X and XI nerves (Vernet syndrome). The hypoglossal nerve leaves through the separate hypoglossal canal, so tongue movement is spared.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (jugular foramen trauma → taste posterior 1/3), 2014 AIIMS

subject: Anatomy
stem: A muscle arises from the medial side of the base of the styloid process and enters the pharynx through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors. Its nerve supply is
explanation:
The muscle is stylopharyngeus — the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which accompanies it through the same gap.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (structure between superior and middle constrictor)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (structure between superior and middle constric

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match the gap in the pharyngeal wall with the structure passing through it.

| Gap | Structure |
|---|---|
| 1. Above the superior constrictor | a. Recurrent laryngeal nerve |
| 2. Between superior and middle constrictors | b. Internal laryngeal nerve |
| 3. Between middle and inferior constrictors | c. Auditory tube |
| 4. Below the inferior constrictor | d. Stylopharyngeus |
explanation:
Above superior: auditory tube and levator veli palatini. Superior–middle: stylopharyngeus and IX nerve. Middle–inferior: internal laryngeal nerve with superior laryngeal vessels. Below inferior: recurrent laryngeal nerve with inferior laryngeal vessels.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET constrictor gap

subject: Anatomy
stem: After a superficial parotidectomy, a patient cannot close the eye tightly on the operated side, but wrinkling of the forehead is normal. The branch of the facial nerve injured is the
explanation:
Frontalis (forehead) is supplied by the temporal branch, which is intact here. Firm eye closure depends on orbicularis oculi, mainly through the zygomatic branch.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (lower lip weakness after parotid surgery), 2015 AIIMS parotid
exam: 2022 INI-CET (lower lip weakness after parotid surgery), 201

subject: Anatomy
stem: During excision of the submandibular gland, the skin incision is placed about two finger-breadths below the lower border of the mandible. This is done mainly to protect the
options: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
Cervical branch of the facial nerve
explanation:
The marginal mandibular branch can loop below the mandible, superficial to the facial vessels. A low incision avoids it; injury causes drooping of the angle of the mouth.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (submandibular excision)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nerve that crosses the submandibular duct twice — first lateral to it, then below and medial to it — is the
explanation:
The lingual nerve spirals around the submandibular (Wharton's) duct and is the nerve most at risk during submandibular gland and duct surgery.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (structure injured in submandibular excision)

subject: Anatomy
stem: In Frey's syndrome, gustatory sweating occurs because of misdirected regrowth of secretomotor fibres. These fibres originally arise from the
options: Superior salivatory nucleus, via the chorda tympani
Superior salivatory nucleus, via the greater petrosal nerve
Inferior salivatory nucleus, via the lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion
Edinger–Westphal nucleus, via the ciliary ganglion
explanation:
Parotid secretomotor pathway: inferior salivatory nucleus → IX → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve. After parotid surgery these fibres regrow into sweat glands of the skin.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (Frey's syndrome), 2021 NEET-PG (parotid nerve supply)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient has an LMN facial palsy with loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and hyperacusis, but lacrimation is normal. The lesion is most likely located
options: Between the geniculate ganglion and the origin of the nerve to stapedius
Between the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani
explanation:
Normal lacrimation means the greater petrosal nerve (given off at the geniculate ganglion) is spared. Hyperacusis means the nerve to stapedius is involved, and taste loss means chorda tympani fibres are involved. The lesion must sit between these points.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (lacrimation lost — greater petrosal)

subject: Anatomy
stem: In a complete oculomotor nerve palsy the eye rests "down and out". Which muscles are responsible for this position?
explanation:
These are the only extraocular muscles not supplied by the III nerve (IV and VI). Unopposed lateral rectus pulls the eye out; unopposed superior oblique pulls it down.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (3rd nerve palsy)

subject: Anatomy
stem: To test the superior oblique muscle in isolation, the patient is asked to look
explanation:
With the eye adducted, the line of pull of the superior oblique aligns with the visual axis, so it acts as a pure depressor. Patients with IV nerve palsy struggle walking downstairs or reading.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (function of superior oblique), 2021 INI-CET (nerve to superior oblique)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A smoker has partial ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis confined to the face and neck on the left side, together with wasting of the small muscles of the left hand. The lesion is most likely at the
options: Internal carotid plexus in the cavernous sinus
Left internal carotid artery in the neck (dissection)
Left lung apex involving the T1 root and sympathetic chain
explanation:
This is a Pancoast tumour. Hand wasting points to T1. A second-order (preganglionic) lesion gives facial anhidrosis; a lateral medullary (first-order) lesion gives anhidrosis of the whole half of the body; a carotid (third-order) lesion spares most facial sweating. The ptosis is from paralysis of Müller's muscle.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (ptosis in Horner's — Müller muscle)

subject: Anatomy
stem: An orbital tumour compresses the nerve to the inferior oblique close to its origin. In addition to weakness of that muscle, the patient will show
options: A dilated pupil with loss of accommodation
explanation:
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus reach the ciliary ganglion along the nerve to the inferior oblique. Interrupting them paralyses the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (Edinger–Westphal fibres via nerve to inferior oblique)

subject: Anatomy
stem: During thyroidectomy, a parathyroid gland is found low in the anterior mediastinum, close to the thymus. This gland is most likely the
options: Superior parathyroid, from the 4th pharyngeal pouch
Superior parathyroid, from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch
Inferior parathyroid, from the 4th pharyngeal pouch
Inferior parathyroid, from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch
explanation:
The 3rd pouch forms both the thymus and the inferior parathyroids. They migrate down together, so the inferior parathyroid is the one found in ectopic, low positions.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (DiGeorge — 3rd pouch defect)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each muscle with its nerve supply (which follows its pharyngeal arch of origin).

| Muscle | Nerve |
|---|---|
| 1. Tensor tympani | a. Facial nerve |
| 2. Stapedius | b. Superior laryngeal nerve (external branch) |
| 3. Stylopharyngeus | c. Mandibular nerve |
| 4. Cricothyroid | d. Glossopharyngeal nerve |
explanation:
1st arch → V3 (tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric). 2nd → VII (stapedius). 3rd → IX (stylopharyngeus). 4th → X via superior laryngeal (cricothyroid).
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (1st arch derivatives), 2018 NEET-PG (arch nerves)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following is NOT derived from the neural crest?
options: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
explanation:
The retinal pigment epithelium comes from the outer layer of the optic cup, which is neuroectoderm (neural tube), not neural crest.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (RPE — neuroectoderm), 2018 NEET-PG (neural crest)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A professional singer cannot reach high-pitched notes after thyroidectomy. Her voice is weak and monotonous, but the vocal cords move normally on laryngoscopy. The nerve injured is the
explanation:
It supplies cricothyroid, the tensor of the vocal cords. It runs close to the superior thyroid artery, so that artery is ligated close to the gland.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (cricothyroid palsy), 2022 INI-CET (nerves at risk in thyroid surgery)

subject: Anatomy
stem: While a fish bone is being removed from the piriform recess, the nerve lying just beneath its mucosa is injured. The expected deficit is
options: Loss of sensation above the vocal cords with an impaired cough reflex
explanation:
The internal laryngeal nerve runs under the mucosa of the piriform recess. It is purely sensory to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds and is the afferent limb of the cough reflex. *Note: the 2020 INI-CET key reads "gag reflex"; standard texts give cough reflex, since the gag reflex afferent is IX.*
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (fish bone in piriform sinus), 2021 INI-CET (piriform fossa)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure is NOT a content of the carotid sheath?
explanation:
The sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, on the prevertebral fascia. The ansa cervicalis is embedded in the anterior wall of the sheath, not inside it.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (contents of carotid sheath)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A retropharyngeal abscess tracks down rapidly into the posterior mediastinum as far as the diaphragm. The space involved lies between the
options: Prevertebral fascia and the vertebral bodies
explanation:
This is the "danger space", which runs from the skull base to the diaphragm. The retropharyngeal space proper (between buccopharyngeal and alar fascia) ends at about T2.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (danger space)

subject: Anatomy
stem: During thyroidectomy, the inferior thyroid artery is ligated well away from the gland, near the carotid sheath. The main reason is to protect the
explanation:
Near the gland, the recurrent laryngeal nerve intertwines with the branches of the inferior thyroid artery. Ligating laterally avoids the nerve and keeps the parathyroid blood supply. The superior thyroid artery is the opposite: it is ligated close to the gland to protect the external laryngeal nerve.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (inferior thyroid artery), 2022 INI-CET (nerves at risk)

subject: Anatomy
stem: All of the following arteries contribute to Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) EXCEPT
options: Septal branch of the superior labial artery
explanation:
Little's area receives the anterior ethmoidal (from the ICA via the ophthalmic artery), the septal branch of sphenopalatine, greater palatine and the septal branch of superior labial (all from the ECA).
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (nasal septum arteries — anterior ethmoidal is the non-ECA one)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each part of the lateral nasal wall with the structure opening into it.

| Site | Opening |
|---|---|
| 1. Inferior meatus | a. Sphenoid sinus |
| 2. Middle meatus (hiatus semilunaris) | b. Posterior ethmoidal air cells |
| 3. Superior meatus | c. Nasolacrimal duct |
| 4. Sphenoethmoidal recess | d. Maxillary sinus |
explanation:
The middle meatus also receives the frontal sinus and the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (opening in inferior meatus)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A muscle arises mainly from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and inserts into the medial surface of the angle of the mandible. Its action is
options: Elevation and protrusion of the mandible
Opening of the mouth against resistance
explanation:
This is medial pterygoid. With masseter it elevates the jaw; with lateral pterygoid it protrudes the jaw and produces side-to-side grinding. Lateral pterygoid is the main opener of the mouth.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (muscle from lateral aspect of lateral pterygoid plate → action), 2014 AIIMS
exam: 2023 INI-CET (muscle from lateral aspect of lateral pterygoi

subject: Anatomy
stem: The mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric share the same nerve supply. That nerve is a branch of the
explanation:
The nerve to mylohyoid leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before it enters the mandibular foramen. Both muscles are 1st-arch derivatives, which explains the shared V3 supply. The posterior belly of digastric is 2nd arch (facial nerve).
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (nerve through mandibular foramen), 2019 NEET-PG (1st arch — anterior digastric)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Stimulating the posterior wall of the external acoustic meatus with an ear bud provokes a cough. The nerve responsible is the
explanation:
Arnold's nerve supplies the concha, the posterior part of the meatus and the outer tympanic membrane. Great auricular supplies the lower pinna on both surfaces; auriculotemporal supplies the upper lateral pinna, tragus and anterior meatus.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (nerve to lower pinna)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Taste from the circumvallate papillae, which lie just in front of the sulcus terminalis, is carried by the
explanation:
Although they sit on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the circumvallate papillae are supplied for both general sensation and taste by IX.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (circumvallate papilla), 2016 AIIMS (taste anterior 2/3)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each foramen with a structure passing through it.

| Foramen | Content |
|---|---|
| 1. Foramen ovale | a. Middle meningeal artery |
| 2. Foramen spinosum | b. Maxillary nerve |
| 3. Foramen rotundum | c. Abducent nerve |
| 4. Superior orbital fissure | d. Lesser petrosal nerve |
explanation:
Foramen ovale (OVALE): Otic ganglion nearby, V3, Accessory meningeal artery, Lesser petrosal nerve, Emissary vein. The superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 branches and VI.
> `HEAD AND NECK` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (foramen rotundum, foramen lacerum)

subject: Anatomy
stem: On attempted gaze to the right, the right eye abducts with nystagmus but the left eye fails to adduct. Convergence is normal. The lesion lies in the
explanation:
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is named after the eye that fails to adduct. Convergence is preserved because the medial rectus nucleus and the III nerve are intact.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (INO), 2014 AIIMS (abducent palsy gaze pattern)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A single pontine lesion damages the right abducent nucleus and the right medial longitudinal fasciculus. Which horizontal eye movement is still possible?
explanation:
This is the "one-and-a-half syndrome": a right horizontal gaze palsy (the "one") plus a right INO (the "half"). The only horizontal movement left is abduction of the opposite eye.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (INO), 2020 INI-CET (facial colliculus)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which feature is NOT seen in occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery?
options: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature over the face
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature over the body
explanation:
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome spares the pyramids, which are supplied medially by the anterior spinal artery. Hoarseness and dysphagia (nucleus ambiguus) and ipsilateral ataxia are typical.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (lateral medullary syndrome — 7X), 2019 NEET-PG, 2023 INI-CET

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient's tongue deviates to the right on protrusion. There is left-sided hemiparesis and loss of proprioception on the left side of the body. The artery occluded is most likely the
explanation:
This is medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome on the right. It damages the right XII nucleus/nerve (tongue deviates to the lesion side), the right pyramid and the right medial lemniscus (both above their decussations, so the deficits appear on the left).
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: lateral medullary cluster 2014–2023

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient has right oculomotor nerve palsy together with left-sided hemiplegia. This is
explanation:
A lesion of the right cerebral peduncle (basis pedunculi) catches the emerging III nerve and the corticospinal fibres above their decussation. Benedikt adds red nucleus involvement (tremor). Millard–Gubler is pontine (VI, VII + hemiplegia).
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: brainstem syndrome cluster (2014, 2019, 2022 INI-CET)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Arrange these nuclei in the floor of the fourth ventricle (medullary part) from medial to lateral.
1. Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus
2. Vestibular nuclei
3. Hypoglossal nucleus
4. Nucleus of the tractus solitarius
explanation:
Medial to lateral: somatic efferent (XII, GSE) → general visceral efferent (DMN X) → visceral afferent (solitary nucleus) → special somatic afferent (vestibular). This matches the hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone and vestibular area.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (arrange columns medial to lateral)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which nucleus is NOT a special visceral efferent (branchial motor) nucleus?
options: Motor nucleus of the facial nerve
Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve
Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
explanation:
The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus is general visceral efferent (parasympathetic). Special visceral efferent nuclei supply muscles of pharyngeal arch origin (V, VII, IX/X via ambiguus).
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (special visceral efferent)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A small haemorrhage involves the facial colliculus. The expected finding is
options: Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy with ipsilateral lateral gaze palsy
Contralateral UMN facial palsy with ipsilateral lateral gaze palsy
Ipsilateral facial palsy with hyperacusis only
Deviation of the tongue to the side of the lesion
explanation:
The facial colliculus, in the floor of the **fourth** ventricle (pons), is formed by facial nerve fibres looping around the abducent nucleus. A lesion of the abducent nucleus causes a horizontal gaze palsy towards that side. *The 2020 INI-CET stem wrongly says "third ventricle".*
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (facial colliculus injury)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A lacunar infarct is confined to the genu of the internal capsule. The fibres mainly affected are the
options: Corticospinal fibres to the lower limb
explanation:
These are projection fibres to the motor cranial nerve nuclei, so the infarct mainly affects the face and tongue. Corticospinal fibres run in the posterior limb; the optic and auditory radiations are retrolentiform and sublentiform.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (fibres in genu — 3X)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following is an example of association fibres?
explanation:
Association fibres connect areas within the same hemisphere (the uncinate links the frontal and temporal lobes). Commissural fibres cross to the other hemisphere; projection fibres link the cortex with lower centres.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (fornix — commissural and association), 2024 INI-CET (projection fibres in genu)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient suddenly cannot read but can write normally (alexia without agraphia), with a right homonymous hemianopia. The artery occluded is the
options: Left middle cerebral artery, superior division
explanation:
The left PCA supplies the left visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum. Visual information reaching the intact right occipital lobe cannot cross the damaged splenium to the left-sided language areas.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (blood supply of splenium)

subject: Anatomy
stem: After a small stroke, a patient develops sudden, violent flinging movements of the left arm. The lesion is in the
explanation:
Hemiballismus is contralateral to the lesion, because basal ganglia circuits act on the motor cortex of the same side, whose corticospinal output then crosses.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (ballistic movements — subthalamic nucleus)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The substantia nigra pars reticulata is functionally equivalent to the
explanation:
Both are the GABAergic output nuclei of the basal ganglia, projecting to the thalamus (and the superior colliculus). The pars compacta is the dopaminergic part that projects to the striatum.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (neurotransmitter of substantia nigra)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Arrange the components of the Papez circuit in sequence, starting from the hippocampus.
1. Cingulate gyrus
2. Mammillary body
3. Fornix
4. Anterior nucleus of the thalamus
explanation:
Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus → parahippocampal gyrus → hippocampus.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (mammillary body → anterior nucleus; limbic system), 2023 INI-CET (thalamic nucleus receiving fornix)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (mammillary body → anterior nucleus; limbic sys

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Arrange the parts of the fornix in the order in which its fibres pass.
1. Fimbria
2. Body
3. Alveus
4. Crus
5. Column
explanation:
Axons from the hippocampus and subiculum gather as the alveus, converge into the fimbria, arch up as the crus, join across the midline as the body (with the hippocampal commissure), and descend as the columns to the mammillary bodies.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (efferents of hippocampus via fornix), 2021 NEET-PG (C-shaped fornix)
exam: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (efferents of hippocampus via forn

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure forms part of the ROOF of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
explanation:
The roof contains the tail of the caudate, the stria terminalis and the tapetum, with the amygdala at the tip. The floor contains the hippocampus, fimbria and collateral eminence.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (structure not in floor of inferior horn)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (structure not in floor of inferior horn)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Climbing fibres of the cerebellum arise from the
explanation:
Olivocerebellar fibres cross, enter through the inferior peduncle and wrap directly around Purkinje cell dendrites. All other afferents (pontine, spinal, vestibular) end as mossy fibres on granule cells.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (molecular layer), 2022 NEET-PG (Purkinje cells), 2021 INI-CET

subject: Anatomy
stem: The only excitatory neurons intrinsic to the cerebellar cortex are the
explanation:
Granule cells are glutamatergic; their parallel fibres run in the molecular layer. Purkinje, basket, stellate and Golgi cells are all inhibitory (GABA). Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cortex.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (molecular layer — basket and stellate cells)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (molecular layer — basket and stellate cells)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Output from the dentate nucleus reaches the motor cortex mainly through the
options: Inferior cerebellar peduncle, to the ipsilateral VL thalamus
Middle cerebellar peduncle, to the contralateral VPL thalamus
Superior cerebellar peduncle, to the contralateral VL thalamus
Middle cerebellar peduncle, to the ipsilateral red nucleus
explanation:
Dentatothalamic fibres leave through the superior peduncle and cross at the level of the inferior colliculus (midbrain), reaching the VL thalamus and then the motor cortex.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (Purkinje fibres relay to dentate), 2022 INI-CET (decussation of superior cerebellar peduncle)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (Purkinje fibres relay to dentate), 2022 INI-CE

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which tract enters the cerebellum through the superior cerebellar peduncle?
explanation:
The superior peduncle is mainly efferent, but the ventral spinocerebellar tract enters through it. Dorsal spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar fibres use the inferior peduncle; pontocerebellar fibres form the middle peduncle.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (middle cerebellar peduncle fibres), 2022 INI-CET (superior peduncle)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A child with a midline posterior fossa tumour (medulloblastoma) arising from the flocculonodular lobe is most likely to show
explanation:
The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) works with the vestibular nuclei (and the fastigial nucleus) on balance and eye movements. Limb signs come from lesions of the cerebellar hemispheres.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (fastigial — saccades), 2018 AIIMS / 2021 NEET-PG (posterior fossa)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A stab wound causes hemisection of the spinal cord on the LEFT side at T8. Which finding is expected?
options: Loss of pain and temperature on the left below the lesion
Loss of vibration sense on the right below the lesion
Spastic paralysis on the right below the lesion
Spastic paralysis on the left below the lesion
explanation:
Brown-Séquard: the lateral corticospinal tract and dorsal columns have already crossed above this level, so motor and vibration/proprioception loss are on the same side. The spinothalamic tract crosses within 1–2 segments, so pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (Brown-Séquard), 2016 AIIMS (spinothalamic)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A young adult has loss of pain and temperature over both shoulders and arms in a cape-like distribution, with touch and proprioception preserved. The structure first damaged is the
explanation:
In syringomyelia, a central cavity first interrupts spinothalamic fibres crossing in front of the central canal. The result is bilateral, segmental, dissociated sensory loss.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (lateral spinothalamic tract), 2019 NEET-PG (Brown-Séquard)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The medial lemniscus is formed by axons of the
options: Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
explanation:
These second-order neurons send internal arcuate fibres that cross in the lower medulla (the sensory decussation) and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the VPL thalamus.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (medial lemniscus is continuation of …)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Arrange the layers pierced by a lumbar puncture needle in the midline, from superficial to deep, starting after skin and fascia.
1. Ligamentum flavum
2. Interspinous ligament
3. Dura mater
4. Supraspinous ligament
5. Arachnoid mater
explanation:
After the ligamentum flavum (a "give"), the needle crosses the epidural space, then the dura and arachnoid into the subarachnoid space. The cord ends at L1–L2 in adults, so LP is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (last layer punctured), 2020 INI-CET / 2016 AIIMS (cord ends at L1)

subject: Anatomy
stem: An elderly man on anticoagulants becomes gradually confused three weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection that crosses suture lines. The source of bleeding is
explanation:
This is a chronic subdural haematoma. Brain atrophy stretches the veins crossing from the cortex to the dural sinuses. Extradural haematomas are lens-shaped and limited by suture lines.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (SDH — bridging veins)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The dura mater of the posterior cranial fossa receives its sensory supply mainly from
options: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
Upper cervical nerves (C1–C3) and the vagus
explanation:
This explains why posterior fossa pathology refers pain to the occiput and back of the neck. The supratentorial dura is supplied by the trigeminal nerve, and its pain refers to the forehead and face.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (referred pain from posterior fossa dura), 2021 INI-CET / 2016 AIIMS (meningeal branch of ICA — T/F)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (referred pain from posterior fossa dura), 2021

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient speaks fluently and understands speech well, but cannot repeat a simple phrase spoken by the examiner. The lesion involves the
options: Posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus
explanation:
This is conduction aphasia: Wernicke's and Broca's areas both work, but the association bundle linking them is cut. Wernicke's lesion (area 22) impairs comprehension; Broca's lesion impairs fluency.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (Brodmann 22 — receptive aphasia), 2020 NEET-PG (Broca's area)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Brodmann areas 44 and 45 correspond to which parts of the inferior frontal gyrus?
options: The precentral gyrus and pars opercularis
explanation:
Area 44 is the pars opercularis and area 45 the pars triangularis; together they form Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere. It is supplied by the superior division of the MCA.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (Broca's area — inferior frontal gyrus)
exam: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (Broca's area — inferior frontal g

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient has a sudden severe headache with ptosis, a dilated pupil and an eye deviated down and out. The aneurysm most likely arises from the
explanation:
The III nerve runs right next to the PComm. Compression affects the superficial pupillomotor fibres first, giving a pupil-involving palsy. An anterior communicating aneurysm instead tends to compress the optic chiasma.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (AComm aneurysm and chiasma), 2024 INI-CET (3rd nerve palsy)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A temporal lobe tumour damaging Meyer's loop produces
explanation:
Meyer's loop carries fibres from the inferior retina (upper visual field) round the temporal horn ("pie in the sky"). Parietal radiation fibres carry the lower field.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (inferior horn relations), 2022 NEET-PG (optic chiasma)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal surface of the brainstem is the
explanation:
It emerges just below the inferior colliculus, after decussating in the superior medullary velum. The abducent nerve emerges at the medial end of the pontomedullary junction; the oculomotor nerve emerges from the interpeduncular fossa.
> `NEUROANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (image — nerve at medial pontomedullary junction), 2021 INI-CET (nerve to superior oblique)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the
explanation:
Anterior: free border of the lesser omentum. Superior: caudate process. Inferior: first part of the duodenum. Posterior: IVC (with the right crus). The foramen lies at about T12.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (superior boundary), 2021 INI-CET (vertebral level)

subject: Anatomy
stem: During a Pringle manoeuvre the surgeon compresses the free border of the lesser omentum. The structure lying most posteriorly in this border is the
explanation:
In the hepatoduodenal ligament, the bile duct lies anterior and to the right, the hepatic artery anterior and to the left, and the portal vein behind both.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2021 INI-CET (epiploic foramen)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The structure most consistently found within the hepatobiliary (Calot's) triangle is the
explanation:
Boundaries: common hepatic duct (medial), cystic duct (lateral), inferior surface of the liver (above). It contains the cystic artery and the cystic lymph node of Lund (Mascagni), and often the right hepatic artery.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (boundary of Calot's triangle — 3X)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which Couinaud segment drains directly into the IVC through its own small veins and receives portal blood from both right and left branches?
explanation:
The caudate lobe is functionally independent of both hemilivers. It is often spared or enlarged in Budd–Chiari syndrome because its outflow bypasses the main hepatic veins.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (structure dividing liver into Couinaud segments)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (structure dividing liver into Couinaud segment

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each portosystemic anastomosis site with the veins forming it.

| Site | Veins |

| 1. Lower oesophagus | a. Superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal |
| 2. Umbilicus | b. Colic veins with lumbar veins (veins of Retzius) |

explanation:
These give oesophageal varices, caput medusae, anorectal varices and retroperitoneal collaterals respectively.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure is in direct contact with the anterior surface of the RIGHT kidney, with no peritoneum in between?
explanation:
The descending duodenum and the hepatic flexure of the colon touch the right kidney directly. The liver is separated from it by the peritoneum of the hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch).
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (viscera related to anterior surface of left kidney)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The most hazardous step in a right adrenalectomy is control of the right adrenal vein, because it
options: Drains into the right renal vein after a long course
Is short and drains directly into the IVC
Passes behind the right crus of the diaphragm
explanation:
The right adrenal vein is very short and enters the back of the IVC. The left adrenal vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein. The right gland is triangular (pyramidal); the left is semilunar.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (right adrenal shape; left inferior phrenic vein drainage)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are innervated by
options: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the coeliac ganglion
Preganglionic sympathetic fibres that do not synapse in any ganglion
Postganglionic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion
explanation:
Chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic neurons (neural crest), so they receive preganglionic splanchnic fibres directly. Those fibres pass through the sympathetic chain and coeliac plexus without relaying.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (preganglionic fibres to adrenals — T/F), 2021 INI-CET (adrenal zones)
exam: 2018 AIIMS (preganglionic fibres to adrenals — T/F), 2021 IN

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each wall of the inguinal canal with the structure forming it.

| Wall | Structure |

| 1. Anterior wall | a. Fascia transversalis and conjoint tendon |
| 2. Posterior wall | b. Inguinal ligament with lacunar ligament |
| 3. Roof | c. Aponeurosis of external oblique |
| 4. Floor | d. Arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis |
explanation:
The deep ring is an opening in the fascia transversalis; the superficial ring is an opening in the external oblique aponeurosis. The lateral part of the anterior wall is reinforced by internal oblique.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (roof of inguinal canal — T/F), 2021 NEET-PG (deep inguinal ring)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lateral boundary of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle is formed by the
explanation:
Direct hernias come through this triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Indirect hernias enter the deep ring, lateral to them. Indirect inguinal hernia is the commonest hernia even in females.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (commonest hernia in female), 2021 NEET-PG (deep ring)

subject: Anatomy
stem: For a transvaginal pudendal nerve block, the needle tip is guided towards the
explanation:
The pudendal nerve crosses the back of the sacrospinous ligament near its attachment to the ischial spine, as it passes from the greater to the lesser sciatic foramen.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (ischial spine crossed by …)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which part of the levator ani forms a U-shaped sling around the anorectal junction and maintains the anorectal angle?
explanation:
It pulls the anorectal junction forward, which is essential for faecal continence. Pubococcygeus damage in childbirth contributes to cystocele, rectocele and stress incontinence.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (pelvic diaphragm — levator ani), 2014 AIIMS (pubococcygeus)

subject: Anatomy
stem: All of the following are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery EXCEPT
explanation:
The posterior division gives only the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries. All the visceral and other parietal branches come from the anterior division.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (branches of posterior division)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient with appendicitis has right iliac pain on passive extension of the right hip (positive psoas sign). The appendix is most likely
explanation:
A retrocaecal appendix lies on the psoas, which is stretched by hip extension. A pelvic appendix irritates obturator internus, giving pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip (obturator sign).
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (match — positions of appendix)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each vitello-intestinal duct anomaly with its result.

| Anomaly | Result |
|---|---|
| 1. Entire duct remains patent | a. Vitelline cyst |
| 2. Only the ileal end persists | b. Volvulus around a band |
| 3. Both ends close, middle stays patent | c. Faecal discharge from the umbilicus |
| 4. Duct persists as a fibrous cord | d. Meckel's diverticulum |
explanation:
Meckel's diverticulum is on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve. It may bleed because of ectopic gastric mucosa.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (faeces from umbilicus), 2015 AIIMS (vitelline cyst), 2023 NEET-PG (Meckel's)

subject: Anatomy
stem: In "nutcracker syndrome", the structure compressed between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta is the
explanation:
It causes haematuria, flank pain and a left varicocele (the left gonadal vein drains into it). Compression of the third part of the duodenum in the same angle is SMA (Wilkie) syndrome.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (compression of 3rd part of duodenum)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The tail of the pancreas lies within which ligament?
explanation:
It also carries the splenic vessels. The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels. The phrenicocolic ligament supports the lower pole of the spleen.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (dorsal mesentery derivatives), 2020 NEET-PG (phrenicocolic ligament)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following develops from the ventral mesogastrium?
explanation:
The ventral mesogastrium forms the lesser omentum, falciform ligament, coronary and triangular ligaments (the liver grows into it). The dorsal mesogastrium forms the greater omentum and the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (falciform — ventral mesogastrium), 2018 NEET-PG (dorsal mesentery)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cells are modified
options: Smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
Epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule
explanation:
The juxtaglomerular apparatus = JG cells + macula densa (modified DCT epithelium that senses NaCl) + extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (glomerulus biopsy), 2019 NEET-PG (duct of Bellini)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The trigone of the urinary bladder is developmentally derived from
options: The endoderm of the urogenital sinus only
The incorporated ends of the mesonephric ducts
explanation:
Most of the bladder comes from the urogenital sinus, but the trigone forms when the mesonephric ducts are absorbed into its wall (mesoderm, later covered by endoderm). The allantois becomes the urachus.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (bladder from urogenital sinus), 2017 AIIMS (T/F — bladder and kidney origin), 2022 NEET-PG (allantois)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Early appendicitis pain is felt around the umbilicus because visceral afferents from the appendix enter the spinal cord at
explanation:
Midgut afferents travel with the lesser splanchnic nerve to T10, the dermatome of the umbilicus. Pain shifts to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum is involved.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (umbilicus — T10 dermatome)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A woman has a cystocele and stress incontinence after a difficult vaginal delivery. The muscle whose damage is most responsible is
explanation:
Its medial fibres (pubovaginalis) support the bladder neck, vagina and perineal body. Their damage loosens support for the anterior and posterior vaginal walls.
> `ABDOMEN AND PELVIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (pubococcygeus — rectocele, cystocele), 2024 INI-CET (pelvic diaphragm)

subject: Anatomy
stem: An ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist produces MORE clawing of the ring and little fingers than a lesion at the elbow. The reason is that in a wrist lesion
options: The ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is spared and flexes the IP joints unopposed
The flexor digitorum superficialis is paralysed
explanation:
This is the "ulnar paradox". In a lesion at the elbow, FDP to the 4th and 5th fingers is also paralysed, so the DIP joints cannot flex and the claw is milder.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (level of ulnar injury — 4X), 2022 INI-CET (medial epicondyle fracture)

subject: Anatomy
stem: When asked to grip a sheet of paper between the thumb and the side of the index finger, a patient flexes the thumb IP joint strongly. The muscle that is weak, and its nerve, are
options: Flexor pollicis longus — anterior interosseous nerve
explanation:
This is Froment's sign: the patient substitutes the median-supplied flexor pollicis longus for the paralysed adductor. The "book test" is the same idea.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2019 NEET-PG (Book test — ulnar nerve)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A long-distance cyclist has weakness of finger abduction and adduction but normal sensation over the little finger. The likely site of compression is the
options: Ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle
Superficial branch of the ulnar nerve
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
explanation:
In or just beyond Guyon's canal the ulnar nerve splits. The deep branch is purely motor (interossei, 3rd and 4th lumbricals, adductor pollicis, usually hypothenar muscles). The superficial branch carries the sensation.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (structures through Guyon's canal), 2023 INI-CET (muscles supplied by ulnar nerve)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ulnar nerve is cut at the wrist by broken glass. Sensation remains normal over which area that the ulnar nerve normally supplies?
options: Palmar surface of the little finger
Palmar surface of the medial half of the ring finger
Dorsal surface of the medial hand
explanation:
The dorsal cutaneous branch leaves the ulnar nerve about 5 cm above the wrist, so a wrist laceration spares it.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (cutaneous supply of hand), 2024 INI-CET (Book test)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A muscle arises from the flexor retinaculum, scaphoid and trapezium and inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Its nerve supply is the
options: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Recurrent (motor) branch of the median nerve
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
explanation:
The muscle is abductor pollicis brevis. Its paralysis is the earliest motor sign of carpal tunnel syndrome, and it is the muscle behind the "can't button the shirt" presentation.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (image — opponens pollicis), 2023 NEET-PG (abductor pollicis brevis palsy)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
options: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
explanation:
It passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so sensation over the central palm and thenar skin is normal in carpal tunnel syndrome.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (Guyon's canal), median nerve cluster

subject: Anatomy
stem: After a supracondylar fracture, a child cannot make the "OK" sign and pinches with flat pads of the thumb and index finger. Sensation over the hand is normal. The nerve injured is the
explanation:
It supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. It has no skin territory, so sensation is normal.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (can't make O sign), 2014 AIIMS (muscles supplied by median nerve)
exam: 2023 NEET-PG (can't make O sign), 2014 AIIMS (muscles suppli

subject: Anatomy
stem: A mid-shaft fracture of the humerus causes wrist drop, but the triceps is largely spared. The best explanation is that
options: Triceps is supplied by the axillary nerve
Triceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
Branches to triceps leave the radial nerve proximal to the spiral groove
Triceps receives a direct branch from the C8 root
explanation:
Branches to the long and medial heads arise in the axilla, before the nerve enters the spiral groove. Extension of the elbow is therefore preserved.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (radial nerve injury near cubital fossa — wrist drop)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A radial neck fracture damages the posterior interosseous nerve. The expected finding is
options: Wrist drop with sensory loss in the first web space
Loss of supination and elbow flexion
Inability to extend the fingers and thumb, with the wrist still extending (radial deviation) and no sensory loss
explanation:
Extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied before the radial nerve divides, so the wrist can still extend, deviating radially. The PIN is purely motor.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (PIN injury — loss of finger extension)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (PIN injury — loss of finger extension)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which finger has NO dorsal interosseous muscle attached to it?
explanation:
Dorsal interossei abduct away from the axis of the middle finger: two attach to the middle finger, one each to the index and ring fingers. The thumb and little finger have their own abductors.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (finger with two dorsal interossei), 2024 INI-CET (dorsal digital expansion)
exam: 2020 INI-CET (finger with two dorsal interossei), 2024 INI-C

subject: Anatomy
stem: In a median nerve lesion at the wrist, which lumbricals are paralysed?
explanation:
The lateral two lumbricals (unipennate) are supplied by the median nerve; the medial two (bipennate) by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Lumbricals uniquely arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (nerve supply of 1st lumbrical)

subject: Anatomy
stem: In Erb's palsy, which muscle is NOT paralysed?
explanation:
Erb's palsy involves the upper trunk (C5, C6): deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, brachialis and brachioradialis. Flexor carpi ulnaris is C7, C8 and T1.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (Erb's palsy — waiter's tip)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A newborn with Klumpke's palsy also has ptosis and miosis on the same side. This additional finding means the injury is
options: At the lower trunk, distal to its divisions
At the T1 root close to the spinal cord, involving the white ramus
At the ulnar nerve in the arm
explanation:
Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head leave through the T1 ventral root and white ramus. Horner's syndrome with Klumpke's palsy suggests root avulsion, which carries a poorer prognosis.
> `UPPER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (Klumpke's palsy — claw hand), 2023 NEET-PG (Horner's)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The axillary artery can be ligated with collateral flow kept through the scapular anastomosis if the ligature is placed
options: Distal to the profunda brachii artery
Distal to the posterior circumflex humeral artery
explanation:
The scapular anastomosis links the first part of the subclavian (suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries) with the third part of the axillary (subscapular artery). The ligature must lie between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery.

Supraspinatus starts abduction (0–15°), deltoid continues it, and trapezius with serratus anterior rotate the scapula above 90°.

It is supplied only by the ulnar artery
It ossifies last among the carpal bones

The long head arises from the supraglenoid tubercle, inside the shoulder joint. The coracoid can be felt in the infraclavicular fossa.

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient walks with a lurching gait. When standing on the LEFT leg, the RIGHT side of the pelvis drops. The nerve injured is the
explanation:
In a positive Trendelenburg sign, the stance-side hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) fail to hold the pelvis level, so the opposite side sags. The lesion is on the side of the supporting leg.

subject: Anatomy
stem: A muscle arises from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines and inserts on the anterior surface of the greater trochanter. Its principal actions are
options: Abduction and medial rotation of the hip
Extension and lateral rotation of the hip
explanation:
The muscle is gluteus minimus (superior gluteal nerve). Its anterior fibres make it a medial rotator, and during walking it keeps the pelvis level.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (action of gluteus minimus), 2021 INI-CET (superior gluteal nerve supplies)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient walks normally on level ground but has great difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. The muscle that is weak, and its nerve, are most likely
explanation:
Gluteus maximus is a powerful extensor of the hip that is not needed for quiet walking. It inserts into the iliotibial tract and the gluteal tuberosity.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (action of muscle on gluteal tuberosity)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (action of muscle on gluteal tuberosity)

subject: Anatomy

explanation:
It winds superficially round the neck of the fibula, where casts and fractures compress it. Both of its branches are lost. Tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) is spared, which rules out a sciatic lesion.

subject: Anatomy
stem: In anterior compartment syndrome of the leg, the earliest sensory loss is in the
explanation:
The deep peroneal nerve runs inside the anterior compartment and its only skin territory is the first web space. Weakness of toe extension follows.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (compartment without neurovascular bundle), 2022 NEET-PG (failure of dorsiflexion)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient cannot evert the foot but dorsiflexion is normal. The nerve injured is the
explanation:
It supplies peroneus longus and brevis (the evertors) and most of the skin of the dorsum of the foot. Dorsiflexion is a deep peroneal (anterior compartment) function.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (evertors), 2022 INI-CET (superficial peroneal supplies)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each compartment of the leg with its neurovascular content.

| Compartment | Content |

| 1. Anterior | a. No neurovascular bundle |
| 2. Lateral | b. Tibial nerve and posterior tibial artery |
| 3. Deep posterior | c. Deep peroneal nerve and anterior tibial artery |
| 4. Superficial posterior | d. Superficial peroneal nerve, no named artery |
explanation:
The superficial posterior compartment (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris) has no main neurovascular bundle running through it. The lateral compartment's blood comes from perforating branches of the peroneal artery.

subject: Anatomy

explanation:
"Tom, Dick, And Nervous Harry": Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, Artery (with veins), Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus.

explanation:
The saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, runs with the great saphenous vein below the knee.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (saphenous nerve with GSV), 2022 INI-CET (nerve block for medial leg — 3X)

subject: Anatomy

explanation:
The psoas sheath runs from the lumbar vertebrae to the lesser trochanter, behind the inguinal ligament. The femoral nerve runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus.

explanation:

subject: Anatomy
stem: The tendons forming the pes anserinus are supplied by three different nerves. Which combination is correct?
explanation:
Sartorius (femoral), gracilis (obturator) and semitendinosus (tibial part of the sciatic nerve) insert together on the upper medial tibia. They represent the three compartments of the thigh.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (sartorius), 2020 NEET-PG (hybrid muscle)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which thigh muscle commonly receives a dual nerve supply from the femoral and obturator nerves?
explanation:
Adductor magnus is the other hybrid, but its two parts are supplied by the obturator nerve and the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. Biceps femoris is a hybrid of the tibial and common peroneal parts.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (hybrid muscle partly spared in sciatica)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A footballer has a positive posterior drawer test. The torn ligament is attached to the femur at the
options: Medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle
Lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle
explanation:
The posterior cruciate ligament runs from the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia upwards, forwards and medially. It is intracapsular but extrasynovial and stops the tibia sliding backwards. The ACL attaches to the medial surface of the lateral condyle.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (posterior cruciate ligament)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The muscle that "unlocks" the fully extended knee does so by
options: Medially rotating the femur on the tibia — supplied by the femoral nerve
Extending the knee — supplied by the tibial nerve
Laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia — supplied by the tibial nerve
Laterally rotating the tibia — supplied by the common peroneal nerve
explanation:
Popliteus reverses the medial rotation of the femur that locks the knee at full extension. Its tendon lies inside the joint capsule and is attached to the lateral meniscus.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (knee ligaments), 2020 INI-CET (lower limb muscle actions)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which intrinsic muscle of the sole is supplied by the medial plantar nerve?
explanation:
The medial plantar nerve supplies only "LAFF": 1st Lumbrical, Abductor hallucis, Flexor digitorum brevis, Flexor hallucis brevis. All other intrinsic muscles, including every interosseous, are lateral plantar.
> `LOWER LIMB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (lateral plantar nerve supplies 1st interossei)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A patient with an acute inferior wall myocardial infarction develops complete heart block. The artery most likely occluded is the
explanation:
In most people (right-dominant circulation), the RCA supplies the inferior wall and gives the AV nodal artery from the crux of the heart.

explanation:
It comes from the RCA in about 60% of hearts and from the circumflex in about 40%. Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery.

On the right, the eparterial (upper lobe) bronchus lies above the pulmonary artery. On both sides, the pulmonary veins are the most anterior and lowest structures.

subject: Anatomy
stem: During a segmentectomy, the surgeon follows which structures to find the plane between bronchopulmonary segments?
options: Segmental branches of the pulmonary artery
explanation:
Each segment has a central (segmental) bronchus and artery. The veins run between segments and drain neighbouring segments.
> `THORAX` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (structure running between bronchopulmonary segments)

subject: Anatomy
stem: An unconscious patient lying supine aspirates gastric contents. The segment most likely to be affected is the
options: Medial basal segment of the right lower lobe
Superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe
Anterior segment of the right upper lobe
explanation:
Its bronchus is the first posterior branch below the hilum and points directly backwards, which is the lowest point when supine. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical.
> `THORAX` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (hilum), 2015 AIIMS (bronchopulmonary segments)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each diaphragmatic opening with its vertebral level and content.

| Opening | Level and content |
|---|---|
| 1. Caval opening | a. T12 — aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein |
| 2. Oesophageal opening | b. Behind the medial arcuate ligament — sympathetic trunk |
| 3. Aortic opening | c. T8 — IVC, branches of right phrenic nerve |
| 4. Medial arcuate ligament | d. T10 — oesophagus, vagal trunks |
explanation:
The caval opening is in the central tendon (it widens during inspiration); the oesophageal opening is in the right crus; the aortic opening lies behind the median arcuate ligament.
> `THORAX` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2016 AIIMS (structures through aortic aperture — 4X), 2014 AIIMS (central tendon — IVC)

stem:

| 4. First arch | d. Proximal part of the right subclavian artery |
explanation:
The left 4th arch forms part of the arch of the aorta. On the right, the distal 6th arch disappears, so the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks round the subclavian. On the left, the nerve hooks round the ligamentum arteriosum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: A "non-recurrent" right inferior laryngeal nerve, which enters the larynx directly from the vagus in the neck, is associated with
explanation:
When the right 4th arch regresses, the right subclavian arises from the descending aorta. There is then no vessel for the nerve to hook round, which is a known hazard in thyroid surgery.
> `THORAX` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (RLN course — 6th arch), 2022 INI-CET (nerves at risk in thyroid surgery)

subject: Anatomy
stem: A persistent left superior vena cava most commonly drains into the
explanation:
It is the persisting left anterior cardinal vein (and common cardinal vein), which normally becomes the oblique vein of the left atrium and the coronary sinus. On echo it gives a dilated coronary sinus.
> `THORAX` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (azygos from supracardinal), 2015 AIIMS (IVC from vitelline), 2021 INI-CET (left superior intercostal vein)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The raised margin (limbus) of the fossa ovalis is derived from the
options: Left valve of the sinus venosus
explanation:
The floor of the fossa ovalis is the septum primum (the valve of the foramen ovale). The free edge of the septum secundum forms the limbus.
> `THORAX` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (fossa ovalis develops from septum primum), 2018 AIIMS (Chiari network — sinus venosus valve)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each joint with its type.

| Joint | Type |
|---|---|
| 1. Pubic symphysis | a. Primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) |
| 2. First sternocostal joint | b. Secondary cartilaginous (symphysis) |
| 3. Inferior tibiofibular joint | c. Pivot (synovial) |
| 4. Median atlanto-axial joint | d. Syndesmosis |
explanation:
Symphyses (pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs, manubriosternal joint) lie in the midline and are permanent. The median atlanto-axial joint performs head rotation ("no" movement).
> `GENERAL ANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (joints of vertebral column — 4X), 2021 INI-CET (middle radioulnar — syndesmosis), 2021 NEET-PG (atlanto-axial)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following is a saddle (sellar) joint?
explanation:
Other saddle joints: the sternoclavicular, incudomalleolar and calcaneocuboid joints. The atlanto-occipital and radiocarpal joints are ellipsoid; the superior radioulnar joint is a pivot.
> `GENERAL ANATOMY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (incudomalleolar — saddle)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Arrange the zones of the epiphyseal growth plate from the epiphyseal side towards the diaphysis.
1. Zone of hypertrophy
2. Zone of proliferation
3. Zone of ossification
4. Reserve (resting) zone
5. Zone of calcification
explanation:
Achondroplasia mainly affects the proliferative zone; rickets disturbs calcification. Fractures through the plate disturb longitudinal growth.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (zone undergoing calcification), 2023 NEET-PG (fracture affecting longitudinal growth)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Match each collagen type with its main location.

| Collagen | Location |
|---|---|
| 1. Type I | a. Basement membrane (lamina densa) |
| 2. Type II | b. Reticular fibres of lymph nodes and blood vessels |
| 3. Type III | c. Bone, tendon and dermis |
| 4. Type IV | d. Hyaline cartilage and vitreous body |
explanation:
Mnemonic "SCAB" for types I–IV: Skeleton, Cartilage, Arteries, Basement membrane.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2017 AIIMS (type II — cartilage), 2015 AIIMS (type IV — basement membrane)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Elastic cartilage is found in the
explanation:
Elastic cartilage is found in the auricle, external acoustic meatus, auditory tube, epiglottis and the corniculate and cuneiform cartilages. The thyroid cartilage is hyaline (it may calcify); the disc is fibrocartilage.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG (fibrocartilage), 2022 INI-CET (ligamentum flavum — elastin)

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ceruminous glands of the external acoustic meatus are modified
explanation:
The glands of Moll (eyelid) and the mammary gland are also modified apocrine glands. Sebaceous glands are holocrine; eccrine sweat glands are merocrine.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: gland-type rotation — 2015 AIIMS (holocrine) → 2020 INI-CET (merocrine) → 2024 INI-CET (apocrine)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which site in the larynx is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium?
explanation:
They withstand mechanical friction and have no submucosal glands or lymphatics in Reinke's space. The rest of the larynx below the inlet is lined by respiratory (pseudostratified ciliated columnar) epithelium.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG (epithelium of hard palate), 2020 INI-CET (transitional epithelium sites)

subject: Anatomy
stem: Club (Clara) cells, which secrete surfactant-like proteins and act as stem cells, are characteristically found in the
explanation:
As the airway narrows, cartilage and goblet cells disappear, and club cells increase in the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. Alveoli open from the walls of the respiratory bronchioles.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (respiratory bronchiole — outpouchings without cartilage)

subject: Anatomy
stem: In bullous pemphigoid, the autoantibodies are directed against which cell junction?
explanation:
Hemidesmosomes anchor basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane, so the blister forms beneath the epidermis. Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmosomes (desmoglein), causing a split within the epidermis.
> `GENERAL HISTOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (desmosome — button-like plaque), 2016 AIIMS (junctions in intercalated discs)

subject: Anatomy
stem:
Arrange these events of oogenesis in chronological order.
1. Extrusion of the first polar body
2. Primary oocyte arrested in diplotene of prophase I
3. Extrusion of the second polar body
4. Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II
explanation:
The diplotene arrest lasts from fetal life until just before ovulation. Meiosis I then completes (first polar body) and the cell is ovulated arrested at metaphase II. Meiosis II completes only after fertilisation (second polar body).
> `GENERAL EMBRYOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (oocyte arrested in diplotene at birth), 2020 NEET-PG (post-ovulation oocyte)
