subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each taste quality with its transduction mechanism.

| Taste | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| 1. Sour | a. ENaC channels |
| 2. Salty | b. T2R G-protein receptors (gustducin) |
| 3. Bitter | c. T1R1/T1R3 heterodimer |
| 4. Umami | d. H⁺-permeable channels (PKD2L1/TRPP3, OTOP1) |
explanation:
Sweet uses T1R2/T1R3. Bitter compounds are typically alkaloids and plant toxins. Filiform papillae carry no taste buds.
> `CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (sour — TRPP3), 2023 INI-CET (bitter — alkaloids), 2023 NEET-PG (filiform papillae)

subject: Physiology
stem: An intense, steady pressure on a limb is applied for a long time. The first modality lost, and the last to be lost, are
options: Proprioception and touch first; pain last
explanation:
Large myelinated A fibres are most susceptible to pressure, and thin unmyelinated C fibres are least. This is why tingling and numbness come before pain fails in a compression palsy (for example, Saturday night palsy).
> `CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (Saturday night palsy — type A fibres)
exam: 2021 NEET-PG (Saturday night palsy — type A fibres)

subject: Physiology
stem: ICF K⁺ is 140 mmol/L and ECF K⁺ is 4 mmol/L. Taking 61 mV for 2.3RT/F at 37°C, the K⁺ equilibrium potential is about
explanation:
Nernst: E = 61 × log([out]/[in]) = 61 × log(4/140) = 61 × (−1.54) ≈ −94 mV. The resting membrane potential (−70 to −90 mV) lies close to E_K because the resting membrane is most permeable to K⁺.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (Cl⁻ equilibrium potential calculation), 2014 AIIMS (Nernst equation), 2023 NEET-PG (K⁺ and RMP)

subject: Physiology
stem: ECF Ca²⁺ is 2 mmol/L and cytosolic free Ca²⁺ is 0.0002 mmol/L. Using 61 mV for 2.3RT/F, the Ca²⁺ equilibrium potential is about
explanation:
E = (61/z) × log(out/in) = (61/2) × log(10⁴) = 30.5 × 4 = +122 mV. Forgetting the valence z = 2 gives the trap answer of +244 mV.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (equilibrium potential calculation)

subject: Physiology
stem: After a crush injury, plasma K⁺ rises to 8 mmol/L. The effect on skeletal and cardiac muscle cells is
options: The RMP becomes more negative, so excitability falls
The RMP becomes more negative, so excitability rises
The RMP becomes less negative; sustained depolarisation inactivates Na⁺ channels, so excitability eventually falls
explanation:
A raised ECF K⁺ shrinks the K⁺ gradient, so E_K and the RMP move towards zero. Mild hyperkalaemia increases excitability; severe hyperkalaemia causes paralysis and cardiac arrest.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (muscle injury and high K⁺ — RMP more positive)
exam: 2023 NEET-PG (muscle injury and high K⁺ — RMP more positive)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each event of the nerve action potential with its ionic basis.

| Event | Ionic basis |
|---|---|
| 1. Depolarisation | a. Slow closure of voltage-gated K⁺ channels |
| 2. Repolarisation | b. Inactivation gates of Na⁺ channels closed |
| 3. After-hyperpolarisation | c. Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated channels (activation gates open) |
| 4. Absolute refractory period | d. Na⁺ channel inactivation plus K⁺ efflux |
explanation:
Na⁺ conductance rises sharply first, then K⁺ conductance rises more slowly. During the relative refractory period some Na⁺ channels have recovered, so a stronger stimulus can fire the cell.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (match — depolarisation/repolarisation, 3X), 2016 AIIMS (absolute refractoriness — Na⁺ inactivation gates)

subject: Physiology
stem: In multiple sclerosis, conduction slows or fails in demyelinated axons mainly because
options: The internodal membrane has very few Na⁺ channels, so current leaks out and cannot reach threshold at the next active site
Na⁺ channel density at the nodes increases
explanation:
Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, which allows saltatory conduction. Once it is lost, the high-capacitance, leaky internode cannot regenerate the impulse. Heat worsens the block (Uhthoff's phenomenon).
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (slow conduction in MS — loss of myelin)
exam: 2022 NEET-PG (slow conduction in MS — loss of myelin)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each nerve fibre type (Erlanger–Gasser) with its function.

| Fibre | Function |
|---|---|
| 1. Aα | a. Preganglionic autonomic |
| 2. Aδ | b. Slow (dull) pain and postganglionic sympathetic |
| 3. B | c. Proprioception and somatic motor |
| 4. C | d. Fast (sharp) pain and cold |
explanation:
Conduction velocity falls from Aα (70–120 m/s) to C (0.5–2 m/s). C fibres are the only unmyelinated group, which is why postganglionic autonomic fibres are the slowest.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (proprioception A-α; pain A-δ), 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (slowest — C fibres)

subject: Physiology
stem: Tetanus toxin produces spastic paralysis, whereas botulinum toxin produces flaccid paralysis, because tetanus toxin
options: Cleaves SNAP-25 at the neuromuscular junction
Travels back to the spinal cord and blocks glycine/GABA release from inhibitory interneurons
explanation:
Both toxins are proteases that cleave SNARE proteins. Tetanus toxin cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP) in Renshaw and other inhibitory interneurons. Botulinum toxin acts peripherally at cholinergic terminals.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (tetanus toxin — synaptobrevin), 2018 NEET-PG (inhibiting vesicle release)

subject: Physiology
stem: 3,4-Diaminopyridine improves strength in Lambert–Eaton syndrome by
options: Blocking presynaptic K⁺ channels, which prolongs the action potential and increases Ca²⁺ entry
explanation:
A longer depolarisation keeps the remaining P/Q-type Ca²⁺ channels open longer, so more ACh vesicles are released.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (increase ACh release by blocking presynaptic K⁺ channels)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (increase ACh release by blocking presynaptic K

subject: Physiology
stem:
Arrange the events of neuromuscular transmission in sequence.
1. ACh binds nicotinic receptors and an end-plate potential develops
2. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open in the nerve terminal
3. A muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma
4. SNARE-mediated exocytosis of ACh vesicles
explanation:
The end-plate potential is always above threshold (a high safety factor). Acetylcholinesterase ends transmission within milliseconds.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (sequence of events at NMJ)

subject: Physiology
stem: A smoker has proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, a dry mouth and depressed reflexes. The antibodies are most likely directed against
explanation:
This is Lambert–Eaton syndrome, often with small cell lung cancer. Repeated activity builds up presynaptic Ca²⁺, so strength improves. Myasthenia gravis (nicotinic receptor antibodies) worsens with use and later in the day.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (myasthenia gravis), 2018 NEET-PG (preventing Ca²⁺ influx)

subject: Physiology
stem: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because facilitated diffusion
options: Shows saturation kinetics with a maximum transport rate
Can move solute against its gradient
Has a rate that rises linearly with concentration at all levels
explanation:
Carrier-mediated transport also shows specificity and competitive inhibition. Glucose entry by GLUT transporters is the classic example. Neither form of diffusion uses ATP.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (saturation curve — glucose), 2014 AIIMS, 2020 NEET-PG (facilitated diffusion)

subject: Physiology
stem: Glucose-containing oral rehydration solution works in cholera because
options: Glucose is absorbed by facilitated diffusion that does not need Na⁺
Na⁺–glucose cotransport by SGLT1 stays intact and draws water with it
explanation:
Cholera toxin raises cAMP and opens CFTR (Cl⁻ secretion), but SGLT1 is unaffected. This is secondary active transport, powered by the Na⁺ gradient created by the basolateral Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (glucose absorption — SGLT1, 5X)

subject: Physiology
stem: A consequence of the Gibbs–Donnan equilibrium across the cell membrane is that
options: The concentrations of each diffusible ion are equal on both sides
The products of diffusible cation and anion concentrations are equal on both sides, and there are slightly more osmotically active particles inside
Intracellular proteins move out of the cell
explanation:
[K⁺]ᵢ[Cl⁻]ᵢ = [K⁺]ₒ[Cl⁻]ₒ. Impermeant anionic proteins inside the cell create the imbalance, and the Na⁺–K⁺ pump stops the resulting osmotic swelling.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (Gibbs–Donnan — intracellular proteins), 2022 INI-CET (assertion on proteins and RMP)

subject: Physiology
stem: 100 mg of inulin is injected intravenously. By the time of equilibrium, 10 mg has been excreted, and the plasma concentration is 0.6 mg/dL. The ECF volume is
explanation:
Volume = amount remaining ÷ concentration = (100 − 10) mg ÷ 6 mg/L = 15 L. Converting 0.6 mg/dL to 6 mg/L is the step most often missed. Ignoring excretion gives the trap answer of 16.7 L.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (mannitol — ECF volume 14 L)

subject: Physiology
stem: 15 mg of Evans blue is injected. The plasma concentration after mixing is 5 mg/L, and the haematocrit is 40%. The total blood volume is
explanation:
Plasma volume = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 L. Blood volume = plasma volume ÷ (1 − Hct) = 3 ÷ 0.6 = 5 L.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (plasma volume from haematocrit), 2021 INI-CET (I-125 albumin — plasma volume)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each body fluid compartment with the indicator used to measure it.

| Compartment | Indicator |
|---|---|
| 1. Total body water | a. Inulin or mannitol |
| 2. ECF | b. ⁵¹Cr-labelled red cells |
| 3. Plasma volume | c. Deuterium oxide or antipyrine |
| 4. Red cell volume | d. Evans blue or ¹²⁵I-albumin |
explanation:
ICF and interstitial fluid cannot be measured directly. They are calculated: ICF = TBW − ECF; interstitial fluid = ECF − plasma.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (I-125 albumin — plasma volume; mannitol — ECF)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (I-125 albumin — plasma volume; mannitol — ECF)

subject: Physiology
stem: Which of the following is an example of POSITIVE feedback?
options: The LH surge triggered by rising oestradiol before ovulation
explanation:
Other positive feedback loops include oxytocin during labour (Ferguson reflex), the clotting cascade and the Na⁺ influx during the AP upstroke. Most homeostatic loops are negative. Salivating in anticipation of food is feedforward.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (baroreceptor — negative feedback), 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (feedforward)

subject: Physiology
stem: A patient with microcytic anaemia has normal ferritin and HbA₂ of 5.2%. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation:
When β-chain production falls, more δ chains pair with α chains, raising HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) above 3.5%. Iron deficiency can falsely lower HbA₂; α-thalassaemia trait has normal HbA₂.
> `BLOOD` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (HbA₂ raised in thalassaemia)

subject: Physiology
stem: A patient's red cells are not agglutinated by anti-A, anti-B or anti-H. The patient's serum agglutinates group O red cells. The blood group is
explanation:
With no H antigen, A and B antigens cannot be made either. The serum carries anti-A, anti-B and anti-H, so these patients can receive only Bombay blood. Normal group O cells are rich in H antigen.
> `BLOOD` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (no agglutination with anti-A, anti-B — O+)
exam: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (no agglutination with anti-A, ant

subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each plasma protein with the substance it carries.

| Protein | Substance carried |
|---|---|
| 1. Transthyretin (prealbumin) | a. Free haem |
| 2. Haptoglobin | b. Copper |
| 3. Haemopexin | c. Thyroxine and retinol-binding protein |
| 4. Ceruloplasmin | d. Free haemoglobin |
explanation:
Haptoglobin falls in intravascular haemolysis because haemoglobin–haptoglobin complexes are rapidly cleared. Albumin carries free fatty acids, bilirubin and many drugs.
> `GENERAL PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (match — prealbumin, albumin, haptoglobin, haemopexin)

subject: Physiology
stem: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is 55 mmHg, Bowman's capsule pressure is 15 mmHg and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure is 30 mmHg. The net filtration pressure is
explanation:
NFP = P_GC − P_BS − π_GC (+ π_BS, which is about 0) = 55 − 15 − 30 = 10 mmHg. Oncotic pressure rises along the glomerular capillary, so filtration falls from the afferent to the efferent end.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (net filtration pressure calculation)

subject: Physiology
stem: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole. The effect on filtration fraction is that it
options: Falls, because GFR falls more than RPF
Rises, because GFR is maintained while RPF falls
explanation:
FF = GFR/RPF. Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure, so GFR is maintained or rises a little, while plasma flow falls. This is why ACE inhibitors can drop GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (efferent constriction — GFR stable or rises), 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (factors increasing GFR, 5X)
exam: 2015 AIIMS (efferent constriction — GFR stable or rises), 20

subject: Physiology
stem: In tubuloglomerular feedback, increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa causes
options: Constriction of the afferent arteriole, mediated by adenosine, and reduced renin release
Constriction of the efferent arteriole and increased renin
explanation:
Macula densa cells sense NaCl through NKCC2 and release ATP/adenosine (A₁ receptors). The macula densa sits where the thick ascending limb meets the early distal tubule, beside its own glomerulus. TGF stabilises GFR.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (TGF — GFR), 2023 INI-CET (macula densa location)

subject: Physiology
stem: Angiotensin II–induced contraction of mesangial cells reduces GFR mainly by
options: Reducing the filtration coefficient (K_f) by shrinking the capillary surface area
explanation:
Mesangial cells are contractile and phagocytic, and the extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells belong to the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Agents such as ANP relax them and raise K_f.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (match — mesangial cell contraction)

subject: Physiology
stem: Urine creatinine is 120 mg/dL, plasma creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL and urine flow is 1 mL/min. The creatinine clearance is
explanation:
C = (U × V)/P = (120 × 1)/1.2 = 100 mL/min. Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR because a small amount of creatinine is secreted by the tubule.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (requirements for creatinine clearance), 2018 AIIMS (GFR markers)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Arrange these substances by renal clearance, from highest to lowest.
1. Urea
2. Glucose (normal plasma level)
3. Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH)
4. Inulin
explanation:
PAH is filtered and secreted (clearance ≈ RPF, about 625 mL/min). Inulin is only filtered (clearance = GFR, about 125). Urea is partly reabsorbed (about 50–70). Glucose is fully reabsorbed (0).
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (maximum clearance — PAH > inulin > bicarbonate > glucose)

subject: Physiology
stem: Glucose begins to appear in the urine at a plasma level of about 200 mg/dL, although the tubular maximum is not reached until about 300 mg/dL. This difference is called
explanation:
Some nephrons saturate earlier than others, and transporter binding is not infinitely tight, so the titration curve is rounded rather than sharp.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (glucose absorbed in S3), 2018 AIIMS (SGLT2 in PCT)
exam: 2016 AIIMS (glucose absorbed in S3), 2018 AIIMS (SGLT2 in PC

subject: Physiology
stem: Gliflozins block the transporter responsible for about 90% of filtered glucose reabsorption. It is
options: SGLT2 in the S1–S2 segments of the PCT, which is low-affinity and high-capacity
SGLT1 in the S3 segment, which is high-affinity and low-capacity
explanation:
SGLT2 moves 1 Na⁺ per glucose; SGLT1 (S3) moves 2 Na⁺ and mops up the remaining roughly 10%. Glucose leaves the cell basolaterally through GLUT2.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (apical PCT transporter — SGLT2), 2016 AIIMS (10% absorbed in S3)

subject: Physiology
stem: Which transporter is NOT present on the apical membrane of the early proximal tubule?
explanation:
NKCC2 is found in the thick ascending limb, the target of loop diuretics. Fluid leaving the PCT is isotonic, because water follows solute in proportion.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (Na⁺ transporters in early PCT), 2024 INI-CET (fluid leaving PCT isotonic)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (Na⁺ transporters in early PCT), 2024 INI-CET (

subject: Physiology
stem: Loop diuretics increase urinary Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ excretion because they
options: Abolish the lumen-positive potential created by K⁺ recycling through ROMK, which drives paracellular Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reabsorption
explanation:
NKCC2 brings in K⁺, which leaks back into the lumen through ROMK, making it positive. That positive charge drives divalent cations through paracellin (claudin-16). Thiazides, by contrast, lower urinary Ca²⁺.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (lumen-positive gradient — K⁺ recycling)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each tubular site with the osmolality of its fluid when ADH is absent.

| Site | Osmolality (mOsm/kg) |
|---|---|
| 1. End of the proximal tubule | a. About 1200 |
| 2. Tip of a juxtamedullary loop | b. About 100 |
| 3. Early distal tubule | c. About 300 |
| 4. Final urine (no ADH) | d. About 50 |
explanation:
The thick ascending limb (the "diluting segment") pumps out solute but is impermeable to water. The thin descending limb is permeable to water, so its fluid concentrates towards the tip.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (fluid leaving PCT — isotonic), 2020 INI-CET (diluting segment), 2019 NEET-PG (descending thin limb permeable)

subject: Physiology
stem: The vasa recta preserve the medullary osmotic gradient mainly because
options: They actively pump NaCl into the interstitium
Their slow flow and hairpin shape let them act as countercurrent exchangers
They carry most of the renal blood flow
explanation:
Solute entering the descending vasa recta leaves again in the ascending limb, so little is washed out. The loop of Henle is the countercurrent multiplier. Medullary blood flow is less than 10% of renal blood flow.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (vasa recta — urine concentration), 2024 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (countercurrent sites)

subject: Physiology
stem: In chronic metabolic acidosis, the main ADAPTIVE increase in renal acid excretion is through
options: Ammonium, from increased glutamine metabolism in the PCT
explanation:
Phosphate buffer supply is limited by dietary intake, whereas ammoniagenesis can increase several-fold over days. Urine pH cannot fall below about 4.5, so free H⁺ excretion is negligible.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (compensation for pH change), 2017 AIIMS (normal H⁺ concentration)

subject: Physiology
stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L. Using Winter's formula, the expected PaCO₂ with appropriate respiratory compensation is about
explanation:
Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2) = 18 + 8 = 26 mmHg. A measured PaCO₂ well above this means a coexisting respiratory acidosis. The compensation is Kussmaul breathing.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (pH 7.4 → 7.3, PCO₂ will reduce)

subject: Physiology
stem: With plasma HCO₃⁻ fixed at 24 mmol/L, PaCO₂ acutely doubles from 40 to 80 mmHg (pK′ = 6.1, CO₂ solubility = 0.03). The pH will be about
explanation:
pH = 6.1 + log[24 ÷ (0.03 × 80)] = 6.1 + log(10) = 7.1. At PaCO₂ 40 the ratio is 20:1, giving pH 7.4. In real acute respiratory acidosis HCO₃⁻ rises slightly, so the measured pH is a little higher.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (pH and PCO₂ relationship), 2023 NEET-PG (respiratory alkalosis — tetany)

subject: Physiology
stem: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by
options: Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts of the renal cortex, under HIF control
explanation:
About 85–90% of EPO comes from the kidney and the rest from the liver; in the fetus the liver is the main source. Hypoxia stabilises HIF-2α, which switches on the EPO gene.
> `RENAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (EPO secreted by liver and kidney), 2016 AIIMS (EPO value)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (EPO secreted by liver and kidney), 2016 AIIMS

subject: Physiology
stem: After resection of the terminal 100 cm of ileum for Crohn's disease, which complication is LEAST expected as a direct result?
explanation:
Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and upper jejunum. The terminal ileum absorbs B₁₂–intrinsic factor (via cubilin) and conjugated bile salts. Losing the bile salt pool causes fat malabsorption and lithogenic bile; colonic bile acids cause secretory diarrhoea.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2019 NEET-PG (ileal resection — B₁₂ deficiency, 3X), 2022 NEET-PG (B₁₂ deficiency)

subject: Physiology
stem: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion MAINLY by
options: Acting directly on H₂ receptors on parietal cells
Inhibiting somatostatin release from D cells
explanation:
Gastrin acts on CCK₂ receptors on ECL cells; the histamine they release acts on H₂ receptors on parietal cells (cAMP). Gastrin and ACh also act directly on parietal cells (Ca²⁺ pathway), with potentiation between all three.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (gastric acid increased by gastrin, histamine, ACh)
exam: 2022 INI-CET (gastric acid increased by gastrin, histamine,

subject: Physiology
stem: When antral pH falls below about 3, further gastrin release is switched off mainly through
explanation:
This is paracrine negative feedback. Acid also reaching the duodenum releases secretin, which inhibits gastrin and acid and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (gastric acid regulation), 2020 NEET-PG (paracrine signalling)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Match each GI hormone with its cell of origin and main action.

| Hormone | Cell and action |
|---|---|
| 1. CCK | a. I cells (duodenum, jejunum) — gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes |
| 2. Secretin | b. M cells — initiates the migrating motor complex |
| 3. GIP | c. S cells — pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion |
| 4. Motilin | d. K cells — glucose-dependent insulin release |
explanation:
GIP and GLP-1 (from L cells) are the incretins, which explains why oral glucose releases more insulin than intravenous glucose.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (CCK — I cells of duodenum and jejunum)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (CCK — I cells of duodenum and jejunum)

subject: Physiology
stem: Erythromycin in low doses is used as a prokinetic for gastroparesis because it
options: Acts as a motilin receptor agonist and triggers migrating motor complexes
explanation:
In the fasting state, MMCs sweep from the stomach to the ileum about every 90–120 minutes, clearing residue (the "housekeeper"). Eating abolishes them.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (migrating motor complexes recur every 90 min)
exam: 2016 AIIMS (migrating motor complexes recur every 90 min)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Arrange these parts of the gut by basal slow-wave frequency, from highest to lowest.
1. Stomach
2. Ileum
3. Duodenum
4. Jejunum
explanation:
Duodenum about 12/min, jejunum about 11, ileum about 8–9, stomach about 3. The interstitial cells of Cajal generate the slow waves; spikes on top of them trigger contraction. The falling gradient along the small bowel helps move contents onward.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (least slow-wave frequency — stomach), 2017 AIIMS (slow waves by ICC)

subject: Physiology
stem: In the peristaltic reflex, contraction of the circular muscle ORAL (behind) to a bolus is mediated by
explanation:
This is the "law of the intestine": excitatory neurons contract the gut behind the bolus, while inhibitory VIP/NO neurons relax the gut ahead of it (the anal side).
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (VIP anterograde to bolus), 2014 AIIMS

subject: Physiology
stem: The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus mainly regulates
options: Local secretion, absorption and mucosal blood flow
Tone of the external anal sphincter
explanation:
The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers, controls motility. In Hirschsprung disease, ganglion cells are absent from both plexuses.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (myenteric plexus location)

subject: Physiology
stem: The most potent stimulus for slowing gastric emptying is
options: Fat in the duodenum, acting mainly through CCK
explanation:
Duodenal fat, acid (via secretin) and hyperosmolar chyme all slow emptying, through hormones and the neural enterogastric reflex. This matches gastric emptying to the duodenum's capacity to digest and absorb.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (enterogastric reflex), 2023 INI-CET (CCK)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Arrange the events of vomiting in sequence.
1. Antiperistalsis carrying small-intestinal contents back into the stomach
2. Deep inspiration with closure of the glottis and elevation of the soft palate
3. Strong contraction of the diaphragm and abdominal muscles
4. Relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and expulsion
explanation:
Antiperistalsis may begin minutes before vomiting (Guyton). The closed glottis and raised palate protect the airway and nasopharynx while abdominal squeezing provides the expulsive force. The vomiting centre is in the medulla, with the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (arrange events during vomiting)

subject: Physiology
stem: During isotonic shortening of a skeletal muscle fibre, which part of the sarcomere stays the SAME length?
explanation:
The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, which do not shorten; the thin filaments slide over them. The I band and H zone narrow. From the edge to the centre of a sarcomere: Z line → I band → A band → H zone → M line.
> `MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (arrange sarcomere parts), 2018 AIIMS (lighter area — I band)

subject: Physiology
stem:
Starting from the rigor (attached) state, arrange the steps of the cross-bridge cycle.
1. Hydrolysis of ATP re-cocks the myosin head
2. Release of Pᵢ triggers the power stroke
3. ATP binds the myosin head, which detaches from actin
4. Release of ADP returns the head to the rigor state
explanation:
Detachment needs ATP binding, not hydrolysis. Without ATP the heads stay locked to actin, which is rigor mortis.
> `MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (detachment of myosin head — ATP binding)
exam: 2020 INI-CET (detachment of myosin head — ATP binding)

subject: Physiology
stem: Vascular smooth muscle maintains tone for long periods using very little ATP because of
options: The latch-bridge state, in which dephosphorylated myosin stays attached to actin
explanation:
Myosin light-chain phosphatase dephosphorylates attached cross-bridges, which then detach very slowly, so force is kept with little cycling. In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase (there is no troponin).
> `MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (latch-bridge mechanism)

subject: Physiology
stem: An isolated skeletal muscle keeps contracting for a while in a Ca²⁺-free bath, whereas cardiac muscle stops almost at once. The reason is that in skeletal muscle
options: Troponin binds Mg²⁺ instead of Ca²⁺
Ca²⁺ is not needed for contraction
The dihydropyridine receptor acts as a voltage sensor mechanically linked to RyR1, releasing Ca²⁺ from the SR without needing extracellular Ca²⁺
explanation:
In cardiac muscle, Ca²⁺ entering through L-type channels triggers RyR2 (Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release), so extracellular Ca²⁺ is essential.
> `MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (match — extracellular Ca²⁺ not important for skeletal contraction), 2023 INI-CET (latent period — excitation–contraction coupling)

subject: Physiology
stem: Shortly after halothane and succinylcholine are given, a patient develops muscle rigidity, rising end-tidal CO₂ and hyperthermia. The defective protein is most commonly
explanation:
This is malignant hyperthermia. A mutant RyR1 lets Ca²⁺ leak uncontrollably from the SR, driving continuous contraction and hypermetabolism. Dantrolene blocks RyR1.
> `MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (skeletal muscle Ca²⁺ release), 2016 AIIMS (energy for exercising muscle)

subject: Physiology
stem: As the force of a voluntary contraction is gradually increased, motor units are recruited
options: From the smallest (slow, fatigue-resistant) to the largest (fast, fatigable)
From the largest to the smallest
All at once, with force graded only by firing rate
explanation:
This is Henneman's size principle: small motor neurons have high input resistance and reach threshold first. Force is graded by both recruitment and rate coding. For the first few seconds of intense effort, ATP is regenerated from phosphocreatine.
> `MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (spindle innervation), 2016 AIIMS (phosphocreatine)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 3-year-old has hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia, raised AST/ALT, ketosis and mild proximal muscle weakness. Blood lactate is normal. Glucagon given 2 hours after a meal raises blood glucose, but glucagon given after an overnight fast does not. The deficient enzyme is
explanation:
This is Cori disease (GSD III). After a meal, phosphorylase can still release glucose from the newly added outer chains. After a fast, only the limit-dextrin branch points remain, and they cannot be broken down. Muscle involvement, ketosis and normal lactate also favour GSD III over von Gierke disease, which has lactic acidosis and no response to glucagon at any time. *Note: the source file keys this exact 8X stem as glucose-6-phosphatase; the clinical pattern described is Cori disease.*
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (GSD case — 8X), 2017 AIIMS (limit dextrin — Cori)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which finding is NOT expected in von Gierke disease (GSD Ia)?
options: A brisk rise in blood glucose after glucagon
explanation:
Glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose, so glucagon only raises lactate. The trapped G6P is pushed into glycolysis (lactate), the HMP shunt (more purine synthesis, so urate), and lipogenesis (TAG). The liver enlarges with glycogen and fat.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (hepatomegaly in G6Pase deficiency), 2017 AIIMS (von Gierke)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each glycogen storage disease with its defect and feature.

| Disease | Defect and feature |
|---|---|
| 1. Pompe | a. Branching enzyme — long unbranched chains, cirrhosis |
| 2. McArdle | b. Debranching enzyme — limit dextrin |
| 3. Cori | c. Lysosomal acid α-1,4-glucosidase — cardiomegaly |
| 4. Andersen | d. Muscle phosphorylase — exercise cramps, "second wind" |
explanation:
Pompe disease is the only GSD that is also a lysosomal storage disease. Its enzyme is acid maltase, not "acid lipase" (the 2017 AIIMS key wording is wrong).
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (match — Pompe, von Gierke, McArdle), 2022 INI-CET (Pompe enzyme), 2017 AIIMS

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In a forearm ischaemic exercise test on a patient with McArdle disease, the expected result is
options: Normal rises in lactate and ammonia
Exaggerated rises in both lactate and ammonia
No rise in lactate, with an exaggerated rise in ammonia
A rise in lactate, with no rise in ammonia
explanation:
Muscle cannot break down glycogen, so no lactate is produced. Extra ATP breakdown drives the purine nucleotide cycle (AMP deaminase), which releases ammonia.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (calf pain on exercise — muscle phosphorylase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During vigorous muscle contraction, glycogen phosphorylase is activated even without adrenaline, mainly because
options: Ca²⁺ binds the calmodulin subunit of phosphorylase kinase, and AMP allosterically activates phosphorylase b
Glucagon receptors on muscle are stimulated
explanation:
Ca²⁺ released from the SR links contraction to fuel supply. Muscle has no glucagon receptors. G6P and ATP inhibit phosphorylase. In the liver, the main route is glucagon → cAMP → PKA.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (phosphorylase activated by calcium; by cAMP-dependent kinase)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (phosphorylase activated by calcium; by cAMP-de

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Arrange the steps by which glucagon activates hepatic glycogenolysis.
1. Phosphorylation of phosphorylase kinase
2. Activation of adenylyl cyclase
3. Conversion of glycogen phosphorylase b to a
4. Activation of protein kinase A
explanation:
Each step amplifies the signal. PKA also phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase, so synthesis and breakdown are not active at the same time.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (correct sequence — adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA), 2024 INI-CET
exam: 2023 INI-CET (correct sequence — adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → P

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During fasting, PFK-1 activity in the liver falls mainly because
explanation:
Glucagon → PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme. Its kinase is switched off and its phosphatase switched on. F-2,6-BP (the strongest activator of PFK-1 and an inhibitor of FBPase-1) falls, so the liver shifts from glycolysis to gluconeogenesis.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (enzyme decreased during fasting — PFK-1)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Arsenite poisoning causes lactic acidosis mainly because arsenite
options: Binds the lipoic acid of pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
explanation:
Arsenite forms a stable complex with the two –SH groups of reduced lipoamide. Pyruvate then builds up and is converted to lactate. Arsenate, by contrast, uncouples substrate-level phosphorylation at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (congenital lactic acidosis — PDH), 2022 INI-CET (thiamine and PDH)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A child with confirmed pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency has persistent lactic acidosis. The most appropriate dietary therapy is
options: A high-protein diet rich in alanine
explanation:
Fatty acids and ketones provide acetyl-CoA without going through PDH, and the lower glucose load reduces pyruvate and lactate. A thiamine trial is also given. Lysine and leucine are purely ketogenic amino acids.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (congenital lactic acidosis — PDH deficiency), 2022 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following CANNOT provide carbon for the net synthesis of glucose?
explanation:
Leucine (and lysine) give only acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate. The two carbons of acetyl-CoA are lost as CO₂ in the TCA cycle, so there is no net gain of oxaloacetate. Propionate (from odd-chain fatty acids) enters through succinyl-CoA, so it is glucogenic.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS (glucogenic substrates — not acetyl-CoA, 3X), 2016 AIIMS (odd-chain fatty acids → propionyl-CoA)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In prolonged fasting, high mitochondrial acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation promotes gluconeogenesis by
options: Allosterically activating pyruvate carboxylase while inhibiting PDH
explanation:
Pyruvate is diverted away from oxidation towards oxaloacetate. Pyruvate carboxylase needs biotin, and its reaction is the classic anaplerotic reaction.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (acetyl-CoA stimulates pyruvate carboxylase — T/F), 2016 AIIMS (anaplerotic reaction)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme does NOT produce cytosolic NADPH?
explanation:
GAPDH produces NADH. NADPH comes from the oxidative HMP shunt (G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase), malic enzyme, and cytosolic NADP⁺-linked isocitrate dehydrogenase. The HMP shunt makes NADPH and ribose-5-P but no acetyl-CoA.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (sources of cytosolic NADPH), 2024 INI-CET (HMP pathway)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): Red cells deficient in G6PD haemolyse after a patient takes primaquine.
Reason (R): NADPH is needed by glutathione reductase to keep glutathione in its reduced form.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
Without NADPH, reduced glutathione falls. H₂O₂ then accumulates, causing **increased** membrane lipid peroxidation, haemoglobin precipitation (Heinz bodies) and bite cells. RBCs depend entirely on the HMP shunt for NADPH.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (G6PD — lipid peroxidation T/F), 2020 NEET-PG (primaquine haemolysis)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Thiamine status is best assessed by measuring
options: Erythrocyte transketolase activity, with and without added TPP
explanation:
A large increase in activity when TPP is added (the "TPP effect") indicates deficiency. Glutathione reductase measures riboflavin status, AST measures B6, and N-methylnicotinamide measures niacin.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (polished rice — transketolase defect), 2021 INI-CET (B2 by glutathione reductase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In galactokinase deficiency, the main clinical problem is cataract. It results from
options: Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the lens
Accumulation of galactitol formed by aldose reductase
Glycation of lens proteins by fructose
explanation:
Galactitol is osmotically active and draws water into the lens. Classic galactosaemia (GALT deficiency) adds liver failure, E. coli sepsis and intellectual disability from galactose-1-phosphate. Urine is Benedict-positive but negative on glucose oxidase (GOD-POD) tests.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (commonest defect in galactosaemia — GALT), 2016 AIIMS (Benedict-positive, GOD-POD normal)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A child with hereditary fructose intolerance develops hypoglycaemia after eating fruit. The main mechanism is
options: Fructose-1-phosphate trapping inorganic phosphate, which depletes ATP and inhibits glycogen phosphorylase and gluconeogenesis
Loss of glucose in the urine
explanation:
The defect is aldolase B. Pᵢ depletion also increases AMP breakdown, leading to hyperuricaemia. Fructokinase deficiency (essential fructosuria) is harmless.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (reducing sugar in urine), 2023 INI-CET (GSD hypoglycaemia mechanisms)
exam: 2016 AIIMS (reducing sugar in urine), 2023 INI-CET (GSD hypo

subject: Biochemistry
stem: If all glycolytic flux in a red cell passes through the Rapoport–Luebering (2,3-BPG) shunt, the net ATP yield per glucose is
explanation:
The shunt bypasses phosphoglycerate kinase, the step that makes 2 ATP per glucose. That leaves only the 2 ATP from pyruvate kinase, which exactly repays the 2 ATP invested. Red cells give up ATP to make 2,3-BPG, which regulates O₂ delivery.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (RBC fuel during fasting — glucose), 2024 INI-CET (2,3-BPG binds globin)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (RBC fuel during fasting — glucose), 2024 INI-C

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Under anaerobic conditions, the net ATP yield per glucose unit taken from glycogen, compared with free blood glucose, is
explanation:
Phosphorolysis by glycogen phosphorylase produces glucose-1-phosphate without spending ATP, which saves the hexokinase step. Glucose-1-P is converted to glucose-6-P by phosphoglucomutase.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (glycogen yields 3 ATP anaerobically), 2015 AIIMS (phosphoglucomutase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A subject consumes 250 mL of O₂ and produces 175 mL of CO₂ per minute. The main fuel being oxidised is
explanation:
RQ = 175/250 = 0.7, which corresponds to fat. Carbohydrate gives 1.0, protein about 0.8 and a mixed diet about 0.85. An RQ above 1 means net lipogenesis from carbohydrate, for example overfeeding with glucose in TPN.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (RQ calculation), 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (RQ of carbohydrate)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In hepatic encephalopathy, ammonia impairs brain energy production mainly by
options: Draining α-ketoglutarate into glutamate and glutamine, which depletes TCA cycle intermediates
explanation:
Glutamate dehydrogenase uses up α-KG, and ammonia also inhibits α-KG dehydrogenase. Glutamine produced in astrocytes is osmotically active and causes cerebral oedema.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (ammonia inhibits α-KG dehydrogenase), 2020 INI-CET (advanced liver disease), 2015 AIIMS

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Fluoroacetate (a rodenticide) blocks the TCA cycle because it is converted into
explanation:
This is "lethal synthesis", and citrate builds up. Fluoride itself inhibits enolase, which is why it is used in sugar sample tubes. Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase competitively.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (fluoroacetate inhibits TCA cycle)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:

| 1. Rotenone | a. Complex IV (cytochrome oxidase) |
| 2. Antimycin A | b. F₀ portion of ATP synthase |
| 3. Cyanide | c. Complex I |
| 4. Oligomycin | d. Complex III |
explanation:
Other complex I inhibitors include amobarbital and other barbiturates. Other complex IV inhibitors are CO, H₂S and azide.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (rotenone — complex I), 2020 INI-CET (cytochrome oxidase inhibitors — 3X), 2019 NEET-PG

subject: Biochemistry
stem: When 2,4-dinitrophenol is given to an animal, the expected changes are
options: O₂ consumption falls, ATP synthesis rises
O₂ consumption rises, ATP synthesis falls, heat production rises
O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis both fall
explanation:
Uncouplers carry protons back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase. The electron transport chain runs unchecked, and the energy is lost as heat. Thermogenin (UCP1) in brown fat does the same thing physiologically.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (uncouplers — thermogenin, 2,4-DNP)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In cyanide poisoning, amyl nitrite or sodium nitrite works by
options: Forming methaemoglobin, which binds cyanide and pulls it away from cytochrome oxidase
explanation:
The Fe³⁺ in methaemoglobin has a high affinity for CN⁻, forming cyanmethaemoglobin. Thiosulfate then lets rhodanese convert cyanide to thiocyanate, which is excreted. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide directly to form cyanocobalamin.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (inhibitors of cytochrome oxidase), 2016 AIIMS (cyanide)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glucose uptake in which tissue depends on insulin?
explanation:
Insulin moves GLUT4 to the membrane in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. The brain (GLUT1/3), RBCs (GLUT1), liver and β-cells (GLUT2) and kidney take up glucose independently of insulin. Insulin does increase liver glucose use, but through glucokinase, not transport.
> `CARBOHYDRATES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (insulin-independent uptake — 2X), 2019 NEET-PG (GLUT4)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: For fatty acid synthesis, acetyl-CoA is carried from the mitochondria to the cytosol in the form of
explanation:
Citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA in the cytosol. The oxaloacetate released returns via malate, which malic enzyme converts with production of NADPH. Synthesis needs ATP, NADPH, biotin (ACC) and Mn²⁺, and its main product is palmitate.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (fatty acid synthesis in cytoplasm), 2017 AIIMS (cofactors), 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (palmitate)

explanation:

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A child has hypoketotic hypoglycaemia on fasting, cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness with lipid vacuoles on muscle biopsy, and a very low plasma free carnitine. The most likely defect is
explanation:
Without carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria for β-oxidation. They are stored as TAG droplets, and ketones cannot be made. MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia but with raised C8-acylcarnitine and usually no myopathy.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (TAG with long-chain FA and muscle fat vacuoles — carnitine deficiency)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): The liver is the main site of ketone body synthesis but cannot use ketone bodies itself.
Reason (R): The liver lacks HMG-CoA synthase.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
The liver has plenty of HMG-CoA synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis. What it lacks is thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA-transferase), which is needed to use ketones. RBCs cannot use ketones because they have no mitochondria.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (liver lacks thiophorase), 2017 AIIMS (liver and RBCs cannot use ketones)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In severe diabetic ketoacidosis, the nitroprusside (Rothera's) test may underestimate the degree of ketosis because
options: β-hydroxybutyrate, which predominates in DKA, is not detected
explanation:
A high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio pushes acetoacetate to β-HB, often in a 3–10:1 ratio. Nitroprusside reacts with acetoacetate and acetone only, forming a purple ring. As DKA is treated, β-HB is converted back to acetoacetate, so the test can paradoxically turn more positive.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (Rothera's test — purple ring), 2015 AIIMS (prolonged starvation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, plasma triglycerides and VLDL rise mainly because
options: Lipoprotein lipase activity falls while hormone-sensitive lipase activity rises
explanation:
LPL needs insulin, so fewer TAG-rich particles are cleared. Unrestrained HSL releases free fatty acids, which the liver re-esterifies and exports as VLDL. Insulin normally suppresses HSL.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (diabetic TAG and VLDL raised), 2021 INI-CET (lipase downregulated by insulin)
exam: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (diabetic TAG and VLDL raised), 20

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each apolipoprotein with its function.

| Apolipoprotein | Function |
|---|---|
| 1. ApoB-48 | a. Activates LCAT |
| 2. ApoB-100 | b. Activates lipoprotein lipase |
| 3. ApoC-II | c. Structural protein of chylomicrons, made by RNA editing |
| 4. ApoA-I | d. Ligand for the LDL receptor |
explanation:
ApoE is the ligand for the remnant receptor. HDL has the highest protein (apoprotein) content of all lipoproteins.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (ApoB-48 by RNA editing), 2020 NEET-PG (ApoC-II), 2015 AIIMS (HDL maximum apoprotein)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which feature is NOT seen in familial chylomicronaemia (type I hyperlipoproteinaemia)?
options: A creamy supernatant layer when plasma is refrigerated overnight
explanation:
Chylomicrons are too large to enter the arterial wall, so atherosclerosis risk is not greatly increased. The cause is LPL or ApoC-II deficiency. Lipaemia retinalis and hepatosplenomegaly also occur.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (type I — chylomicrons), 2015 AIIMS (milky blood case), 2022 NEET-PG (LPL deficiency)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient has very high LDL-cholesterol and tendon xanthomas. Fibroblasts show normal LDL-receptor number and function, and PCSK9 is normal. The most likely defect is in
explanation:
In familial defective apoB-100, LDL particles cannot bind normal receptors, so they are cleared slowly. Classic familial hypercholesterolaemia is a receptor defect. Gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations raise LDL by degrading receptors.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (high LDL with normal receptors — ApoB-100), 2022 INI-CET / 2023 NEET-PG (FH — LDL receptor)
exam: 2014 AIIMS (high LDL with normal receptors — ApoB-100), 2022

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A fasting lipid profile shows total cholesterol 260 mg/dL, HDL 40 mg/dL and triglycerides 200 mg/dL. The calculated LDL-cholesterol is
explanation:
Friedewald formula: LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5 = 260 − 40 − 40 = 180 mg/dL. It is valid only when TG is below 400 mg/dL.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (LDL calculation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The ABCA1 transporter, which is defective in Tangier disease, normally
options: Transfers cholesteryl ester from HDL to VLDL
Moves cellular cholesterol and phospholipid out to lipid-poor apoA-I, forming nascent HDL
explanation:
Without it, HDL is almost absent and cholesteryl esters build up in macrophages. This produces large orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly and neuropathy. Option B is CETP.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (ABCA1 mutation, orange tonsils — Tangier)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): Familial LCAT deficiency causes a high plasma HDL-cholesterol.
Reason (R): LCAT esterifies free cholesterol on HDL, and is activated by apoA-I.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
Without esterification, HDL cannot mature into spherical particles, so HDL-C is very **low**. Free cholesterol accumulates and causes corneal opacities, haemolytic anaemia and renal failure. *Note: the 2021 NEET-PG key ("increases HDL") is incorrect.*
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (LCAT deficiency), 2017 AIIMS (LCAT expansion)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for the metabolic syndrome (NCEP ATP III / IDF)?
explanation:
The criteria are central obesity, TG ≥ 150 mg/dL, HDL below 40 (men) or 50 (women), BP ≥ 130/85 and fasting glucose ≥ 100 mg/dL. LDL is a separate risk factor.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (criteria of metabolic syndrome)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each peroxisomal disorder with its defect.

| Disorder | Defect |
|---|---|
| 1. Zellweger syndrome | a. ABCD1 transporter for very-long-chain fatty acids |
| 2. Refsum disease | b. Failure of peroxisome assembly (PEX genes) |
| 3. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy | c. Alanine–glyoxylate aminotransferase |
| 4. Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 | d. Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (α-oxidation) |
explanation:
VLCFAs accumulate in both Zellweger syndrome and X-ALD. In Refsum disease, dietary phytanic acid accumulates because its β-methyl group blocks β-oxidation until α-oxidation removes one carbon.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (Refsum — α-oxidation), 2020 INI-CET / 2016 AIIMS (Zellweger — VLCFA), 2021 NEET-PG (peroxisomes)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each sphingolipidosis with its enzyme and hallmark.

| Disease | Enzyme and hallmark |
|---|---|
| 1. Tay–Sachs | a. Glucocerebrosidase — "crumpled tissue paper" macrophages |
| 2. Niemann–Pick | b. Galactocerebrosidase — globoid cells |
| 3. Gaucher | c. Hexosaminidase A — cherry-red spot without organomegaly |
| 4. Krabbe | d. Sphingomyelinase — cherry-red spot with hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells |
explanation:
All are autosomal recessive. Gaucher disease is the commonest, and type 1 has no CNS involvement. Fabry disease is the X-linked exception.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (Gaucher; Niemann–Pick case), 2022 NEET-PG (Tay–Sachs), 2021 INI-CET (Gaucher), 2017 AIIMS (Krabbe)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 16-year-old boy has burning pain in his hands and feet, reduced sweating, dark red papules in the bathing-trunk area, and proteinuria. The enzyme deficiency and inheritance are
explanation:
This is Fabry disease. Globotriaosylceramide builds up in vessels, kidney, heart and nerves. Enzyme replacement or chaperone therapy (migalastat) is available. Arylsulfatase A deficiency is metachromatic leukodystrophy.
> `LIPIDS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: sphingolipidosis cluster — 2024 INI-CET, 2022 NEET-PG, 2021 INI-CET

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Fetal lung maturity is assessed from amniotic fluid by
explanation:
A ratio above 2 suggests mature surfactant, which is mainly dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine made by type II pneumocytes. Phosphatidylglycerol is an additional marker of maturity.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (preterm ARDS — DPPC deficiency)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The phospholipid found almost only in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is also the antigen detected by the VDRL test, is
explanation:
Cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol) holds the respiratory chain complexes in place. In Barth syndrome, defective tafazzin causes abnormal cardiolipin, with cardiomyopathy, neutropenia and myopathy.
> `LIPIDS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (Barth syndrome — cardiolipin)

subject: Biochemistry

explanation:

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Nitisinone, now approved for alkaptonuria, lowers homogentisic acid production by inhibiting
explanation:
Blocking the step just before homogentisate production prevents it from forming. Alkaptonuria itself is a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase, causing urine that darkens on standing and ochronosis of cartilage. Nitisinone is also the main treatment for tyrosinaemia type I.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (alkaptonuria — 4X)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An infant has liver failure, renal Fanconi syndrome, a "cabbage-like" odour and raised urinary succinylacetone. The deficient enzyme is
explanation:
This is tyrosinaemia type I (hepatorenal). Succinylacetone is diagnostic and also inhibits ALA dehydratase, causing porphyria-like crises. Tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency is type II (oculocutaneous).
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (tyrosinosis — fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A child with hyperphenylalaninaemia deteriorates neurologically despite a strict low-phenylalanine diet. Phenylalanine hydroxylase activity is normal. Effective treatment must also include
explanation:
This is BH₄ deficiency (for example DHPR deficiency). BH₄ is also the cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so dopamine and serotonin must be replaced. Lowering phenylalanine alone is not enough.

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): The urine and sweat of untreated phenylketonuric children have a "mousy" odour.
Reason (R): Excess phenylalanine is diverted to phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate, which are excreted.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

explanation:
Phenylacetate causes the odour. In 2023 the reason given was low tyrosine, dopamine and noradrenaline. Those are real features (fair skin, neurological effects), but they do not explain the odour.

subject: Biochemistry
stem:

explanation:
Tyrosine also gives catecholamines and melanin. Tryptophan also gives serotonin and niacin. Glutamate gives GABA, and glycine is used for haem, creatine and glutathione.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A child has a pellagra-like photosensitive rash, intermittent cerebellar ataxia and large amounts of neutral amino acids in the urine. Plasma amino acids are normal. The defect is in
explanation:
This is Hartnup disease. Tryptophan is poorly absorbed in the gut and lost in the urine, which limits niacin synthesis. It responds to nicotinamide and a high-protein diet.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (Hartnup — SLC6A19)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is NOT excreted in excess in cystinuria?
explanation:
"COLA": Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine share a dibasic transporter in the PCT and gut. Only cystine is insoluble, forming hexagonal stones; the cyanide–nitroprusside test is positive.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (cystinuria — 6X), 2023 NEET-PG (hexagonal crystals)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which is deficient in maple syrup urine disease, needs all of the following cofactors EXCEPT
explanation:
Like PDH and α-KGDH, it needs TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺. Some patients respond to thiamine. Treatment restricts valine, leucine and isoleucine.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (MSUD restriction), 2016 AIIMS (thiamine cofactor for BCKAD)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A tall boy with downward lens dislocation and a recent venous thrombosis is found to have cystathionine β-synthase deficiency. Which of the following is NOT part of management?
explanation:
Methionine is **restricted** and cysteine supplemented, since cysteine becomes essential. Betaine remethylates homocysteine to methionine. About half of patients respond to B₆, the cofactor of CBS. Marfan syndrome, by contrast, causes upward lens dislocation.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (vitamin in homocystinuria treatment)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A newborn boy has hyperammonaemia, a low plasma citrulline and very high urinary orotic acid. The deficient enzyme is
explanation:
Carbamoyl phosphate cannot enter the urea cycle, so it spills into pyrimidine synthesis and produces orotic acid. CPS-I and NAGS defects cause hyperammonaemia without orotic aciduria. OTC deficiency is the only X-linked urea cycle defect.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (glutamine raised — CPS-I deficiency)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Arrange the urea cycle enzymes in the order in which they act.
1. Argininosuccinate lyase
2. Ornithine transcarbamoylase
3. Arginase
4. Argininosuccinate synthetase
explanation:
The cycle starts with CPS-I and OTC in mitochondria, then continues with ASS, ASL and arginase in the cytosol. ASL releases fumarate, which links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (urea cycle enzymes), 2021 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (fumarate as linking compound)

stem: Sodium phenylbutyrate removes waste nitrogen in urea cycle disorders because its metabolite phenylacetate conjugates with
explanation:
Each conjugate removes 2 nitrogen atoms, which makes it more efficient than sodium benzoate. Benzoate conjugates with glycine to form hippurate, removing 1 N.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (benzoate takes N from glycine), 2020 INI-CET / 2016 AIIMS (phenylbutyrate)

stem: Cerebral oedema in acute hyperammonaemia is mainly due to
options: Direct disruption of the blood–brain barrier by ammonia
Osmotic swelling of astrocytes as glutamine synthetase converts ammonia and glutamate into glutamine
explanation:
The brain has no urea cycle, so ammonia is detoxified as glutamine. This also uses up glutamate and α-ketoglutarate.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (ammonia removed from brain as glutamine)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycine has a pK₁ (–COOH) of 2.34 and a pK₂ (–NH₃⁺) of 9.60. Its isoelectric pH is
explanation:
For an amino acid with no ionisable side chain, pI = (pK₁ + pK₂)/2 = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97. At its pI a molecule carries no net charge and does not move in an electric field.
> `PROTEINS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (charged amino acids), 2017 AIIMS (pH calculation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: On haemoglobin electrophoresis at alkaline pH (8.6), HbS moves
options: Faster towards the anode than HbA
More slowly towards the anode than HbA
At the same rate as HbA
explanation:
Replacing glutamate with valine at β6 (a point missense mutation) removes a negative charge. HbC (Glu→Lys) is even slower because it gains a positive charge.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (mobility of HbS decreased), 2020 INI-CET (sickle cell — point mutation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Proteins destined for proteasomal degradation are tagged with a polyubiquitin chain attached to
options: Lysine residues of the target protein
explanation:
The E1–E2–E3 enzyme cascade links ubiquitin's C-terminal glycine to the ε-amino group of lysine. The 26S proteasome then degrades short-lived, misfolded or regulatory proteins in the cytosol using ATP. The "N-end rule" links the N-terminal residue to protein half-life.
> `PROTEINS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (function of proteasomes), 2018 AIIMS (protein folding enzymes)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An infant boy with kinky, brittle hair, hypotonia and arterial tortuosity has low serum copper and ceruloplasmin. The connective tissue defect is due to reduced activity of the copper-dependent enzyme
explanation:
This is Menkes disease (ATP7A, X-linked): copper cannot be exported from enterocytes. Lysyl oxidase forms the cross-links of collagen and elastin. Prolyl hydroxylase needs vitamin C and Fe²⁺.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (Menkes — lysyl oxidase), 2017 AIIMS (Menkes features), 2020 INI-CET (copper deficiency)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In a diabetic patient with sickle cell disease, HbA1c is unreliable. Fructosamine is used instead. It reflects glycaemic control over the previous
explanation:
Fructosamine is mainly glycated albumin, which has a half-life of about 20 days. HbA1c depends on red cell lifespan (about 120 days), so it is falsely low in haemolysis or after recent transfusion.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (fructosamine — glycated albumin)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Insulin lispro acts faster than regular insulin because reversing the order of Pro(B28) and Lys(B29)
options: Increases its affinity for the receptor
Reduces the tendency to form dimers and hexamers in the injection depot
explanation:
The C-terminal part of the B chain (B26–B30) helps with self-association, but not with receptor binding, so changes here leave biological activity intact. Adding a fatty acid (option D) is how detemir and degludec are made long-acting.
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (changes at B29–B30 do not alter activity)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (changes at B29–B30 do not alter activity)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Specific dynamic action (diet-induced thermogenesis) is highest for protein mainly because
options: Deamination, urea synthesis and protein turnover consume a lot of ATP
Protein has the highest calorific value
explanation:
SDA is about 20–30% of the energy in protein, compared with about 5–10% for carbohydrate and 0–3% for fat. Fat has the highest calorific value (9 kcal/g).
> `PROTEINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (thermogenic food — high-protein diet, 3X)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme does NOT require thiamine pyrophosphate?
explanation:
Pyruvate carboxylase needs biotin. The TPP-dependent enzymes are PDH, α-KGDH, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (thiamine is cofactor for PDH, α-KGDH, BCKAD)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In a malnourished alcoholic presenting with confusion, thiamine must be given before intravenous glucose because
options: Glucose inactivates thiamine in the blood
Thiamine is needed for glucose uptake into neurons
A glucose load increases flux through TPP-dependent enzymes, using up the remaining thiamine and precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy
explanation:
Wernicke's triad is confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff psychosis (amnesia with confabulation).
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (thiamine before dextrose), 2024 INI-CET (Korsakoff features)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The high-output cardiac failure of wet beriberi is mainly caused by
options: Peripheral vasodilatation from accumulated pyruvate and lactate, lowering systemic vascular resistance
explanation:
The circulation behaves like an arteriovenous shunt, so cardiac output rises and causes oedema and cardiomegaly. Dry beriberi is a peripheral neuropathy. Polished rice and alcohol are classic causes.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2019 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (wet beriberi — B1)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Riboflavin status is assessed by measuring
options: The erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity coefficient (stimulation by FAD)
The urinary xanthurenic acid after a tryptophan load
explanation:
Glutathione reductase is FAD-dependent. A coefficient above 1.2–1.4 indicates deficiency. The xanthurenic acid test assesses B₆ status.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (B2 status — glutathione reductase, 3X)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with metastatic carcinoid tumour develops dermatitis, diarrhoea and confusion. The vitamin deficiency arises because
options: Most dietary tryptophan is diverted to serotonin instead of niacin synthesis
explanation:
Normally about 60 mg of tryptophan yields 1 mg of niacin. Pellagra also occurs with maize diets (bound niacytin), Hartnup disease and isoniazid (via B₆ deficiency). A necklace-shaped neck rash (Casal's necklace) is typical.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (Casal's necklace — tryptophan/niacin), 2023 NEET-PG (maize diet)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient on isoniazid develops microcytic anaemia with ringed sideroblasts in the marrow. It responds to pyridoxine because PLP is the cofactor for
explanation:
Without ALA synthase activity, haem synthesis fails and iron piles up in mitochondria around the nucleus. Isoniazid forms an inactive hydrazone with PLP, which also causes peripheral neuropathy.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (vitamin for sideroblastic anaemia — B6), 2021 NEET-PG (ATT neuropathy — B6)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which reaction does NOT require pyridoxal phosphate?
explanation:
Prolyl hydroxylase needs vitamin C, Fe²⁺, α-ketoglutarate and O₂. PLP serves transamination, decarboxylation, transsulfuration, deamination of hydroxy amino acids, ALA synthase and glycogen phosphorylase.
> `VITAMINS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (pyridoxine required for transamination, decarboxylation, transsulfuration), 2017 AIIMS (glycogen phosphorylase cofactor)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A bodybuilder eating a dozen raw egg whites daily develops dermatitis, alopecia and lethargy. Which enzyme is NOT affected?
explanation:
Avidin in raw egg white binds biotin, the cofactor for all carboxylases (CO₂ transfer). Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs B₁₂ (adenosylcobalamin).
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (raw eggs — pyruvate carboxylase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with megaloblastic anaemia has raised serum homocysteine and NORMAL methylmalonic acid. The most likely deficiency is
explanation:
B₁₂ is needed by two enzymes, methionine synthase (homocysteine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMA), so B₁₂ deficiency raises both. Folate is needed only for methionine synthase.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (folate — high homocysteine, low MMA), 2022 INI-CET (enzymes affected by B12)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In B₁₂ deficiency, DNA synthesis is impaired even when folate intake is adequate. This is because of the
options: "Methyl-folate trap": N⁵-methyl-THF cannot be demethylated, so the THF available for thymidylate synthesis falls
explanation:
N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF is the methyl donor for thymidylate synthase (dUMP → dTMP). Uracil is then wrongly built into DNA and cell division is delayed, giving megaloblasts.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (deficiencies preventing thymine insertion — folate and B12)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord in B₁₂ deficiency is best explained by
options: Impaired methionine synthase (less SAM for methylation) together with methylmalonyl-CoA accumulation causing abnormal myelin lipids
Hyperhomocysteinaemia causing thrombosis of spinal arteries
explanation:
Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts degenerate. Giving folate alone can correct the anaemia while the neurological damage progresses.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA needs B12), 2022 NEET-PG (B12 paraesthesia)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Leucovorin (folinic acid) "rescues" normal cells after high-dose methotrexate because it
options: Is a reduced folate that supplies THF without needing dihydrofolate reductase
explanation:
Methotrexate blocks DHFR, so THF and thymidylate (TMP) cannot be regenerated. Leucovorin is 5-formyl-THF, which enters the folate pool after the blocked step.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (methotrexate reduces TMP synthesis)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Perifollicular haemorrhages, "corkscrew" hairs and swollen bleeding gums in scurvy are due to
options: Defective collagen cross-linking by lysyl oxidase
Defective hydroxylation of proline and lysine, producing an unstable collagen triple helix
explanation:
Ascorbate keeps the iron of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the Fe²⁺ state. Without it, the weak capillary walls bleed. Option A is vitamin K; option B is copper.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (collagen defect — scurvy), 2021 NEET-PG (bleeding gums), 2016 AIIMS (hydroxyproline — post-translational)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Warfarin produces its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting
explanation:
Vitamin K hydroquinone is the cofactor for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in factors II, VII, IX and X and in proteins C and S. Each carboxylation turns vitamin K into the epoxide, which must be recycled. VKORC1 variants explain differences in warfarin dose between patients.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (vitamin K — factors II, VII, IX, X), 2015 AIIMS (γ-carboxylation)
