subject: Biochemistry
stem: The EARLIEST clinical sign of vitamin A deficiency in a child is usually
explanation:
Rod function needs 11-cis-retinal to regenerate rhodopsin. Bitot's spots (conjunctival xerosis) and corneal changes come later. Follicular hyperkeratosis of the skin (phrynoderma) is an extra-ocular sign.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (night blindness, Bitot spots, toad skin), 2018 AIIMS (provitamin A — β-carotene)
exam: 2020 NEET-PG (night blindness, Bitot spots, toad skin), 2018

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A child with fat malabsorption, acanthocytes and absent plasma apoB-containing lipoproteins develops ataxia, loss of position sense and haemolysis. The vitamin deficiency responsible for the neurological features is
explanation:
This is abetalipoproteinaemia (MTP defect). Vitamin E, a lipid-soluble antioxidant, cannot be transported, so spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, peripheral nerves and the retina degenerate, and red cells undergo oxidative haemolysis.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (vitamin E deficiency features)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): Humans must obtain ascorbic acid from the diet.
Reason (R): Ascorbic acid is the cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
Humans need dietary vitamin C because they lack L-gulonolactone oxidase, the last enzyme of the synthesis pathway. Its role in prolyl hydroxylation is true but unrelated. Intakes above about 100 mg/day saturate tissues, and the excess is excreted.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (L-gulonolactone oxidase), 2020 INI-CET (vitamin C above 100 units)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A breast-fed infant develops a rash around the mouth and anus, diarrhoea, alopecia and poor wound healing after weaning. The defect is in
explanation:
This is acrodermatitis enteropathica. Breast milk contains a zinc-binding ligand that helps absorption, so symptoms appear after weaning. Zinc deficiency also causes hypogonadism, loss of taste and growth failure.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (perioral scaly patches — zinc), 2024 INI-CET (zinc — hypogonadism)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A teenager with chronic hepatitis and Kayser–Fleischer rings has low serum ceruloplasmin. The defective protein is
options: ATP7B, a hepatocyte copper transporter for biliary excretion and ceruloplasmin loading
explanation:
This is Wilson disease (autosomal recessive). Copper builds up in liver, brain (basal ganglia) and cornea. The ATP7A defect in Menkes disease causes copper **deficiency**.
> `VITAMINS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (copper deficiency — Menkes), 2017 AIIMS (Menkes copper ATPase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A young woman from a selenium-poor region develops dilated cardiomyopathy. The selenium-dependent enzymes include
explanation:
This is Keshan disease. These enzymes contain selenocysteine (the "21st amino acid") at the active site, encoded by UGA. Zinc is in option A, copper in B, and molybdenum in C.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (selenocysteine enzyme — glutathione peroxidase), 2014 AIIMS (codon for selenocysteine)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient whose sweat and breath smell of rotting fish is advised to restrict dietary choline. The defective enzyme is
explanation:
This is trimethylaminuria. Gut bacteria make trimethylamine from choline and carnitine, and the liver normally oxidises it to odourless TMA N-oxide.
> `VITAMINS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (fish odour disease — restrict choline)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hepcidin lowers plasma iron by
options: Inhibiting DMT1 on the apical membrane of enterocytes
Binding ferroportin and causing it to be internalised and degraded
explanation:
With ferroportin gone, iron is trapped in enterocytes and macrophages. Inflammation (via IL-6) raises hepcidin, causing anaemia of chronic disease. Hepcidin deficiency causes haemochromatosis. Haem iron and Fe²⁺ are absorbed in the duodenum.
> `VITAMINS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (ileal resection — vitamin deficiencies), mineral cluster 2020–2024

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each type of enzyme inhibition with its effect.

| Inhibition | Effect |
|---|---|
| 1. Competitive | a. Both Km and Vmax decrease |
| 2. Non-competitive | b. Irreversible covalent inactivation after the enzyme acts on the inhibitor |
| 3. Uncompetitive | c. Km increases, Vmax unchanged |
| 4. Suicide (mechanism-based) | d. Km unchanged, Vmax decreases |
explanation:
Raising [S] overcomes competitive inhibition but not non-competitive inhibition. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the ES complex.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (Vmax decreases, Km same — 3X), 2020 NEET-PG (competitive), 2024 INI-CET (suicide inhibition)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, lines for an enzyme with and without a competitive inhibitor
options: Intersect in the second quadrant above the x-axis
explanation:
The y-intercept (1/Vmax) is unchanged, and the x-intercept (−1/Km) moves towards the origin. Non-competitive inhibition gives lines that meet on the x-axis; uncompetitive inhibition gives parallel lines.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (competitive — Vmax same, Km increases)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: For an enzyme following Michaelis–Menten kinetics, when [S] = 4 × Km the reaction velocity is
explanation:
v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 4Km/5Km × Vmax = 0.8 Vmax. At [S] = Km, v = ½ Vmax; at [S] = 9 Km, v = 0.9 Vmax.
> `ENZYMES` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (catalytic efficiency), 2020 INI-CET (kinetics calculation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An enzyme works with substrate at 1000 × Km and converts 1% of it to product in 10 minutes. If the enzyme concentration is doubled and the substrate is halved (still far above Km), the time to form the same amount of product is
explanation:
At [S] far above Km the enzyme is saturated, so the reaction is zero order in substrate: rate = kcat[E] and does not depend on [S]. Doubling [E] doubles the rate and halves the time. This is the same logic as the 2020 question (enzyme reduced to ⅓ → 3 × 9 = 27 min).
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (substrate 1000 × Km — 27 min)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The best single measure of an enzyme's catalytic efficiency and substrate preference is
explanation:
A high kcat and a low Km together give high efficiency. The upper limit is about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹, set by diffusion, and is reached by "catalytically perfect" enzymes such as triose phosphate isomerase and carbonic anhydrase.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (highest catalytic efficiency — kcat high, Km low)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (highest catalytic efficiency — kcat high, Km l

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which drug is NOT a suicide (mechanism-based) inhibitor of its target enzyme?
explanation:
Methotrexate is a tight-binding competitive substrate analogue and is not chemically changed by DHFR. Suicide inhibitors are processed by the enzyme into a reactive form that inactivates it: allopurinol becomes oxypurinol, and 5-FU becomes FdUMP. Aspirin acetylates COX irreversibly.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (suicidal inhibition)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Allosteric regulatory enzymes such as aspartate transcarbamoylase show a sigmoid velocity–substrate curve because
options: They have several subunits with cooperative binding
They are inhibited by their substrate
explanation:
Effectors bind at a site other than the active site and shift the curve (K-type) or change Vmax (V-type). ATCase is inhibited by CTP and activated by ATP.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (allosteric inhibitors bind another site), 2015 AIIMS (modifier at allosteric site — T/F)
exam: 2018 AIIMS (allosteric inhibitors bind another site), 2015 A

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Five days after an MI, a patient has new chest pain. The best biochemical marker for diagnosing reinfarction is
explanation:
CK-MB returns to normal within 48–72 hours, so a fresh rise means a new infarct. Troponins stay raised for 7–14 days. The LDH "flip" (LDH₁ > LDH₂) appears at 12–24 hours and lasts more than a week.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (LDH flip in MI)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A raised serum alkaline phosphatase can come from bone or liver. The enzyme that confirms a hepatobiliary source is
explanation:
GGT (or 5′-nucleotidase) rises with ALP in cholestasis but not in bone disease. GGT is also induced by alcohol, making it the most characteristic enzyme rise in alcoholic liver disease.
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (bile duct obstruction — GGT), 2017 AIIMS (alcoholic hepatitis — GGT)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each enzyme with its metal cofactor.

| Enzyme | Metal |
|---|---|
| 1. Carbonic anhydrase | a. Molybdenum |
| 2. Glutathione peroxidase | b. Copper and iron |
| 3. Cytochrome c oxidase | c. Zinc |
| 4. Xanthine oxidase | d. Selenium |
explanation:
Other zinc enzymes include alcohol dehydrogenase, ALP and carboxypeptidase. Copper enzymes include tyrosinase, lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase (cytosolic, Cu/Zn).
> `ENZYMES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (zinc enzyme — carbonic anhydrase), 2023 INI-CET (selenocysteine — glutathione peroxidase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In Lesch–Nyhan syndrome, uric acid overproduction is mainly due to
options: Failure of purine salvage, which leads to accumulation of PRPP and loss of feedback inhibition, accelerating de novo purine synthesis
explanation:
HGPRT deficiency is X-linked. It causes self-mutilation, choreoathetosis, intellectual disability and gout. Overactive PRPP synthetase also causes hyperuricaemia, by the same mechanism.
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (Lesch–Nyhan case), 2017 AIIMS (hyperuricaemia — HGPRT, PRPP synthase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Binge drinking precipitates an attack of gout mainly because
options: Alcohol contains purines only in wine
Alcohol increases urate binding to albumin
Lactate competes with urate for renal excretion, and alcohol metabolism speeds ATP breakdown to purines
explanation:
A high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio turns pyruvate into lactate, which is exchanged for urate in the tubule and so reduces urate secretion. Converting acetate to acetyl-CoA uses ATP, producing AMP and then urate. Beer also contains guanosine.
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (alcoholic gout — raised urate and lactate)
exam: 2022 NEET-PG (alcoholic gout — raised urate and lactate)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An infant has megaloblastic anaemia that does not respond to B₁₂ or folate, with crystals of orotic acid in the urine and normal ammonia. The appropriate treatment is
explanation:
This is hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency). Uridine supplies pyrimidines through salvage and, by feedback, switches off CPS-II. Orotic aciduria with **hyperammonaemia** points instead to OTC deficiency.
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (CPS-I deficiency), 2020 NEET-PG (methotrexate and TMP)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Basophilic stippling of red cells in lead poisoning results from inhibition of
explanation:
Without it, ribosomal RNA breakdown products are not cleared and clump as basophilic dots. Inherited deficiency of the enzyme causes a haemolytic anaemia with the same stippling.
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (basophilic stippling — pyrimidine-specific 5′-nucleotidase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Spontaneous deamination of cytosine in DNA produces uracil. This lesion is removed first by
options: Uracil-DNA glycosylase, through base excision repair
explanation:
Deamination of **5-methylcytosine** gives thymine, a normal DNA base, which is much harder to recognise. This is why methylated CpG sites are mutation hotspots (C→T transitions).
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (deamination of methylcytosine → thymine), 2015 AIIMS (CpG islands)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hydroxyurea, used in sickle cell disease and myeloproliferative disorders, inhibits
explanation:
Ribonucleotide reductase makes all the deoxyribonucleotides (using thioredoxin as reductant). Hydroxyurea quenches its tyrosyl free radical. In sickle cell disease it also raises HbF.
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (methotrexate — TMP synthesis), nucleotide synthesis cluster

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In which genome would the content of adenine NOT equal that of thymine, and guanine NOT equal that of cytosine?
explanation:
Chargaff's rules (A = T, G = C) apply only to double-stranded DNA, where hydrogen-bonded base pairing enforces them. Parvovirus has single-stranded DNA. HIV's RNA genome has no thymine at all.
> `NUCLEOTIDES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (virus in which A ≠ T — HIV), 2016 AIIMS (base pairing — hydrogen bonds)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Arrange these enzymes of haem synthesis in the order in which they act.
1. Porphobilinogen deaminase
2. Ferrochelatase
3. δ-ALA dehydratase
4. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
explanation:
ALA synthase (glycine + succinyl-CoA, PLP-dependent) acts first, in mitochondria. The middle steps are cytosolic, and the last steps return to mitochondria. Mature RBCs cannot make haem because they have no mitochondria.
> `HEME` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (TCA intermediate in haem synthesis — succinyl-CoA), 2016 AIIMS (RBC not a site of haem synthesis)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (TCA intermediate in haem synthesis — succinyl-

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): In chronic lead poisoning, urinary δ-aminolevulinic acid is raised.
Reason (R): Lead inhibits δ-ALA dehydratase.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
Lead also inhibits ferrochelatase, so zinc protoporphyrin rises and microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling develops. Urinary coproporphyrin also rises. Eosinophilia is not a feature, as the 2022 assertion tested.
> `HEME` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (assertion — lead and ALA dehydratase), 2018 NEET-PG (urinary coproporphyrin), 2016 AIIMS (lead — ALA synthase activity)
exam: 2022 INI-CET (assertion — lead and ALA dehydratase), 2018 NE

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A young woman has an attack of severe abdominal pain, psychosis and dark urine after starting barbiturates. Giving intravenous haemin helps because it
options: Represses hepatic ALA synthase-1 by feedback
explanation:
This is acute intermittent porphyria (PBG deaminase deficiency). Drugs that induce cytochrome P450 deplete haem, which induces ALAS1 and floods the pathway with ALA and PBG. Glucose also represses ALAS1. There is no photosensitivity, because the block comes before porphyrin rings form.
> `HEME` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (ALA synthase activity increased), 2021 INI-CET (haem synthesis)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each porphyria with its enzyme and hallmark.

| Porphyria | Enzyme and hallmark |
|---|---|
| 1. Acute intermittent porphyria | a. Ferrochelatase — painful, non-blistering photosensitivity |
| 2. Porphyria cutanea tarda | b. PBG deaminase — neurovisceral attacks, no skin lesions |
| 3. Congenital erythropoietic porphyria | c. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase — blistering of sun-exposed skin |
| 4. Erythropoietic protoporphyria | d. Uroporphyrinogen III synthase — red teeth and red urine from infancy |
explanation:
PCT is the commonest porphyria and is linked to hepatitis C, alcohol, oestrogens and iron overload. Photosensitivity comes from porphyrins that absorb light around 400 nm (the Soret band).
> `HEME` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: haem synthesis cluster — 2022 INI-CET, 2018 NEET-PG, 2016 AIIMS
exam: haem synthesis cluster — 2022 INI-CET, 2018 NEET-PG, 2016 AI

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The only reaction in the body that produces carbon monoxide endogenously is catalysed by
explanation:
Haem oxygenase opens the haem ring to give biliverdin, Fe²⁺ and CO; biliverdin reductase then forms bilirubin. Endogenous CO is a vasodilator and signalling molecule, and it explains raised carboxyhaemoglobin in haemolysis.
> `HEME` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (products of haem catabolism — Fe²⁺, biliverdin, CO)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (products of haem catabolism — Fe²⁺, biliverdin

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher O₂ affinity than HbA because
options: Its γ chains bind 2,3-BPG weakly, because His143 of the β chain is replaced by serine
explanation:
2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity between the two β chains of deoxy-HbA and stabilises the T (taut) state. With fewer positive charges there, HbF binds it weakly, so the curve shifts left and O₂ moves from mother to fetus.
> `HEME` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (2,3-BPG binds globin), 2023 INI-CET (β globin)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In E. coli, the RNA primers of Okazaki fragments are removed and replaced with DNA by
options: DNA polymerase I, using its 5′→3′ exonuclease activity
explanation:
Ligase then seals the nick, using NAD⁺ in bacteria and ATP in eukaryotes. In eukaryotes, RNase H and FEN1 remove primers. Okazaki fragments form on the lagging strand, which is made discontinuously.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (Okazaki fragments — 6X), 2022 NEET-PG (DNA Pol I proofreading)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Klenow fragment of DNA polymerase I keeps which activities?
explanation:
Protease cleavage removes the N-terminal domain that carries 5′→3′ exonuclease activity. Klenow is used to fill in sticky ends and was used in early Sanger sequencing.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (Klenow lacks 5′→3′ exonuclease)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Telomerase is best described as
options: A ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template and adds TTAGGG repeats to the 3′ end
A DNA ligase that joins chromosome ends
explanation:
It solves the end-replication problem. It is active in germ cells, stem cells and most cancers, but inactive in most somatic cells, which therefore age.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein — T/F)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each disorder with the defective DNA repair pathway.

| Disorder | Repair pathway |
|---|---|
| 1. Xeroderma pigmentosum | a. Homologous recombination |
| 2. Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) | b. ATM kinase signalling of double-strand breaks |
| 3. BRCA1/2-associated breast cancer | c. Nucleotide excision repair |
| 4. Ataxia telangiectasia | d. Mismatch repair |
explanation:
Double-strand breaks are repaired by homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Mismatch repair does not handle them. UV-induced thymine dimers need NER, which is why xeroderma pigmentosum causes skin cancers in sun-exposed areas.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (photosensitivity — NER, 3X), 2023 NEET-PG (HNPCC — mismatch), 2024 INI-CET (not useful in dsDNA break)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Arrange the steps of base excision repair.
1. DNA polymerase β fills the single-nucleotide gap
2. A DNA glycosylase removes the damaged base
3. DNA ligase seals the nick
4. AP endonuclease cuts the backbone at the abasic site
explanation:
BER repairs small, non-distorting lesions such as uracil, oxidised bases (8-oxoguanine) and abasic sites. Bulky, helix-distorting lesions go to NER.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (DNA repair mechanisms), 2022 INI-CET (methylcytosine deamination)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: To correct a single point mutation exactly using CRISPR–Cas9 and a donor DNA template, the cell must repair the Cas9 cut by
explanation:
HDR copies the donor template and works mainly in the S and G2 phases. NHEJ is error-prone and introduces small insertions or deletions, which is used to knock genes out.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS (CRISPR nick → NHEJ knockout)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The key mechanistic difference between siRNA and miRNA is that
options: siRNA acts in the nucleus, miRNA in mitochondria
miRNA is double-stranded while siRNA is single-stranded
Only miRNA uses the RISC complex
siRNA pairs perfectly and directs cleavage of its target mRNA, whereas miRNA pairs imperfectly, usually in the 3′ UTR, and mainly represses translation
explanation:
Both are processed by Dicer and loaded onto Argonaute in RISC. Both "knock down" genes, unlike CRISPR, which knocks them out. One miRNA can regulate hundreds of mRNAs.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (miRNA binds 3′ UTR), 2023 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS (RNAi — knockdown)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The template strand of a gene reads 5′-TACGGA-3′. The mRNA transcribed from it is
explanation:
mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template. Pairing gives 3′-AUGCCU-5′, which written 5′→3′ is UCCGUA. Option B is the trap of writing the complement in the same direction. The mRNA matches the coding strand with U in place of T.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (template GATCTAC → RNA product)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The 7-methylguanosine cap on eukaryotic mRNA does all of the following EXCEPT
options: Help the ribosome recognise the mRNA through eIF4E
Promote nuclear export and splicing of the first intron
explanation:
Cleavage and polyadenylation are signalled by AAUAAA near the 3′ end. Capping, splicing, polyadenylation and editing are post-transcriptional changes; glycosylation is post-translational. tRNA and rRNA are not capped.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (mRNA binds ribosome via 7-methylguanosine cap), 2024 INI-CET (post-transcriptional modification), 2017 AIIMS (RNAs without cap)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the intestine, apoB-48 is produced from the same gene as apoB-100 because
options: Alternative splicing removes the exons after exon 26
APOBEC-1 deaminates cytidine to uridine, turning a CAA codon into the stop codon UAA
A proteolytic enzyme cleaves apoB-100 after translation
explanation:
The protein is cut off at 48% of apoB-100's length and lacks the LDL-receptor-binding domain. This is classic RNA editing. The liver does not edit, so it makes apoB-100.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (ApoB-48 — RNA editing), 2021 INI-CET (RNA editing)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Antibodies against the Sm proteins of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), which form the spliceosome, are highly specific for
explanation:
The spliceosome (U1, U2, U4/U6, U5 snRNPs) removes introns at GU…AG boundaries. Anti-U1 RNP antibodies define mixed connective tissue disease. Splice-site mutations cause some forms of β-thalassaemia.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (post-transcriptional processing), 2022 NEET-PG (RNA processing)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In human mitochondria, UGA codes for tryptophan instead of acting as a stop codon. This is an exception to which property of the genetic code?
explanation:
Mitochondria also read AUA as methionine and AGA/AGG as stop. Degeneracy, explained by wobble at the third base, means several codons code for one amino acid.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (wobble — degeneracy), 2018 AIIMS (stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Peptide bond formation on the eukaryotic ribosome is catalysed by
explanation:
Peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme (23S rRNA in prokaryotes). RNase P and self-splicing introns are other ribozymes. eEF-2 drives translocation.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (ribozymes — RNase P, peptidyl transferase)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each agent with its effect on protein synthesis.

| Agent | Effect |
|---|---|
| 1. Diphtheria toxin | a. Aminoacyl-tRNA analogue that causes premature chain release |
| 2. Shiga toxin / ricin | b. Binds the 30S subunit and causes misreading (prokaryotes) |
| 3. Puromycin | c. ADP-ribosylates eEF-2 |
| 4. Streptomycin | d. Depurinates an adenine in 28S rRNA |
explanation:
Pseudomonas exotoxin A also ADP-ribosylates eEF-2 (at diphthamide). Puromycin acts on both prokaryotic and eukaryotic ribosomes.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (ribozymes — peptidyl transferase), translation cluster 2017–2021

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The commonest CFTR mutation (ΔF508) is a deletion of three nucleotides. Its consequence is
options: Loss of a single phenylalanine without a frameshift, producing a misfolded protein that is degraded in the ER
A frameshift with premature stop codon
explanation:
Deletions in multiples of three keep the reading frame. This is a class II (processing/trafficking) defect, the target of corrector drugs. Sickle cell disease is a missense point mutation; a nonsense mutation creates a stop codon.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (CF — phenylalanine deletion at 508), 2020 INI-CET / NEET-PG (mutation types)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): Acetylation of histone tails increases gene transcription.
Reason (R): Acetylation neutralises the positive charge of lysine residues, loosening histone binding to DNA.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
Open euchromatin lets the transcription machinery in. By contrast, methylation of cytosine at CpG islands and histone deacetylation silence genes, which is how X-inactivation and imprinting work.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (methylation does not favour euchromatin), 2019 NEET-PG (cytosine methylation lowers expression)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A hypotonic newborn with feeding difficulty becomes a hyperphagic, obese child with hypogonadism. Testing shows a 15q11–q13 deletion. The deleted copy was inherited from the
explanation:
This is genomic imprinting: the maternal genes in this region are silenced by methylation. Losing the paternal copy (or having maternal uniparental disomy) causes Prader–Willi syndrome. Losing the maternal UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome (a happy demeanour, seizures and ataxia).
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (CpG methylation), 2021 INI-CET (epigenetic methylation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Transcription of the lac operon in E. coli is maximal when
options: Glucose is high and lactose is absent
Glucose is absent and lactose is present
Both glucose and lactose are high
explanation:
Allolactose releases the repressor (negative control). Low glucose raises cAMP, so the CAP–cAMP complex activates the promoter (positive control).
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (thyroid hormone as transcription factor), gene regulation cluster
exam: 2021 INI-CET (thyroid hormone as transcription factor), gene

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Assertion (A): Retroviruses carry the enzyme reverse transcriptase.
Reason (R): The retroviral genome is double-stranded DNA.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation:
Retroviruses have two copies of single-stranded (+) RNA. Reverse transcriptase copies it into DNA, which integrase inserts into the host genome. Because the genome is RNA, A ≠ T in HIV.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (assertion — central dogma and retroviruses), 2023 INI-CET (HIV — A ≠ T)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Thyroid hormone, steroid and vitamin D receptors bind DNA through which structural motif?
explanation:
These receptors are ligand-activated transcription factors that bind hormone response elements. Leucine zippers are found in AP-1 (Fos/Jun) and CREB; helix–turn–helix in homeodomain and bacterial repressors.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (T3/T4 act as transcription factor)
exam: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (T3/T4 act as transcription factor

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which mucopolysaccharidosis is inherited as X-linked recessive?
explanation:
Hunter syndrome (iduronate-2-sulfatase) causes no corneal clouding, and patients are aggressive ("hunters see clearly"). Hurler syndrome (α-L-iduronidase) is autosomal recessive with corneal clouding. Fabry disease is the other X-linked lysosomal disorder.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (Hurler case), 2018 AIIMS (X-linked disorder)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Children of a mother with MELAS are affected to very different degrees. The main reason is
options: Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance
Heteroplasmy, with a threshold effect for the proportion of mutant mtDNA
explanation:
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother, and different cells carry different mixes of normal and mutant copies. mtDNA mutates faster than nuclear DNA because it lacks histones, is exposed to reactive oxygen species and has limited repair.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (mtDNA higher mutation rate — T/F)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Human Genome Project estimated the number of protein-coding genes in the human genome at about
explanation:
The international project published a draft in 2001 and was declared complete in 2003. Coding exons are only about 1–2% of the genome. The largest gene family encodes olfactory receptors. *Note: the 2023 INI-CET key gives "1 lakh genes", which was a pre-project estimate.*
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (Human Genome Project), 2016 AIIMS (largest gene family — odorant receptors)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), lysosomal enzyme levels are very high in plasma because
options: The enzymes are not glycosylated at all
N-acetylglucosamine phosphotransferase is deficient, so the enzymes lack the mannose-6-phosphate tag and are secreted instead of being sent to lysosomes
explanation:
The defect is in the Golgi, but the organelle affected is the lysosome. Cells fill with inclusions, giving coarse features, gingival hyperplasia, joint contractures and early death.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (organelle in I-cell disease — lysosomes)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Selenocysteine is built into proteins at a UGA codon, rather than translation stopping there, because of
options: A special aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase acting on UAA
A SECIS element in the mRNA (3′ UTR in eukaryotes) together with a dedicated tRNA^Sec
RNA editing of UGA to UGG
explanation:
Serine is loaded onto tRNA^Sec and converted to selenocysteine on the tRNA. Pyrrolysine (UAG) is the "22nd amino acid", found only in some archaea and bacteria.
> `MOLECULAR BIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (codon for selenocysteine — UGA), 2023 INI-CET (selenocysteine enzyme)

subject: Biochemistry
stem:
Match each blotting technique with the molecule it detects.

| Technique | Detects |
|---|---|
| 1. Southern blot | a. Protein |
| 2. Northern blot | b. DNA-binding proteins |
| 3. Western blot | c. DNA |
| 4. Southwestern blot | d. RNA |
explanation:
Western blot uses antibodies (for example, confirming HIV). An "Eastern" blot looks for post-translational modifications.
> `TECHNIQUES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (match — Southern, Northern, Western), 2021 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS (Northern — RNA)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In real-time quantitative PCR, sample A reaches threshold at cycle 22 and sample B at cycle 25 (100% efficiency). Compared with B, sample A contains
explanation:
Each cycle doubles the product, so a difference of 3 cycles means 2³ = 8-fold. A lower Ct means more starting template. This is why the 2024 answer was 25 cycles: one cycle earlier means half the amount.
> `TECHNIQUES` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (qPCR cycles for half the DNA amount)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (qPCR cycles for half the DNA amount)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: To measure how much of a particular mRNA a tissue is expressing by real-time PCR, the first essential step is
options: Reverse transcription of the RNA into cDNA
explanation:
Taq polymerase cannot copy RNA, so RT-qPCR is used. It is the standard way to quantify RNA (for example, viral load or BCR-ABL transcripts). Bisulfite treatment is used to study DNA methylation.
> `TECHNIQUES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (technique to quantify RNA — real-time PCR, 3X)
exam: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (technique to quantify RNA — real-

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Digital droplet PCR can detect a mutant allele present at 0.1% in circulating tumour DNA mainly because it
options: Splits the sample into thousands of droplets, each amplified separately, and counts positives for absolute quantification without a standard curve
Sequences each molecule by the Sanger method
explanation:
Partitioning spreads the rare mutant molecules thinly, so the many wild-type molecules do not swamp them. Poisson statistics then give the exact copy number. This is the basis of liquid biopsy for minimal residual disease.
> `TECHNIQUES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (low allele frequency — digital droplet PCR)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (low allele frequency — digital droplet PCR)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Dideoxynucleotides terminate chain growth in Sanger sequencing because they
options: Lack the 3′-OH group needed to form the next phosphodiester bond
explanation:
Each fluorescent ddNTP stops a fragment at a specific base, and capillary electrophoresis reads off the sequence. Sanger sequencing is still the gold standard for confirming a known variant.
> `TECHNIQUES` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (dideoxynucleotides in Sanger — 3X)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which abnormality can FISH NOT detect?
explanation:
FISH probes are thousands of bases long, so they detect copy number and structural changes (aneuploidy, deletions such as 22q11, translocations, amplification) but cannot resolve point mutations. Those need sequencing or allele-specific PCR.

stem: Which of these sequences is most likely to be the recognition site of a type II restriction endonuclease?
explanation:
Restriction sites are usually palindromes: the sequence reads the same 5′→3′ on both strands. The complement of GAATTC, read 5′→3′, is again GAATTC (the EcoRI site). AAGCTT (HindIII) was the 2022 example.

DNA is negatively charged (phosphate backbone) and moves towards the anode. The gel acts as a sieve, so small fragments move fastest and large ones stay near the start.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In hybridoma technology, only fused cells survive in HAT medium because
options: Hypoxanthine is toxic to myeloma cells
Aminopterin blocks de novo nucleotide synthesis; the HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells cannot use the salvage pathway, while hybrids get HGPRT from the B cell
explanation:
Unfused B cells die naturally because their lifespan in culture is limited. The hybridoma combines immortality (from the myeloma) with antibody specificity (from the B cell).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ammonium sulphate precipitates proteins without denaturing them because it
options: Competes for water of hydration, reducing protein solubility ("salting out")
Forms insoluble salts with the protein's carboxyl groups, as heavy metals do
Changes the pH to the isoelectric point
explanation:
The protein can be redissolved with its activity intact. TCA, heavy metal salts, alcohol, acetone and heat precipitate proteins by denaturing them or forming insoluble salts.

explanation:
Large molecules cannot enter the pores of the beads, so they travel only in the space between beads and come out first. This is the opposite of gel electrophoresis, where small molecules move fastest.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An acetate buffer (pKa 4.76) contains 10 times as much acetate as acetic acid. Its pH is
explanation:
Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log 10 = 5.76. A buffer works best within ±1 unit of its pKa. Bicarbonate (pKa 6.1) is still the main body buffer because the lungs and kidneys can each adjust one of its components.
> `TECHNIQUES` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ best buffer), 2017 AIIMS (pH calculation)

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The normality of 0.5 M H₂SO₄ is
explanation:
Normality = molarity × replaceable H⁺ per molecule = 0.5 × 2 = 1 N. Likewise, 1 mM H₂SO₄ and 2 mM HCl have the same normality (2 mN).

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each condition with its iron profile.

| Condition | Profile |
|---|---|
| 1. Iron-deficiency anaemia | a. Ferritin raised, TIBC low, transferrin saturation low |
| 2. Anaemia of chronic disease | b. Ferritin normal, iron studies normal, HbA₂ raised |
| 3. β-thalassaemia trait | c. Ferritin raised, transferrin saturation raised, ring sideroblasts |
| 4. Sideroblastic anaemia | d. Ferritin low, TIBC raised, transferrin saturation low |
explanation:
Ferritin is the best single test for iron deficiency, but it is an acute-phase reactant and rises in inflammation. In anaemia of chronic disease, iron is plentiful but locked away in macrophages.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (IDA iron profile — 7X), 2020 INI-CET (ACD — 5X)

stem: A 22-year-old has Hb 10.8 g/dL, MCV 64 fL and an RBC count of 5.8 million/µL. The Mentzer index and the most likely diagnosis are
explanation:
Mentzer index = MCV ÷ RBC count (millions) = 64 ÷ 5.8 ≈ 11. Below 13 suggests thalassaemia trait, where many small red cells are made; above 13 suggests iron deficiency. Confirm with HbA₂ by HPLC.

subject: Pathology
stem: The key mediator that traps iron in macrophages in anaemia of chronic disease is
options: Hepcidin, induced by IL-6, which degrades ferroportin
explanation:
Ferroportin is the only cellular iron exporter. Without it, both gut absorption and release from macrophages are blocked. Iron overload also raises hepcidin, while hypoxia and active erythropoiesis (via erythroferrone) lower it.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (hepcidin downregulates ferroportin — 3X), 2021 INI-CET (ferritin raised in ACD)

subject: Pathology
stem: The earliest peripheral smear finding of a developing megaloblastic anaemia, which may appear before macrocytosis, is
explanation:
This means at least one neutrophil with 6 or more lobes, or more than 5% with 5 lobes. It reflects impaired DNA synthesis in all dividing cells. The marrow shows nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony and giant metamyelocytes.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (hypersegmented neutrophils — B12), 2022 NEET-PG (B12 deficiency case)

subject: Pathology
stem: A young software engineer living on fast food develops macrocytic anaemia within a few months, while his B₁₂ is normal. Folate deficiency appears so quickly because
options: Folate is absorbed only in the terminal ileum
Body folate stores last only about 3–4 months, whereas B₁₂ stores last 3–5 years
Folate is destroyed by gastric acid
explanation:
Folate comes from green vegetables and fruit, is destroyed by cooking, and is absorbed in the jejunum. Giving folate alone to a B₁₂-deficient patient can correct the anaemia while the neurological damage gets worse.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (junk food, raised MCV — folate, 4X), 2021 NEET-PG (folate therapy worsening neurology)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 2-year-old with frontal bossing and a transfusion-dependent anaemia has HbF of 92% on HPLC. The investigation that identifies the exact defect, for prenatal counselling of the family, is
options: Repeat HPLC of both parents only
β-globin gene mutation analysis (ARMS-PCR or sequencing)
explanation:
HPLC and the smear (target cells, microcytes, nucleated RBCs, teardrop cells) establish β-thalassaemia major. Prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling needs the specific mutations to be known.

explanation:
Parvovirus B19 causes a transient aplastic crisis. It is dangerous in conditions with a short red-cell lifespan (spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia). Giant pronormoblasts are seen in the marrow. CD21 is the EBV receptor; Duffy is the receptor for *P. vivax*.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (virus causing aplasia in thalassaemia — parvovirus), 2020 INI-CET (EBV receptor CD21)

subject: Pathology
stem: Hydroxyurea reduces vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell anaemia mainly by
options: Increasing HbF, which inhibits HbS polymerisation
explanation:
It also lowers neutrophil counts and adhesion. Polymerisation is promoted by deoxygenation, dehydration (raised MCHC) and acidosis. The underlying lesion is a missense point mutation (Glu6Val).
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (hydroxyurea reduces crises), 2023 INI-CET / 2024 INI-CET (sickle mutation)

subject: Pathology
stem: The smear of a 10-year-old with sickle cell anaemia shows small, round, dark-purple inclusions in many red cells. These indicate
explanation:
These are Howell–Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants), normally removed by the spleen. Loss of splenic function predisposes to infection with encapsulated organisms. Salmonella is the classic cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (Howell–Jolly — nuclear remnants), 2021 NEET-PG (small spleen), 2020 NEET-PG (Salmonella osteomyelitis)

subject: Pathology
stem: The most sensitive and specific screening test for hereditary spherocytosis is
explanation:
EMA binds band 3; spherocytes show reduced fluorescence. Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects of ankyrin, spectrin, band 3 or protein 4.2, is mostly autosomal dominant, and characteristically has a raised MCHC. A negative DAT helps rule out autoimmune haemolysis.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (EMA flow — hereditary spherocytosis), 2021 NEET-PG (HS — osmotic fragility), 2020 INI-CET (family history in HS)

subject: Pathology
stem: In a G6PD-deficient patient with acute haemolysis, Heinz bodies are best demonstrated with
options: A supravital stain such as crystal violet or new methylene blue
explanation:
Heinz bodies are precipitates of denatured haemoglobin and are not seen with Romanowsky stains. When splenic macrophages pluck them out, "bite cells" form. G6PD deficiency is X-linked, so males are mainly affected.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (G6PD — males and females equally affected T/F), 2021 INI-CET (G6PD features)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (G6PD — males and females equally affected T/F)

subject: Pathology
stem: Which statement about paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is FALSE?
options: It is caused by an acquired somatic PIGA mutation in a stem cell
Cells lack GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59
Thrombosis, especially of hepatic and abdominal veins, is the main cause of death
It is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern
explanation:
PIGA is on the X chromosome, but the mutation is acquired, not inherited. That is why PNH is "the haemolytic anaemia that is not inherited" (an intracorpuscular yet acquired defect). Flow cytometry (CD55/CD59, FLAER) is the gold standard. Eculizumab blocks C5.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (not an inherited disorder — PNH), 2022 INI-CET / NEET-PG (PNH features; flow cytometry), 2019 NEET-PG (CD59)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (not an inherited disorder — PNH), 2022 INI-CET

explanation:
In cold agglutinin disease, the IgM antibody binds red cells in cool peripheral blood, fixes complement and then falls off on warming, leaving only C3d. Causes include *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, EBV and lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Warm AIHA (IgG) causes spherocytes and splenic destruction.

subject: Pathology
stem: A patient has a reticulocyte count of 10% and a haematocrit of 22% (normal 45%). The corrected reticulocyte count is about
explanation:
Corrected count = observed × (patient Hct ÷ normal Hct) = 10 × 22/45 ≈ 4.9%. Dividing further by the maturation factor (about 2 at this Hct) gives a reticulocyte production index of about 2.4. An index above 2–3 indicates an adequate marrow response, as in haemolysis.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (corrected reticulocyte count calculation)

subject: Pathology
stem: A patient has pancytopenia, a reticulocyte count of 0.3% and no splenomegaly. Aspiration gives a dry tap, and trephine biopsy shows more than 75% fat with no abnormal cells. The diagnosis is
explanation:
Splenomegaly argues against aplastic anaemia. A dry tap with a **fibrotic, cellular** trephine suggests myelofibrosis or hairy cell leukaemia. Aplastic anaemia is mostly immune-mediated (T-cell attack on stem cells).
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (fatty marrow — aplastic anaemia), 2021 INI-CET (splenomegaly not seen in aplastic anaemia)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 55-year-old with isolated severe anaemia has a reticulocyte count close to zero, normal WBC and platelets, and a marrow almost devoid of erythroid precursors. CT shows an anterior mediastinal mass. The mass is most likely a
explanation:
Thymoma is associated with pure red cell aplasia, myasthenia gravis and hypogammaglobulinaemia (Good syndrome). Removing the tumour can reverse the aplasia.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (mediastinal mass and red cell aplasia), 2020 INI-CET (thymoma vs ALL — cytokeratin)

subject: Pathology
stem: "Spur cell" anaemia, with numerous acanthocytes on the smear, is classically seen in
explanation:
An excess of membrane cholesterol produces irregular spiky cells, which the spleen destroys. Acanthocytes are also seen in abetalipoproteinaemia, McLeod phenotype and neuroacanthocytosis (PKAN). Echinocytes ("burr cells") have regular short spines.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (acanthocytes — abetalipoproteinaemia, PKAN)

subject: Pathology
stem: Schistocytes on a peripheral smear are expected in all of the following EXCEPT
explanation:
Schistocytes are red cells cut by fibrin strands or abnormal flow (microangiopathic or macroangiopathic haemolysis), with raised LDH and low haptoglobin. Spherocytosis is a membrane defect without fragmentation.
> `RBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (schistocytes — mechanical valve), 2024 INI-CET (TTP — MAHA)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 9-year-old has an abdominal mass. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized cells with a "starry sky" pattern, Ki-67 close to 100%, CD10 positive and BCL2 negative. The characteristic genetic lesion is
explanation:
This is Burkitt lymphoma, the fastest-growing human tumour. The "stars" are tingible-body macrophages that have engulfed apoptotic cells. The endemic African form is associated with EBV and involves the jaw; the sporadic form involves the abdomen (ileocaecal region).
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (starry sky — c-MYC, 10X), 2019 NEET-PG (CD19+, CD10+ — Burkitt)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each lymphoma with its characteristic translocation.

| Lymphoma | Translocation |
|---|---|
| 1. Follicular lymphoma | a. t(11;18) API2–MALT1 |
| 2. Mantle cell lymphoma | b. t(14;18) IGH–BCL2 |
| 3. Gastric MALT lymphoma not responding to H. pylori eradication | c. t(8;14) MYC–IGH |
| 4. Burkitt lymphoma | d. t(11;14) CCND1–IGH |
explanation:
BCL2 is anti-apoptotic and located on the mitochondrial membrane, so follicular lymphoma grows slowly by escaping cell death. t(11;14) also marks a good-prognosis subgroup of myeloma.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (follicular lymphoma — BCL-2), 2017 AIIMS (myeloma t(11;14)), 2016 AIIMS (BCL2 in mitochondria)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 65-year-old man has generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Lymph node cells are CD5+, CD23−, CD10− and cyclin D1+. The diagnosis is
explanation:
CLL is also CD5+, but it is CD23+ and cyclin D1−. In the few cyclin D1-negative mantle cell lymphomas, nuclear SOX11 confirms the diagnosis. Lymphomatous polyposis of the gut is a classic presentation.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (cyclin D1-negative mantle cell lymphoma — SOX11), 2021 INI-CET (CLL — flow cytometry)

subject: Pathology
stem: A woman with known CLL develops rapidly enlarging neck nodes, fever and weight loss over 6 weeks, with a sharp rise in LDH. Node biopsy will most likely show
explanation:
Transformation occurs in about 5–10% of CLL and carries a poor prognosis. Smudge cells on the smear and CD5+/CD23+ flow cytometry establish the original CLL, which arises from mature naïve or memory B cells.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (CLL with rapid nodes — Richter), 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (smudge cells — flow, 3X), 2022 INI-CET (CLL origin)

subject: Pathology
stem: A man has massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, monocytopenia and a dry tap. Circulating cells have hair-like cytoplasmic projections. The most specific molecular abnormality is
explanation:
Hairy cell leukaemia is CD11c+, CD25+, CD103+, annexin A1+ and TRAP-positive, and is present in almost all classic cases. Reticulin fibrosis causes the dry tap. Cladribine is the treatment, and BRAF inhibitors are used when it relapses.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (hair-like projections), 2023 INI-CET (dry tap — hairy cell)

subject: Pathology
stem: The immunophenotype of a classic Reed–Sternberg cell is
options: CD15+, CD30+, CD45−, CD20 usually negative
explanation:
The "popcorn" (L&H) cells of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma have the opposite profile: CD20+, CD45+, CD15−, CD30−. They are EBV-negative and have a good prognosis.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (NLPHL — popcorn cells CD20+), 2019 NEET-PG (L&H cells), 2015 AIIMS (EBV not with NLPHL)

subject: Pathology
stem: Which feature favours non-Hodgkin lymphoma over Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Localised to a single axial group of nodes
Involvement of Waldeyer's ring and mesenteric nodes
explanation:
NHL spreads non-contiguously and is often extranodal. Hodgkin lymphoma typically involves cervical and mediastinal nodes, spreads in an orderly way, and rarely involves Waldeyer's ring or the mesentery.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (Waldeyer's ring in Hodgkin — false)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 15-year-old boy has a large anterior mediastinal mass and a high WBC count. The blasts are TdT+, CD7+ and cytoplasmic CD3+. The diagnosis is
explanation:
TdT marks lymphoblasts (precursors). B-ALL is CD19+, CD10+, CD22+ and TdT+. Thymoma also contains TdT+ thymocytes, but its epithelial cells are cytokeratin-positive, which separates it from lymphoblastic lymphoma.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (CD10, CD19, CD22, TdT — B-ALL), 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (ALL vs thymoma — cytokeratin)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (CD10, CD19, CD22, TdT — B-ALL), 2020 INI-CET /

subject: Pathology
stem: Which finding indicates a POOR prognosis in childhood B-ALL?
explanation:
Other poor-prognosis features are age under 1 or over 10, very high WBC, t(9;22), hypodiploidy and poor early response to steroids or therapy (minimal residual disease). Hyperdiploidy and ETV6–RUNX1 are favourable.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (good prognosis in ALL — hyperploidy), 2015 AIIMS (most important prognostic factor — steroid response)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 30-year-old presents with gum bleeding and DIC. The marrow is packed with hypergranular promyelocytes containing bundles of Auer rods. The drug that induces maturation of the leukaemic cells is
explanation:
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia carries t(15;17) PML–RARA. ATRA and arsenic trioxide release the block on differentiation. DIC comes from procoagulants and annexin II in the granules, and is a medical emergency.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (Auer rods — AML t(15;17)), 2021 NEET-PG (ATRA — PML–RARA)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 2-year-old with Down syndrome has acute leukaemia. The blasts show cytoplasmic blebs and express CD41 and CD61. The mutation typically involved is
explanation:
Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (AML-M7) is about 500 times more common in Down syndrome. It may follow transient abnormal myelopoiesis in the newborn. Marrow fibrosis often causes a dry tap.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (blebbed blasts — 47,XY,+21 megakaryoblastic), 2023 INI-CET (dry tap in AML-M7)

subject: Pathology
stem: In chronic myeloid leukaemia, which finding defines blast crisis (WHO)?
options: Basophils of 20% or more in blood
Blasts of 20% or more in blood or marrow, or extramedullary blast proliferation
explanation:
Options A, B and D are features of accelerated phase (with blasts 10–19%), together with new clonal abnormalities and resistance to TKIs. About two-thirds of blast crises are myeloid and one-third lymphoid.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (accelerated phase of CML), 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (CML t(9;22)), 2017 AIIMS (p190 BCR–ABL)

subject: Pathology
stem: A man from a hilly region has Hb 19 g/dL with normal WBC and platelet counts. The single best test to separate polycythaemia vera from secondary polycythaemia is
explanation:
In PV (JAK2 V617F in more than 95%), EPO is low because red cell production is autonomous. In hypoxic or EPO-secreting causes such as high altitude or renal tumours, it is normal or high. Aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia suggest PV.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (hilly area polycythaemia — EPO levels), 2023 INI-CET (PV — JAK2, pruritus after bath)
exam: 2016 AIIMS (hilly area polycythaemia — EPO levels), 2023 INI

subject: Pathology
stem: A "dry tap" on bone marrow aspiration is expected in all of the following EXCEPT
explanation:
ITP marrow is normal or hypercellular with increased megakaryocytes and aspirates easily. Dry taps result from fibrosis or a tightly packed marrow, as in metastases or some CML and ALL. Trephine biopsy is then essential.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (dry tap — hairy cell, AML-M7, CML), 2024 INI-CET (ITP marrow)
exam: 2023 INI-CET (dry tap — hairy cell, AML-M7, CML), 2024 INI-C

subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following indicates a POOR prognosis in multiple myeloma?
explanation:
The International Staging System uses β₂-microglobulin and albumin. High-risk cytogenetics include del(17p), t(4;14) and t(14;16). Myeloma presents with CRAB features (hyperCalcaemia, Renal failure, Anaemia, lytic Bone lesions).
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (myeloma case — 5X), 2020 NEET-PG (poor prognosis — β₂-microglobulin), 2017 AIIMS (t(11;14) good)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 68-year-old has blurred vision, headache and nosebleeds. Serum shows an IgM M-spike, and the marrow has lymphoplasmacytic cells without lytic bone lesions. The mutation found in more than 90% of such cases is
explanation:
This is Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, which arises from post-germinal-centre B cells. Large pentameric IgM causes hyperviscosity, which is treated urgently with plasmapheresis. Unlike myeloma, lytic bone lesions are absent.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (Waldenström — post-germinal centre B cells), myeloma cluster 2014–2023
exam: 2016 AIIMS (Waldenström — post-germinal centre B cells), mye

subject: Pathology
stem: Besides Birbeck granules on electron microscopy, the most specific immunohistochemical marker of Langerhans cell histiocytosis is
explanation:
Langerin is the protein that forms the tennis-racket Birbeck granules. LCH is also CD1a+ and S100+, and over half of cases carry BRAF V600E. Lytic skull lesions, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos form the Hand–Schüller–Christian triad.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (LCH — Birbeck granules)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each inclusion with what it is.

| Inclusion | Nature |
|---|---|
| 1. Döhle bodies | a. Fused primary (azurophilic) granules |
| 2. Auer rods | b. Iron-containing (siderotic) granules |
| 3. Howell–Jolly bodies | c. Remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum in toxic neutrophils |
| 4. Pappenheimer bodies | d. Nuclear (DNA) remnants in red cells |
explanation:
Pappenheimer bodies stain with Perls' Prussian blue (when they are called siderotic granules). Basophilic stippling is aggregated ribosomal RNA, as seen in lead poisoning and thalassaemia.
> `WBC DISORDERS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (match — Howell–Jolly, Döhle, flame bodies), 2021 INI-CET (match — granulocyte granules)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 24-year-old woman has menorrhagia and easy bruising. Her father and sister have similar symptoms. Platelet count is normal, bleeding time is prolonged and aPTT is mildly prolonged. The test that best confirms the diagnosis is
options: vWF antigen with ristocetin cofactor activity
explanation:
von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and is mostly autosomal dominant, affecting both sexes. vWF also carries factor VIII, so the aPTT may be prolonged. Type 1 is a mild quantitative defect, type 2 qualitative and type 3 severe.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (father and sister affected — vWD), 2023 NEET-PG (vWD types; raised BT), 2020 INI-CET (commonest inherited bleeding disorder)
exam: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (father and sister affected — vWD)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each platelet disorder with its laboratory feature.

| Disorder | Feature |
|---|---|
| 1. Bernard–Soulier syndrome | a. No aggregation with ADP, collagen or epinephrine; normal ristocetin response |
| 2. Glanzmann thrombasthenia | b. Absent ristocetin response that corrects with normal plasma |
| 3. von Willebrand disease | c. Giant platelets, thrombocytopenia, absent ristocetin response not corrected by plasma |
| 4. Storage pool disease | d. Absent secondary wave of aggregation (dense-granule deficiency) |
explanation:
Bernard–Soulier is a defect of GPIb–IX–V (the receptor for vWF). Glanzmann is a defect of GPIIb/IIIa (the fibrinogen receptor). In vWD the platelets are normal and the plasma factor is missing, so adding normal plasma corrects it.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (Bernard–Soulier — GpIb/IX), 2022 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (Glanzmann — GpIIb/IIIa)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 5-year-old develops petechiae two weeks after a viral illness. Platelets are 8,000/µL, other counts and the smear are normal, and there is wet purpura with mucosal bleeding. The most appropriate first-line treatment is
explanation:
Acute childhood ITP usually resolves on its own. Observation is enough when only skin bleeding is present, but mucosal bleeding with very low counts needs IVIG or steroids. The marrow shows increased megakaryocytes and is rarely needed. Splenectomy is for chronic, refractory adult ITP.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (ITP — IVIG), 2022 NEET-PG (acute ITP — IVIG), 2015 AIIMS (ITP treatment)

subject: Pathology
stem: Platelet transfusion is relatively CONTRAINDICATED in
options: Dengue with platelets of 15,000/µL and active severe bleeding
explanation:
In TTP, transfused platelets feed more microthrombi. HIT is the other classic contraindication, and transfusion is usually ineffective in ITP. TTP is treated with urgent plasma exchange, which removes anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies and replaces the enzyme. A stable dengue patient without significant bleeding needs only observation and fluids.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (contraindications to platelet transfusion), 2023 INI-CET (plasma in TTP; dengue with platelets 14,000)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 4-year-old develops acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis a week after bloody diarrhoea. ADAMTS13 activity is normal. The cause is most likely
explanation:
This is typical haemolytic uraemic syndrome: the toxin damages glomerular endothelium. TTP has ADAMTS13 below 10% with more neurological features. Atypical HUS (complement dysregulation, such as factor H) has no diarrhoeal prodrome. In DIC, PT and aPTT are prolonged.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (TTP triad), 2023 INI-CET (ADAMTS13 in TTP)

subject: Pathology
stem: A patient has delayed bleeding after surgery and poor wound healing. Platelet count, bleeding time, PT, aPTT and fibrinogen are all normal. The most useful screening test is
options: Clot solubility test in 5 M urea or 1% monochloroacetic acid
explanation:
Factor XIII deficiency gives normal routine coagulation tests. Without XIIIa cross-linking, the fibrin clot dissolves in urea. Umbilical stump bleeding in newborns and intracranial bleeding are classic.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (umbilical bleeding, normal PT/aPTT — factor XIII), 2015 AIIMS (factor XIII cross-links clot)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (umbilical bleeding, normal PT/aPTT — factor XI

subject: Pathology
stem: A man found to have a markedly prolonged aPTT before surgery has never had abnormal bleeding, even after tooth extraction. The most likely deficiency is
explanation:
Contact activation by factor XII is important in the test tube but not for haemostasis in the body, where coagulation starts with tissue factor and factor VIIa. Factor XI deficiency (haemophilia C) causes mild bleeding after trauma.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (factor deficiency not affecting coagulation in vivo — XII), 2021 INI-CET (factor VII in extrinsic pathway)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Arrange these clotting factors in the order in which they act along the intrinsic pathway to fibrin.
1. Factor IX
2. Factor X
3. Factor XI
4. Prothrombin (factor II)
explanation:
Factor XIIa activates XI, XIa activates IX, and IXa with VIIIa (the tenase complex) activates X. Xa with Va (prothrombinase) converts II to thrombin, which forms fibrin and activates XIII. The aPTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways; the PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (arrange clotting factors 12-9-10-5-13), 2023 INI-CET (aPTT measures intrinsic pathway)

subject: Pathology
stem: A woman with recurrent miscarriages has a prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct when her plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal plasma. She has had a deep vein thrombosis. The most likely cause is
explanation:
If the mixing study corrects, a factor is missing; if it does not, an inhibitor is present. The antiphospholipid antibody prolongs phospholipid-dependent tests in vitro but causes **thrombosis** in vivo. It is confirmed with the dRVVT test.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (thrombophilia — lupus anticoagulant), 2023 INI-CET (aPTT), 2016 AIIMS (DIC labs)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each thromboelastography (TEG) parameter with what it mainly reflects.

| TEG parameter | Reflects |
|---|---|
| 1. R time | a. Fibrinolysis |
| 2. K time / α-angle | b. Platelet number and function |
| 3. Maximum amplitude (MA) | c. Clotting factor activity (time to first fibrin) |
| 4. LY30 | d. Fibrinogen level (speed of clot build-up) |
explanation:
TEG gives a rapid, whole-blood picture of clot formation, strength and lysis. It guides targeted replacement in trauma, cardiac surgery and liver transplantation: FFP for a long R, cryoprecipitate for a low angle, platelets for a low MA, and tranexamic acid for a high LY30.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (MA in TEG — platelet function), 2022 INI-CET / NEET-PG (TEG — whole coagulation)
exam: 2020 INI-CET (MA in TEG — platelet function), 2022 INI-CET /

subject: Pathology
stem: In suspected DIC, the most useful single laboratory evidence of ongoing intravascular coagulation and fibrinolysis is
explanation:
D-dimer comes from plasmin breaking down cross-linked fibrin. DIC also shows falling platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen and schistocytes. Fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant and may be falsely normal early on.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (best test for bleeding in DIC — raised FDP)
exam: 2016 AIIMS (best test for bleeding in DIC — raised FDP)

subject: Pathology
stem: Factor V Leiden predisposes to venous thrombosis because
options: Factor V levels are greatly increased
Mutant factor Va resists inactivation by activated protein C
explanation:
The Arg506Gln point mutation destroys the APC cleavage site. It is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in white populations. Protein C deficiency, by contrast, predisposes to warfarin-induced skin necrosis, because protein C falls before the procoagulant factors.
> `HAEMOSTASIS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (commonest hypercoagulable state — factor V Leiden, 3X), 2018 AIIMS (thrombophilia through protein C), 2014 AIIMS (warfarin necrosis — protein C)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each vacutainer cap colour with its additive and a typical use.

| Cap | Additive and use |
|---|---|
| 1. Lavender | a. Sodium fluoride with potassium oxalate — plasma glucose |
| 2. Light blue | b. Lithium heparin — plasma electrolytes, ammonia |
| 3. Grey | c. K₂/K₃ EDTA — CBC, HbA1c |
| 4. Green | d. 3.2% trisodium citrate — PT, aPTT |
explanation:
Fluoride inhibits enolase, which stops glycolysis in the tube. Citrate is used for coagulation tests at a 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio. *The 2023 INI-CET stem pairs "blue cap" with plasma glucose; glucose samples go in grey-cap fluoride tubes.*
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (EDTA for HbA1c; green for electrolytes), 2023 INI-CET (blue cap — trisodium citrate), 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (grey cap — fluoride)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (EDTA for HbA1c; green for electrolytes), 2023

subject: Pathology
stem:
Arrange the CLSI order of draw for venepuncture with multiple tubes.
1. Lavender (EDTA)
2. Light blue (citrate)
3. Grey (fluoride/oxalate)
4. Plain red / gold (serum)
explanation:
Full order: blood cultures → citrate → serum → heparin → EDTA → fluoride. Following it prevents additives carrying over between tubes; for example, EDTA carried over chelates calcium and gives a falsely low calcium. Prolonged tourniquet time also falsely raises calcium and proteins.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (serum calcium sampling — release tourniquet, 3X), 2016 AIIMS (sequence of events in sample collection)

subject: Pathology
stem: Platelet concentrates are stored at 20–24 °C with constant agitation rather than refrigerated, because cold storage
options: Clusters GPIb on platelets, which are then quickly cleared by hepatic macrophages after transfusion
explanation:
The price of room-temperature storage is a higher risk of bacterial contamination and a shelf life of only about 5 days. Red cells are stored at 2–6 °C and FFP at −18 °C or colder. Platelets left over in an emergency should be kept at room temperature, never in the fridge.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2015 AIIMS (storage temperatures — 3X), 2018 AIIMS (product not refrigerated — platelets), 2020 INI-CET (store platelets at room temperature)

subject: Pathology
stem: In an emergency when the patient's blood group is unknown, the "universal" donor groups for packed red cells and for plasma are, respectively
explanation:
O red cells lack A and B antigens. AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies. Rh matters for red cells, especially in women of child-bearing age, but not for plasma. ABO inheritance is codominant.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (FFP for unknown group — AB, 4X), 2016 AIIMS (ABO codominance)
exam: 2022 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (FFP for unknown group — AB, 4X),

subject: Pathology
stem: Gamma irradiation of cellular blood components is done primarily to prevent
explanation:
Irradiation stops donor T lymphocytes from dividing. Options B to D are prevented by **leucodepletion**. *The 2021 INI-CET key credits irradiation with preventing HLA sensitisation and CMV, which mixes up the two methods.* Indications include immunodeficiency, intrauterine transfusion, transfusion from relatives, and stem cell transplant.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (irradiated blood prevents …), 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (leucodepleted and irradiated blood — 3X)

subject: Pathology
stem: Two hours into a plasma transfusion, a patient develops sudden breathlessness, fever and hypotension with bilateral infiltrates. BNP is normal, and there is no response to diuretics. The mechanism is
options: Donor anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the lungs
explanation:
This is TRALI, which occurs within 6 hours. Plasma from women who have had several pregnancies carries the highest risk. TACO, by contrast, causes hypertension, a raised BNP and improvement with diuretics.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (TRALI onset within 6 h), 2018 NEET-PG (TACO case)
exam: 2018 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (TRALI onset within 6 h), 2018 NEE

subject: Pathology
stem: Ten days after transfusion, a previously pregnant woman has a falling Hb, mild jaundice (raised unconjugated bilirubin) and a positive DAT. The antibody most often responsible for this delayed haemolytic reaction is
explanation:
Kidd antibodies drop to undetectable levels and are missed at cross-match, then return in an anamnestic response 3–14 days later. Kell is the most immunogenic system after ABO and D.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (delayed haemolytic reaction — unconjugated bilirubin), 2018 AIIMS (most immunogenic — Kell)

subject: Pathology
stem: With CPDA-1 anticoagulant–preservative, the permitted shelf life of whole blood or packed red cells is
explanation:
Adenine allows ATP to be regenerated, extending storage from 21 days (CPD) to 35 days. Additive solutions such as SAGM give 42 days. During storage, 2,3-BPG falls (left shift of the curve), and K⁺ and free Hb rise.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (CPDA for 35 days), 2023 NEET-PG (CPD vs ACD), 2024 INI-CET (stored blood left shift)
