subject: Pathology
stem: In flow cytometry, forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) are proportional, respectively, to
explanation:
An FSC versus SSC dot plot separates lymphocytes, monocytes and granulocytes. Antigen expression is shown on fluorescence histograms and dot plots. Flow cytometry is the gold standard for PNH and for immunophenotyping CLL.
> `TRANSFUSION AND LAB` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 AIIMS (forward scatter — cell size), 2022 INI-CET (flow shown by histogram and dot plot)

subject: Pathology
stem: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of apoptosis and NOT of necrosis?
options: A diffuse "smear" of DNA on agarose gel
A "ladder" of DNA fragments in multiples of about 180–200 bp
Release of cell contents with inflammation
explanation:
Caspase-activated DNase cuts DNA between nucleosomes. Apoptotic cells shrink, keep their membranes intact, show phosphatidylserine for phagocytosis, and cause no inflammation. Enzyme activation occurs in both forms of death, so it does not separate them.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (not a difference — enzyme activation), 2018 AIIMS (electrophoresis pattern of necrosis), 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (apoptosis features — 3X)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (not a difference — enzyme activation), 2018 AI

subject: Pathology
stem:
Arrange the events of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis after DNA damage.
1. Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria
2. Activation of BAX/BAK by BH3-only proteins (such as PUMA, NOXA)
3. Activation of executioner caspase-3
4. Formation of the apoptosome (APAF-1 + caspase-9)
explanation:
p53 switches on PUMA and NOXA. Anti-apoptotic BCL2, BCL-XL and MCL-1 normally hold BAX/BAK in check. The extrinsic (Fas/TNF receptor) pathway goes through caspase-8 and joins at caspase-3.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (anti-apoptotic gene MCL-1), 2017 AIIMS (BCL2, BCL-XL, MCL1), 2020 INI-CET (apoptosis activated intrinsically or extrinsically)

subject: Pathology
stem: Venetoclax, used in CLL and AML, kills tumour cells by
options: Acting as a BH3 mimetic that inhibits BCL2, freeing BAX/BAK to trigger apoptosis
explanation:
CLL cells depend heavily on BCL2. Tumour lysis syndrome is the main early risk. BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib), anti-CD20 antibodies (rituximab) and proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib) act differently.
> `CELL INJURY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (anti-apoptotic genes), 2016 AIIMS (BCL2 in mitochondria)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each form of regulated cell death with its defining feature.

| Cell death | Feature |
|---|---|
| 1. Pyroptosis | a. Iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, prevented by GPX4 |
| 2. Necroptosis | b. One live cell invades and dies inside another |
| 3. Ferroptosis | c. Caspase-1 activated by the inflammasome, releasing IL-1β |
| 4. Entosis | d. RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL signalling, independent of caspases |
explanation:
Caspase-1 also converts pro-IL-1β into IL-1β. In emperipolesis, by contrast, the engulfed cell (for example a lymphocyte inside a histiocyte or megakaryocyte) survives and passes through.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (caspase-1 — pyroptosis), 2022 INI-CET (cell-in-cell — entosis), 2021 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (IL-1 activated by caspase-1)

subject: Pathology
stem: Prominent emperipolesis of lymphocytes within large S100-positive histiocytes in massively enlarged cervical lymph nodes is the hallmark of
explanation:
This is sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy. The histiocytes are S100+, CD68+ and CD1a−. Emperipolesis (one viable cell passing through another) is also seen in megakaryocytes and in autoimmune hepatitis.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (one viable cell within another — emperipolesis), 2016 AIIMS (emperipolesis in autoimmune hepatitis)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (one viable cell within another — emperipolesis

subject: Pathology
stem: The ultrastructural change most reliably indicating IRREVERSIBLE cell injury is
options: Cell swelling with loss of microvilli
Large, amorphous flocculent densities in mitochondria
Dilated endoplasmic reticulum with detached ribosomes
explanation:
Irreversibility comes from severe mitochondrial dysfunction (failure to make ATP) and membrane damage, including lysosomal rupture. Nuclear pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis follow. The other options are features of reversible injury.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (signs of reversible injury)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each type of necrosis with its classic setting.

| Necrosis | Setting |
|---|---|
| 1. Coagulative | a. Brain infarct, abscess |
| 2. Liquefactive | b. Tuberculosis |
| 3. Caseous | c. Immune complex vasculitis, malignant hypertension |
| 4. Fibrinoid | d. Myocardial or renal infarct (outlines preserved) |
explanation:
In coagulative necrosis, protein denaturation outpaces enzyme digestion, so "ghost" cell outlines remain, as in a wedge-shaped adrenal or renal infarct. Fat necrosis (pancreatitis) shows chalky saponification.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (necrosis in vessels — fibrinoid), 2015 AIIMS (wedge-shaped area with outlines — coagulative)

subject: Pathology
stem: Psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid carcinoma are an example of
explanation:
Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead or damaged tissue with normal serum calcium: atheromas, damaged valves, TB caseation, psammoma bodies. Metastatic calcification affects normal tissues in hypercalcaemia (lungs, kidneys, gastric mucosa). *Myositis ossificans, keyed in 2021, is heterotopic ossification, a different process.*
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (dystrophic calcification seen in …)

subject: Pathology
stem: Calorie restriction prolongs lifespan in experimental models, partly by activating sirtuins. Sirtuins are
options: NAD⁺-dependent protein deacetylases that promote DNA repair and insulin sensitivity
explanation:
Calorie restriction also dampens IGF-1/insulin signalling and mTOR. Ageing involves telomere shortening (telomerase activity falls with age), accumulated DNA damage (Werner syndrome, WRN helicase), and failing protein homeostasis.
> `CELL INJURY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (sirtuins), 2023 NEET-PG (calorie restriction), 2022 NEET-PG (telomerase with ageing), 2021 NEET-PG (Werner — helicase)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Arrange the steps of leucocyte recruitment in acute inflammation.
1. Firm adhesion by integrins binding ICAM-1
2. Rolling mediated by selectins
3. Transmigration (diapedesis) mediated by PECAM-1
4. Margination
explanation:
After transmigration, chemotaxis (driven by C5a, IL-8, LTB₄ and bacterial peptides) guides cells to the site. Chemokines switch integrins to a high-affinity state, which links rolling to firm adhesion.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (sequence of acute inflammation — 3X), 2021 INI-CET (PECAM-1)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each adhesion molecule with its role.

| Molecule | Role |
|---|---|
| 1. P- and E-selectin | a. Transmigration through intercellular junctions |
| 2. LFA-1 (β2 integrin) | b. Initial rolling of leucocytes |
| 3. VLA-4 (β1 integrin) | c. Firm adhesion of neutrophils to ICAM-1 |
| 4. PECAM-1 (CD31) | d. Adhesion of lymphocytes, monocytes and eosinophils to VCAM-1 |
explanation:
VLA-4 is the target of natalizumab (multiple sclerosis, Crohn's disease). Selectins bind sialyl-Lewis X on leucocytes; failure of that binding is leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 2.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (adhesion molecule — VLA), 2021 INI-CET (PECAM-1)

subject: Pathology
stem: A newborn's umbilical cord has not separated by 4 weeks. He has recurrent bacterial skin infections without pus formation, and a very high neutrophil count. The defect is in
explanation:
This is leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1: neutrophils cannot adhere firmly and leave the vessels, so blood counts are high but tissues contain no pus. NADPH oxidase defects cause CGD; LYST defects cause Chédiak–Higashi syndrome.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (adhesion molecules), 2024 INI-CET (CGD)

subject: Pathology
stem: Vascular leakage that starts 2–12 hours after sunburn and lasts for hours to days is the
explanation:
It is due to direct endothelial damage in capillaries and venules (mild heat, UV, X-rays). Histamine (for example a thorn prick with mast cell release) gives the immediate transient type in venules. Severe burns give the immediate sustained type.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (match — endothelial injury: sunburn, thorn prick)
exam: 2020 INI-CET (match — endothelial injury: sunburn, thorn pri

subject: Pathology
stem: Anti-TNF therapy for rheumatoid arthritis can reactivate latent tuberculosis because TNF
options: Maintains granuloma structure and macrophage activation
explanation:
IL-12 from macrophages drives Th1 cells, whose IFN-γ turns macrophages into epithelioid cells and giant cells. TNF holds the granuloma together. Caseation reflects a type IV hypersensitivity response.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (caseous granuloma — IFN-γ), 2024 INI-CET (caseous granuloma — TB), 2017 AIIMS (caseous TB pathogenesis)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each type of granuloma with its usual cause.

| Granuloma | Cause |
|---|---|
| 1. Caseating with Langhans giant cells | a. Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) |
| 2. Stellate with central neutrophils (suppurative) | b. Sarcoidosis |
| 3. Ring of fibrin around a central lipid vacuole ("doughnut") | c. Tuberculosis |
| 4. Non-caseating with asteroid and Schaumann bodies | d. Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) |
explanation:
Stellate suppurative granulomas are also seen in lymphogranuloma venereum and tularaemia. Asteroid bodies are not specific to sarcoidosis, but they suggest it in the right clinical setting.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2016 AIIMS (stellate granuloma — cat scratch), 2016 AIIMS (doughnut granuloma — Q fever)

subject: Pathology
stem: Compared with healing by first intention, healing by second intention is characterised mainly by
options: Wound contraction by myofibroblasts and much more granulation tissue
explanation:
Large wounds with lost tissue heal from the base upwards. Myofibroblasts (α-SMA positive) pull the edges together. "Tertiary intention" (delayed primary closure) is when a contaminated wound is left open for a few days and then sutured.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (wound sutured after 5 days — tertiary intention), 2014 AIIMS (collagen fibrils at 4–5 days)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (wound sutured after 5 days — tertiary intentio

subject: Pathology
stem: When skin sutures are removed at the end of the first week, the wound's tensile strength is about what percentage of unwounded skin?
explanation:
Strength rises steeply over the next 4 weeks and plateaus at about 70–80% by 3 months. It never returns to 100%. Granulation tissue is rich in type III collagen, which is later replaced by type I collagen with lysyl oxidase cross-links.
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (collagen type III in granulation tissue), 2019 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (tensile strength — tropocollagen cross-linking)
exam: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (collagen type III in granulation

subject: Pathology
stem: Hepatic synthesis of acute-phase proteins such as CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A and hepcidin is driven mainly by
explanation:
IL-1 and TNF also contribute. Fever is produced by PGE₂ in the hypothalamus. IL-4 drives Th2 responses (eosinophils, IgE). IL-8 is the main neutrophil chemokine (important in ARDS).
> `INFLAMMATION` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2016 AIIMS (fever — PGE₂), 2020 NEET-PG (IL-1 endogenous pyrogen), 2023 NEET-PG (IL-8 in ARDS; IL-4 eosinophils)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each primary immunodeficiency with its defect.

| Disorder | Defect |
|---|---|
| 1. Bruton agammaglobulinaemia | a. MHC class II not expressed (CIITA/RFX) |
| 2. Chronic granulomatous disease | b. Btk — B cells fail to mature |
| 3. Bare lymphocyte syndrome (type II) | c. CD40 ligand on activated T cells |
| 4. X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome | d. NADPH oxidase |
explanation:
In bare lymphocyte syndrome, the lack of MHC means HLA-mismatched transplants are poorly recognised, so rejection is least likely. CGD patients are infected by catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia).
> `IMMUNITY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (CGD; bare lymphocyte transplant; CD19+ CD40−), 2022 INI-CET (bare lymphocyte — MHC non-expression), 2023 INI-CET (CD40 — class switching)

subject: Pathology

options: Nitroblue tetrazolium test giving a blue colour
explanation:

explanation:

subject: Pathology
stem: With Congo red, amyloid appears salmon-pink in ordinary light and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. The birefringence is due to
options: The high iron content of amyloid
The cross-β-pleated sheet structure of the fibrils
explanation:

Marfan syndrome is caused by FBN1 (fibrillin). Rett syndrome (MECP2) is lethal in males, so mostly girls are affected. Albinism is also autosomal recessive.

subject: Pathology
stem: In a pedigree, an affected father passes the trait to ALL his daughters and to NONE of his sons. Affected mothers pass it to half of their children of either sex. The pattern is
explanation:
A father gives his X only to daughters. In mitochondrial inheritance, affected **mothers** pass the trait to all their children and affected fathers to none. In X-linked recessive inheritance, mostly males are affected and carrier mothers transmit it.

subject: Pathology

subject: Pathology
stem: Anticipation in Huntington disease (earlier and more severe onset in later generations) is most marked when the gene is inherited from the
options: Father, because CAG repeats are unstable during spermatogenesis
explanation:
Juvenile Huntington disease is usually paternally inherited. Fragile X expands mainly during **maternal** transmission, through the premutation stage. Anticipation itself is defined as earlier and more severe disease in successive generations.

subject: Pathology
stem: The most common cardiovascular abnormality in Turner syndrome (45,X) is
explanation:
Bicuspid valve (about 30%) and preductal coarctation are typical, with a risk of aortic dissection. Other features: short stature (SHOX), webbed neck (cystic hygroma), widely spaced nipples, short 4th metacarpals, horseshoe kidney and streak ovaries.

subject: Pathology
stem: How many Barr bodies are present in the somatic cells of a 48,XXXY male?
explanation:
Number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1. Classic Klinefelter (47,XXY) has 1, and features gynaecomastia, long limbs, small firm testes and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Each extra X makes intellectual disability more likely.
> `GENETICS` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (XXY — Klinefelter), 2024 INI-CET (aneuploidy — Klinefelter)

subject: Pathology
stem: A couple has had two children with Down syndrome. The mother is 26. The most likely karyotype finding in one parent is
options: Normal karyotype, because recurrence is due only to age
explanation:
About 95% of Down syndrome is free trisomy from maternal meiotic non-disjunction, linked to maternal age and with a low recurrence risk. About 4% is translocation Down syndrome, which carries a high familial recurrence risk, especially when the mother is the carrier.
> `GENETICS` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (aneuploidy — trisomy 21), 2021 INI-CET (partial aneuploidy)

subject: Pathology
stem:

1. Arrest cells in metaphase with colcemid
2. Culture heparinised blood with phytohaemagglutinin for about 72 hours
3. G-band the chromosomes with trypsin–Giemsa and analyse
4. Swell cells in hypotonic KCl and fix in methanol–acetic acid
explanation:
Phytohaemagglutinin makes T lymphocytes divide. Heparin is used because EDTA damages viable cells. C-banding stains centromeric heterochromatin (useful for dicentric chromosomes). Standard banding resolution (about 5–10 Mb) misses microdeletions.

explanation:
A balanced translocation has no net gain or loss of DNA, so arrays miss it, while karyotype and FISH detect it. FISH cannot detect point mutations, and Sanger sequencing misses mosaic or low-level variants below about 15–20%.

1. Cyclin B–CDK1
2. Cyclin E–CDK2
3. Cyclin D–CDK4/6

explanation:

stem: On colonic biopsy, which finding most strongly favours Crohn's disease over ulcerative colitis?
explanation:
Granulomas are found in only about 35% of Crohn's cases, but they are specific when present. Crohn's disease is also transmural with skip lesions, fissures, fistulae and creeping fat, and aphthous ulcers are its earliest lesion. UC is continuous from the rectum, limited to the mucosa, forms pseudopolyps and is linked to PSC.
> `GASTROINTESTINAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (UC vs Crohn's — pseudopolyps), 2018 NEET-PG (first feature of Crohn's — aphthous ulcer), 2016 AIIMS (UC features)

explanation:
BRCA2 carries the greater risk of male breast cancer, and also of prostate and pancreatic cancer. BRCA1 is tested first in young women with a strong family history and triple-negative tumours. Both genes repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, which is why PARP inhibitors work against them.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (breast lump, mother died young — test BRCA1), 2024 INI-CET (BRCA1 DSB repair), 2020 INI-CET (BRCA testing — sequencing)
exam: 2022 INI-CET (breast lump, mother died young — test BRCA1),

subject: Pathology
stem: A breast carcinoma shows weak-to-moderate complete membrane staining for HER2 in more than 10% of cells (IHC 2+). The next step is
options: Report as HER2 positive and start trastuzumab
Repeat IHC with a different chromogen
In-situ hybridisation (FISH or SISH) for HER2 gene amplification
explanation:
IHC 3+ is positive and 0 or 1+ is negative; 2+ is equivocal and needs ISH. The brown colour on IHC comes from the DAB (diaminobenzidine) chromogen reacting with peroxidase.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (stain giving brown colour to HER2 — DAB)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (stain giving brown colour to HER2 — DAB)

subject: Pathology
stem: A breast carcinoma shows small, uniform cells infiltrating in single file with no tubules, and the tumour cells are negative for E-cadherin. The diagnosis is
options: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type
explanation:
Loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) stops the cells sticking together. The tumour is often multicentric and bilateral, and spreads unusually to peritoneum, ovary and GI tract. Mucinous carcinoma shows clusters of cells floating in pools of mucin.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (cells floating in mucin — colloid carcinoma), 2021 INI-CET (EMT and E-cadherin)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each ovarian tumour with its hallmark.

| Tumour | Hallmark |
|---|---|
| 1. Granulosa cell tumour | a. Schiller–Duval bodies, raised AFP |
| 2. Yolk sac tumour | b. Psammoma bodies, WT1+, raised CA-125 |
| 3. Dysgerminoma | c. Call–Exner bodies, inhibin+, oestrogen excess |
| 4. High-grade serous carcinoma | d. Large clear cells with lymphocytes, OCT3/4+, raised LDH |
explanation:
Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of seminoma and is very radiosensitive. High-grade serous carcinoma is the commonest malignant ovarian tumour, is often bilateral, and frequently starts in the fallopian tube (STIC).
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (granulosa — Call–Exner, inhibin; bilateral cysts with CA-125 — serous), 2020 INI-CET (Schiller–Duval — endodermal sinus)

subject: Pathology
stem: The most common testicular tumour in a man over 60 years old is
explanation:
It is often bilateral and spreads to the CNS. Seminoma (OCT3/4, KIT, PLAP, with lymphocytes in the septa) peaks at 30–40 years. Leydig cell tumours contain Reinke crystals.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (70-year-old, testicular swelling — NHL), 2022 INI-CET (seminoma markers), 2023 INI-CET (Reinke crystals)

subject: Pathology
stem: Strong, diffuse ("block") p16 staining in a cervical biopsy with CIN 3 indicates
options: Transforming high-risk HPV infection, with E7 inactivating RB
explanation:
When RB is inactivated, the cell overexpresses the CDK inhibitor p16. This makes p16 a surrogate marker for high-risk HPV. Multinucleated cells with intranuclear inclusions on a Pap smear suggest herpes simplex infection instead.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (HPV E7 acts on RB), 2023 INI-CET (HPV 16 and 18), 2018 NEET-PG (herpes on Pap smear)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (HPV E7 acts on RB), 2023 INI-CET (HPV 16 and 1

subject: Pathology
stem: A 70-year-old woman has a uterine cancer arising in an atrophic endometrium. It has a papillary architecture, marked nuclear atypia and a diffuse, strong ("all-or-none") p53 pattern. This tumour is
options: Endometrioid carcinoma linked to unopposed oestrogen and PTEN loss
Serous carcinoma (type II), driven by TP53 mutation
Clear cell carcinoma caused by DES exposure
explanation:
Type I endometrioid carcinomas arise from atypical hyperplasia in younger, obese women and carry a better prognosis. Serous carcinoma spreads early to the peritoneum even when it invades the uterine wall only slightly. DES is linked to clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina and cervix.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (DES — clear cell carcinoma), 2024 INI-CET (p53 role)

subject: Pathology
stem: In a prostate needle biopsy, the most helpful immunohistochemical support for invasive adenocarcinoma is
options: Absence of basal cells (p63 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin negative), with AMACR positivity
explanation:
Benign glands keep a layer of basal cells; invasive carcinoma loses it. Corpora amylacea (eosinophilic, laminated concretions) are common in benign glands. PSA confirms prostatic origin but not malignancy.
> `BREAST AND GENITAL` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (prostate biopsy — corpora amylacea)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each glomerular disease with its electron microscopy finding.

| Disease | EM finding |
|---|---|
| 1. Minimal change disease | a. Subendothelial deposits with "tram-track" GBM duplication |
| 2. Membranous nephropathy | b. Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes only |
| 3. Post-streptococcal GN | c. Subepithelial deposits with intervening GBM "spikes" |
| 4. MPGN type I | d. Subepithelial "humps" |
explanation:
Membranous nephropathy is linked to anti-PLA2R antibodies, hepatitis B, SLE, drugs and tumours. Minimal change disease responds to steroids. Post-streptococcal GN presents with cola-coloured urine, hypertension and periorbital puffiness.
> `RENAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG (foot process loss — MCD), 2018 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (membranous — spike and dome, 3X), 2022 NEET-PG (PSGN — subepithelial deposits)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 28-year-old woman with SLE has nephrotic-range proteinuria, active urinary sediment and falling GFR. Biopsy shows proliferation in more than 50% of glomeruli and "wire-loop" capillaries. The wire loops are caused by
explanation:
This is ISN/RPS class IV diffuse lupus nephritis, the commonest and most severe class. Immunofluorescence is "full house" (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q). Anti-dsDNA is associated with nephritis, whereas anti-La is linked to a lower risk.
> `RENAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (full-house IF — lupus nephritis, 3X), 2015 AIIMS (anti-La lower risk)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 60-year-old has haemoptysis, rapidly progressive renal failure and positive MPO-ANCA. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN, and there are no granulomas anywhere. The diagnosis is
explanation:
RPGN is classified by immunofluorescence: type I is linear anti-GBM, type II is granular immune complex (lupus, PSGN, IgA), and type III is pauci-immune ANCA disease. GPA is usually PR3-ANCA with granulomas. Crescents are the most consistent feature of RPGN.
> `RENAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (pauci-immune crescentic GN — ANCA), 2018 NEET-PG (p-ANCA, pulmonary–renal — MPA), 2015 AIIMS (type II RPGN), 2014 AIIMS (crescents in RPGN)

subject: Pathology
stem: The earliest morphological change in diabetic nephropathy, seen on electron microscopy, is
options: Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane
explanation:
Diffuse mesangial expansion follows, then nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules). Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of **both** afferent and efferent arterioles and loss of podocytes are typical.
> `RENAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (diabetic nephropathy — podocyte loss, mesangial widening, GBM thickening)

subject: Pathology
stem: A patient develops fever, rash and rising creatinine 10 days after starting a β-lactam antibiotic for tonsillitis. The most characteristic urine finding is
options: Red cell casts with dysmorphic RBCs
Heavy proteinuria with oval fat bodies
explanation:
This is drug-induced acute (tubulo)interstitial nephritis, a type IV (± type I) reaction. NSAIDs, PPIs, β-lactams and rifampicin are common causes. Red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs point to glomerular disease, and muddy-brown casts to ATN.
> `RENAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (antibiotics, eosinophilia, WBC casts — TIN), 2016 AIIMS (dysmorphic RBCs — glomerular)

subject: Pathology
stem: A renal tumour shows large cells with pale reticulated cytoplasm, prominent cell membranes ("plant-cell" look), perinuclear halos and diffuse Hale's colloidal iron positivity. The diagnosis is
explanation:
It has extensive chromosome loss (hypodiploidy) and a good prognosis. Clear cell RCC (VHL, 3p loss) arises from the PCT and is full of glycogen and lipid. Oncocytoma is benign and has a central scar. Angiomyolipoma is the classic renal tumour of tuberous sclerosis.
> `RENAL` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG (perinuclear halo — chromophobe), 2020 INI-CET (clear cell RCC features), 2016 AIIMS (tuberous sclerosis — angiomyolipoma)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match the age of a myocardial infarct with its dominant histological feature.

| Infarct age | Histology |
|---|---|
| 1. 1–3 days | a. Dense collagenous scar |
| 2. 3–7 days | b. Early granulation tissue at the margins |
| 3. 7–10 days | c. Coagulative necrosis with neutrophilic infiltrate |
| 4. More than 2 months | d. Macrophages removing dead myocytes (maximum softening) |
explanation:
Rupture of the free wall, septum or papillary muscle is most likely at 3–7 days, when macrophages have softened the infarct. In the first 4 hours, light microscopy may show only wavy fibres.
> `CARDIOVASCULAR` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (coagulative necrosis with neutrophils — day 1–3), 2017 AIIMS (rupture 2–4 days)

subject: Pathology
stem: After thrombolysis, the reperfused myocardium shows intensely eosinophilic transverse bands in necrotic myocytes. These are caused by
options: Calcium influx causing hypercontraction of myofibrils
explanation:
Contraction band necrosis is the hallmark of reperfusion. Reperfusion injury also involves oxygen free radicals and the mitochondrial permeability transition. The hydroxyl radical is the most reactive free radical.
> `CARDIOVASCULAR` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (post-MI reperfusion — contraction bands), 2015 AIIMS (most reactive free radical)

subject: Pathology
stem: At autopsy, a heart slice is incubated in triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC). An infarct about 6 hours old appears pale because
options: Dehydrogenase enzymes have leaked out of the dead myocytes, so the dye is not reduced to red formazan
explanation:
Viable myocardium stains brick-red. TTC shows infarcts only 2–3 hours old, well before the changes visible on routine histology.
> `CARDIOVASCULAR` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (TTC — viable myocardium red)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each type of endocarditis with its vegetations.

| Endocarditis | Vegetations |
|---|---|
| 1. Rheumatic | a. Small, warty, along the lines of closure, with commissural fusion |
| 2. Infective | b. Small, sterile, on both surfaces of the leaflets |
| 3. Libman–Sacks (SLE) | c. Small, bland, sterile, loosely attached, in cancer or hypercoagulable states |
| 4. Non-bacterial thrombotic (marantic) | d. Large, bulky, friable and destructive |
explanation:
In acute rheumatic carditis, Aschoff bodies containing Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells are diagnostic. Chronic rheumatic disease causes fish-mouth mitral stenosis.
> `CARDIOVASCULAR` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (vegetations along lines of closure, commissural fusion — rheumatic), 2019 NEET-PG (bulky friable — infective; Aschoff bodies), 2018 AIIMS (fish-mouth)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 19-year-old athlete collapses and dies on the field. The heart shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy. The characteristic histology and the most commonly mutated gene are
options: Lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis — coxsackievirus
Fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricle — plakophilin-2
Disorganised myocytes (myofibre disarray) with interstitial fibrosis — MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain, chromosome 14)
explanation:
HCM is autosomal dominant, mostly from sarcomere gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3). Large "box-car" nuclei show myocyte hypertrophy of any cause, including hypertension. Option B is arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy, and option D causes a restrictive cardiomyopathy.
> `CARDIOVASCULAR` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (young athlete — HOCM), 2021 INI-CET (match — myocyte disarray HOCM, box-car hypertension), 2017 AIIMS (MYH7 on chromosome 14)

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each thyroid carcinoma with its hallmark.

| Carcinoma | Hallmark |
|---|---|
| 1. Papillary | a. Calcitonin-derived amyloid stroma, RET mutation |
| 2. Follicular | b. Older patients, very aggressive, TP53 loss |
| 3. Medullary | c. Capsular or vascular invasion, blood-borne spread to bone, RAS mutation |
| 4. Anaplastic | d. Ground-glass "Orphan Annie" nuclei, psammoma bodies, BRAF V600E, lymphatic spread |
explanation:
Follicular carcinoma can present with punched-out lytic deposits in the skull. Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells.
> `ENDOCRINE` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (amyloid — parafollicular cells), 2023 NEET-PG (papillary — BRAF), 2021 INI-CET (Orphan Annie), 2020 INI-CET (skull lytic lesions — follicular), 2015 AIIMS (lymphatic spread — papillary)

subject: Pathology
stem: FNAC of a solitary thyroid nodule shows a "follicular neoplasm" (Bethesda IV). FNAC cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma because
options: Diagnosing carcinoma needs capsular or vascular invasion, which can only be assessed on the excised specimen
Follicular carcinoma has no distinctive nuclei
explanation:
Diagnostic lobectomy is therefore needed. Papillary carcinoma, by contrast, **can** be diagnosed on FNAC from its nuclear features (grooves, pseudo-inclusions, ground-glass chromatin).
> `ENDOCRINE` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (FNAC not enough for follicular carcinoma), 2016 AIIMS (follicular vs benign — invasion), 2022 NEET-PG (Orphan Annie — FNAC)
exam: 2015 AIIMS (FNAC not enough for follicular carcinoma), 2016

subject: Pathology
stem: The features that separate MEN 2B from MEN 2A are
options: Mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus, with no primary hyperparathyroidism
Parathyroid hyperplasia and cutaneous lichen amyloidosis
explanation:
Both types are caused by RET gain-of-function mutations (classically M918T in MEN 2B) and both include medullary carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma. MEN 1 (menin) comprises parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.
> `ENDOCRINE` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG / 2014 AIIMS (MEN 2B — 3X), 2020 NEET-PG (phaeochromocytoma — MEN 2A)

subject: Pathology
stem: In a phaeochromocytoma, the chief cells are arranged in nests ("Zellballen"). The S100-positive cells at the edge of each nest are
explanation:
Chief cells are chromogranin- and synaptophysin-positive. Raised urinary or plasma metanephrines and VMA support the diagnosis. Up to 40% of cases are hereditary (MEN 2, VHL, NF1, SDH), so the old "rule of 10s" is outdated.
> `ENDOCRINE` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (raised VMA, Zellballen — phaeochromocytoma), 2022 INI-CET (paraganglioma neurosecretory granules)

subject: Pathology
stem: A woman with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis develops a rapidly enlarging, painless thyroid mass. The tumour she is at specific increased risk of is
options: Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma or DLBCL of the thyroid
explanation:
Hashimoto thyroiditis shows lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and Hürthle (oncocytic) cells. Chronic antigen stimulation of the acquired lymphoid tissue predisposes to lymphoma. A small increase in papillary carcinoma is also reported.
> `ENDOCRINE` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centres — Hashimoto, 3X)

subject: Pathology
stem: A smoker has a central lung mass. Biopsy shows a poorly differentiated non-small cell carcinoma that is p40+ and CK5/6+, and TTF-1 and Napsin A negative. The tumour is
explanation:
p40 is the most specific squamous marker. Adenocarcinoma is TTF-1+ and Napsin A+ and is tested for EGFR, ALK and ROS1. Small cell carcinoma is TTF-1+, neuroendocrine-marker positive and has a very high Ki-67. PTHrP-related hypercalcaemia favours squamous cell carcinoma.
> `RESPIRATORY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (TTF-1 — adenocarcinoma), 2021 NEET-PG (smoker with hypercalcaemia — SCC)

subject: Pathology
stem: A bronchial neuroendocrine tumour with organoid nests has 4 mitoses per 2 mm² and focal punctate necrosis. It is classified as
explanation:
Typical carcinoid has fewer than 2 mitoses per 2 mm² and no necrosis. Atypical carcinoid has 2–10 and/or necrosis. More than 10 means a high-grade carcinoma (small cell or large cell neuroendocrine). Carcinoids often present as intrabronchial polypoid masses and are chromogranin-positive.
> `RESPIRATORY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (intrabronchial polyp, chromogranin — atypical carcinoid), 2018 AIIMS (carcinoid cell of origin)

subject: Pathology
stem: In workers exposed to asbestos, the most common asbestos-related MALIGNANCY is
explanation:
Asbestos and smoking together multiply the risk of lung cancer. Mesothelioma is more **specific** to asbestos but less common. Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies are golden-brown and beaded, and stain with Prussian blue. Pleural plaques are the commonest lesion overall.
> `RESPIRATORY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (golden-brown beaded bodies — asbestosis), 2020 NEET-PG (asbestos bodies)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 40-year-old non-smoker with lower-lobe panacinar emphysema also has cirrhosis. Liver biopsy is expected to show
options: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes
explanation:
In α1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ), misfolded protein is trapped in the ER of hepatocytes, causing liver damage. The lack of circulating protease inhibitor allows neutrophil elastase to destroy the lungs. Smoking-related emphysema is centriacinar and affects the upper lobes.
> `RESPIRATORY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (panacinar emphysema — α1-AT deficiency), 2022 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (α1-AT inhibits proteases)

subject: Pathology
stem: A 25-year-old has bilateral vestibular schwannomas and a meningioma. The defective gene product is
explanation:
Schwannomas show cellular Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies, loose Antoni B areas, and diffuse S100. They cause tinnitus and hearing loss at the cerebellopontine angle. NF1 causes neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules.
> `CNS BONE AND SKIN` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (CP angle — Verocay bodies, schwannoma), 2020 INI-CET (Verocay bodies — schwannoma), 2017 AIIMS (CP angle schwannoma)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (CP angle — Verocay bodies, schwannoma), 2020 I

subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each sarcoma with its characteristic translocation.

| Sarcoma | Translocation |
|---|---|
| 1. Ewing sarcoma | a. t(11;22) EWSR1–FLI1 |
| 2. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma | b. t(12;16) FUS–DDIT3 |
| 3. Synovial sarcoma | c. t(2;13) PAX3–FOXO1 |
| 4. Myxoid liposarcoma | d. t(X;18) SS18–SSX |
explanation:
Ewing sarcoma is a diaphyseal small round blue cell tumour with an onion-skin periosteal reaction, CD99+ and NKX2.2+. FISH (EWSR1 break-apart) or RT-PCR confirms these translocations.
> `CNS BONE AND SKIN` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / NEET-PG (Ewing — t(11;22), MIC-2), 2023 NEET-PG (t(12;16) — myxoid liposarcoma), 2016 AIIMS (FISH for t(11;22))

subject: Pathology
stem: A 30-year-old has an expansile lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal femur, extending to the subchondral bone. Biopsy shows many osteoclast-like giant cells evenly scattered among mononuclear stromal cells. The neoplastic cell and the targeted therapy are
options: The mononuclear stromal cell (H3F3A G34W mutation, RANKL-expressing) — denosumab
explanation:
In giant cell tumour of bone, the stromal cells recruit the reactive giant cells through RANKL. The tumour typically occurs after the growth plate closes (age 20–40), around the knee.
> `CNS BONE AND SKIN` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (knee swelling, giant cells among mononuclear cells — GCT)

subject: Pathology
stem: Basal cell carcinoma of the face rarely metastasises. The pathway most consistently disrupted in it, which is targeted by vismodegib, is
options: Hedgehog signalling (PTCH1 loss or SMO activation)
explanation:
Histology shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact. Germline PTCH1 mutation causes Gorlin syndrome (multiple BCCs, jaw keratocysts). BCC is the malignancy least likely to spread by lymphatics.
> `CNS BONE AND SKIN` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET / 2016 AIIMS (least lymphatic spread — BCC), 2023 NEET-PG (palisading nests — BCC)

subject: Pathology
stem: A patient has long-standing eczema-like patches progressing to plaques. Skin biopsy shows atypical CD4⁺ T cells with cerebriform nuclei collected in small clusters within the epidermis. These clusters are called
explanation:
This is mycosis fungoides, the commonest primary cutaneous lymphoma (a T-cell lymphoma, also called Alibert–Bazin disease). Sézary syndrome is the leukaemic form, with erythroderma and circulating Sézary cells. Munro microabscesses and Kogoj pustules are neutrophil collections in psoriasis; Civatte bodies are found in lichen planus.
> `CNS BONE AND SKIN` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 NEET-PG / 2017 AIIMS (commonest skin lymphoma — mycosis fungoides), 2017 AIIMS (Alibert–Bazin — T lymphocyte)

subject: Microbiology
stem: The biological indicator used to check ethylene oxide sterilisation is spores of
explanation:
B. atrophaeus (formerly *B. subtilis* var. *niger*) is used for ethylene oxide and dry heat. *G. stearothermophilus* is used for autoclaves and hydrogen peroxide plasma (STERRAD).
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (autoclave indicator), 2016 AIIMS (STERRAD — H₂O₂)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each item with the correct method of sterilisation.

| Item | Method |
|---|---|
| 1. Inoculating wire loop | a. Inspissation |
| 2. Glass Petri dishes and syringes | b. Ethylene oxide |
| 3. Löwenstein–Jensen (egg-based) medium | c. Red heat (flaming) |
| 4. Heat-sensitive plastic cardiac catheters | d. Hot air oven |
explanation:
Inspissation (80–85 °C on 3 successive days) coagulates media containing egg or serum without destroying them. The hot air oven runs at 160 °C for 2 hours.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (wire loop — heat till red), 2023 INI-CET (glass pipette mouthpiece; cold sterilisation)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Which agent is NOT sporicidal?
explanation:
Alcohol is both an antiseptic and a disinfectant, but it does not kill spores. Sterilants (autoclave, ethylene oxide, plasma, and glutaraldehyde with long exposure) destroy spores.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (spores destroyed by ETO), 2021 INI-CET (ethanol — disinfectant and antiseptic)

subject: Microbiology
stem: After caring for a patient with Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea, hands should be cleaned with soap and water rather than alcohol rub because
options: Alcohol does not kill the spores, and washing removes them mechanically
explanation:
Soap and water are also needed when hands are visibly soiled. Otherwise, alcohol-based rubs are the WHO standard for the "5 moments" of hand hygiene.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (sanitiser not useful with visibly soiled hands)
exam: 2021 INI-CET (sanitiser not useful with visibly soiled hands

subject: Microbiology
stem: A large spill of blood in the operating theatre should be disinfected with sodium hypochlorite containing available chlorine of
explanation:
The spill is covered with absorbent material, flooded with 1% hypochlorite, left for 10–30 minutes, then wiped. 0.1% is enough for routine surfaces. Bleaching powder acts by releasing hypochlorous acid.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG / 2015 AIIMS (blood spill — hypochlorite), 2016 AIIMS (cover with absorbent), 2022 NEET-PG (bleaching powder — HOCl)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each organism or sample with the biosafety level needed to handle it.

| Organism / work | Biosafety level |
|---|---|
| 1. Non-pathogenic E. coli K-12 | a. BSL-4 |
| 2. Routine HIV and HBV blood samples | b. BSL-3 |
| 3. Culture of XDR M. tuberculosis | c. BSL-1 |
| 4. Ebola or Nipah virus | d. BSL-2 |
explanation:
BSL-3 is for organisms spread by aerosol that can be treated (TB culture, Brucella, Coxiella). BSL-4 is for life-threatening agents with no treatment and needs positive-pressure suits.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (BSL-3 — XDR TB)

subject: Microbiology
stem: An E-test strip is placed on a lawn of bacteria. After incubation, the result is read as
options: The diameter of the zone of inhibition
The MIC, at the point where the elliptical zone meets the strip
explanation:
The E-test combines a concentration gradient with diffusion and gives a quantitative MIC. Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion gives a zone diameter (a qualitative result). Broth microdilution is the reference method for MIC.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (E-test — antibiotic sensitivity), 2020 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (disc diffusion — Kirby–Bauer)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Whether milk has been adequately pasteurised is checked with the
explanation:
Alkaline phosphatase is destroyed at pasteurisation temperatures, so remaining activity means heating was inadequate. Holder method: 63 °C for 30 minutes; HTST: 72 °C for 15–20 seconds. The methylene blue test measures bacterial load (keeping quality).
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (pasteurisation 63 °C for 30 min)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A PCR starts with 10 copies of target DNA and runs at 100% efficiency. How many copies are present after 10 cycles?
explanation:
Copies = N₀ × 2ⁿ = 10 × 2¹⁰ = 10 × 1,024 = 10,240. One cycle less gives half the product, which is why the 2024 answer was 26 cycles for half of what 27 cycles produce.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (PCR cycles for half the product)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (PCR cycles for half the product)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A child has suspected meningitis. The single test that can detect several possible bacteria and viruses directly from CSF at once is
explanation:
Multiple primer sets amplify different targets in one reaction. RNA viruses (enteroviruses, influenza, SARS-CoV-2) need reverse transcription first (RT-PCR).
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (syndromic PCR — multiplex), 2021 INI-CET (RNA viruses — RT-PCR), 2020 INI-CET (RSV needs RT step)

subject: Microbiology
stem: The endotoxic activity of the lipopolysaccharide of Gram-negative bacteria lies in
options: Lipid A, which acts through TLR4
explanation:
Lipid A triggers TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 release, causing fever, shock and DIC. The O antigen determines the serotype. Teichoic acid is found only in Gram-positive walls.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (lipid A — Gram-negative wall), 2017 AIIMS (Gram-negative wall — not teichoic acid)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each mechanism of gene transfer with its description.

| Mechanism | Description |
|---|---|
| 1. Transformation | a. DNA carried by a bacteriophage |
| 2. Transduction | b. Transfer through a sex pilus, as with R-plasmids |
| 3. Conjugation | c. "Jumping genes" moving within the same cell |
| 4. Transposition | d. Uptake of naked DNA from the environment |
explanation:
Conjugation is the main way multidrug resistance spreads. Phage conversion, a special case of transduction, gives diphtheria, cholera and botulinum toxins and Shiga-like toxins.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2014 AIIMS (phage-mediated change — transduction), 2017 AIIMS (mechanisms of resistance)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Biofilm formation on catheters and prosthetic valves is coordinated by bacteria through
options: Quorum sensing using autoinducer signalling molecules
explanation:
Biofilms resist antibiotics through poor penetration, slow growth (persister cells) and a protective matrix. This is why infected devices usually have to be removed.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (functions of biofilm)

subject: Microbiology
stem: In Indian ICUs, the organisms most often responsible for ventilator-associated pneumonia are
options: Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae
explanation:
Late-onset VAP (5 days or more after admission) is dominated by these multidrug-resistant Gram-negatives. Healthcare-associated infections are those that appear 48 hours or more after admission.
> `GENERAL MICROBIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (VAP organisms), 2023 NEET-PG (nosocomial infection after 48 h)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Undiluted serum from a patient with secondary syphilis gives a negative VDRL, but the test turns strongly positive at a 1:64 dilution. This is called
options: Prozone phenomenon, caused by antibody excess
explanation:
Too much antibody coats each antigen particle separately, so no lattice (visible clumping) forms. It is classic in secondary syphilis and brucellosis, so serial dilutions are tested.
> `IMMUNOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (negative till 1:40 — excess antibody), 2019 NEET-PG (brucella — prozone)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each preparation or event with the type of immunity it gives.

| Preparation / event | Immunity |
|---|---|
| 1. Tetanus toxoid | a. Natural passive |
| 2. Anti-tetanus immunoglobulin | b. Natural active |
| 3. Maternal IgG crossing the placenta | c. Artificial active |
| 4. Recovery from measles | d. Artificial passive |
explanation:
Active immunity takes time to develop but leaves memory. Passive immunity is immediate but short-lived. Tetanus-prone wounds in unimmunised people receive both, given at different sites.
> `IMMUNOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (toxoid — active immunity)

subject: Microbiology
stem: The secretory component of secretory IgA comes from
options: The J chain made by plasma cells
The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor of mucosal epithelial cells
explanation:
The plasma cell makes dimeric IgA joined by the J chain. The epithelial poly-Ig receptor carries it across the cell (transcytosis), and its cleaved part stays on as the secretory component, protecting IgA from proteases.
> `IMMUNOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (dimeric immunoglobulin — IgA)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Antibodies in a secondary immune response bind antigen more strongly than those in the primary response because of
options: Somatic hypermutation with selection of high-affinity B cells in germinal centres (affinity maturation)
explanation:
The secondary response is faster and larger, mostly IgG, and of higher affinity. Both affinity maturation and class switching need T-cell help (CD40L–CD40).
> `IMMUNOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (affinity low in primary, high in secondary response)
exam: 2020 INI-CET (affinity low in primary, high in secondary res

subject: Microbiology
stem: A dengue NS1 antigen ELISA uses a capture antibody on the plate and a second, enzyme-labelled antibody against another part of the antigen. This format is called
explanation:
Sandwich ELISA detects antigen. Indirect ELISA detects antibody (as in HIV screening). IgM-capture ELISA (MAC-ELISA) detects class-specific antibody, as used for dengue after day 5 and for JE.
> `IMMUNOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (dengue — IgM capture ELISA), 2023 INI-CET (technique for autoantibodies)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Staphylococcal and streptococcal superantigens activate up to 20% of all T cells because they
options: Are processed and presented in the MHC class I groove
Bind the Vβ region of the T-cell receptor and MHC class II outside the peptide groove
explanation:
This polyclonal activation releases huge amounts of cytokines (IL-2, TNF), causing toxic shock. Examples are TSST-1, staphylococcal enterotoxins and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (SpeA, SpeC).
> `IMMUNOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (superantigen — S. pyogenes), 2021 NEET-PG (superantigen producers), 2021 INI-CET (MHC-I → CD8)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each Staphylococcus aureus toxin with the disease it causes.

| Toxin | Disease |
|---|---|
| 1. TSST-1 | a. Necrotising pneumonia and furunculosis (CA-MRSA) |
| 2. Exfoliative toxin | b. Food poisoning with vomiting within 1–6 hours |
| 3. Enterotoxin B | c. Toxic shock syndrome |
| 4. Panton–Valentine leukocidin | d. Scalded skin syndrome (cleaves desmoglein-1) |
explanation:
These are toxin-mediated diseases. Staphylococcal enterotoxins are heat-stable, so reheating food does not prevent illness. Septicaemia, by contrast, is invasive infection, not a toxin effect.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (toxin-mediated effects of S. aureus), 2021 NEET-PG (vomiting 3 h after food)
exam: 2015 AIIMS (toxin-mediated effects of S. aureus), 2021 NEET-

subject: Microbiology
stem: Several guests start vomiting 2 hours after eating fried rice left out at room temperature overnight. The cause is
explanation:
Spores survive cooking, germinate and make heat-stable toxin in the rice. The diarrhoeal form of B. cereus (8–16 hours, meat and vegetables) resembles C. perfringens. *V. parahaemolyticus* (seafood) takes 12–24 hours.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (B. cereus emetic toxin), 2021 NEET-PG (vomiting 3 h — S. aureus), 2016 AIIMS (seafood — V. parahaemolyticus)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A β-haemolytic streptococcus isolated from rapidly spreading necrotising fasciitis is presumptively identified as S. pyogenes by
options: Bacitracin sensitivity and a positive PYR test
explanation:
Group A streptococci produce superantigens (SpeA) and tissue-destroying enzymes (streptokinase, hyaluronidase). The CAMP test is for group B, optochin for pneumococcus, and 6.5% NaCl for enterococcus.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (necrotising fasciitis — S. pyogenes), 2016 AIIMS (bacitracin test)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A neonate develops sepsis and meningitis in the first 24 hours of life. The organism grown is CAMP-test positive and hydrolyses hippurate. Screening the mother at 35–37 weeks involves
options: A combined lower-vaginal and rectal swab cultured in enrichment broth
explanation:
The organism is *Streptococcus agalactiae* (group B), the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis. Carriers receive intrapartum penicillin.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (S. agalactiae — neonatal sepsis)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Cephalosporins are useless against enterococcal infections because
options: Enterococci have intrinsically low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins (PBP5)
The drugs cannot reach the urine
explanation:
Enterococci grow in 6.5% NaCl and on bile esculin and cause UTIs, endocarditis and prostatitis. Treatment is ampicillin with gentamicin, or vancomycin in penicillin-allergic patients (VRE carry *vanA*).
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET (enterococcal endocarditis with penicillin allergy — vancomycin), 2018 AIIMS (acute prostatitis — Enterococcus)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci from a pneumonia patient are separated from viridans streptococci by
explanation:
Autolysin makes pneumococcal colonies "draughtsman"-shaped and bile-soluble. The polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor, demonstrated by the Quellung reaction. Pneumococcus is the commonest cause of community pneumonia, even in HIV.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2015 AIIMS (lanceolate Gram-positive diplococci), 2022 NEET-PG / 2020 NEET-PG (pneumococcal pneumonia), 2023 INI-CET (capsulated organisms)

subject: Microbiology
stem: An isolate of C. diphtheriae from a throat swab is confirmed as toxin-producing by
options: Elek gel precipitation test (or PCR for the tox gene)
explanation:
Albert stain (toluidine blue and malachite green) shows metachromatic granules but not toxin production. The toxin gene comes from a β-phage, and the toxin ADP-ribosylates EF-2, stopping protein synthesis.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (stain for C. diphtheriae), 2022 INI-CET (ADP-ribosylation of EF-2)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A pregnant woman who eats soft cheese develops febrile illness. Blood culture grows a Gram-positive bacillus with tumbling motility at 25 °C but not at 37 °C. The drug of choice is
options: Ampicillin, with gentamicin in severe infection
explanation:
*Listeria monocytogenes* is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. It grows in the cold (cold enrichment) and spreads from cell to cell on actin tails (ActA), avoiding antibodies. It causes neonatal meningitis and stillbirth.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (motile at 22 °C, not at 37 °C — Listeria), 2022 INI-CET (cell-to-cell spread by actin)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A 4-month-old with constipation, poor feeding, weak cry and a "floppy" body was recently given honey. The pathogenesis is
options: Inhibition of glycine release in the spinal cord
Spores germinating in the infant gut and producing toxin that blocks acetylcholine release
explanation:
This is infant botulism. Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins at cholinergic terminals, causing descending flaccid paralysis with dilated pupils. Tetanus toxin blocks glycine and GABA release instead, causing spasms.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (child with blurred vision, dilated pupils — botulism), 2018 NEET-PG (botulinum blocks ACh), 2024 INI-CET (tetanus toxin — glycine/GABA)
exam: 2017 AIIMS (child with blurred vision, dilated pupils — botu

subject: Microbiology
stem: In gas gangrene, the α-toxin of Clostridium perfringens is a lecithinase. It is demonstrated in the laboratory by
options: The Nagler reaction, which is inhibited by antitoxin
explanation:
On egg-yolk agar, lecithinase makes an opaque zone, which antitoxin prevents on half the plate. *C. perfringens* also gives double-zone haemolysis and "stormy clot" in litmus milk, and its type A strains cause food poisoning.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2016 AIIMS (gas gangrene — C. perfringens), 2021 NEET-PG (superantigens include C. perfringens)

subject: Microbiology
stem: The recommended first-line treatment for an initial non-severe episode of C. difficile infection is
explanation:
IV vancomycin does not reach the gut lumen. Diagnosis is two-step: GDH antigen or NAAT, then toxin EIA. Antibodies (IgM) have no diagnostic role.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG (pseudomembranous colitis — GDH and toxin assay; IgM false), 2015 AIIMS (PCR for toxin genes)
exam: 2018 NEET-PG (pseudomembranous colitis — GDH and toxin assay

subject: Microbiology
stem: A renal transplant recipient has a cavitating lung lesion and a brain abscess. Sputum shows thin, branching Gram-positive filaments that stain with modified Ziehl–Neelsen (1% H₂SO₄). The organism and treatment are
explanation:
Nocardia is aerobic and partially acid-fast and spreads by blood to the brain. Actinomyces is anaerobic, non-acid-fast, part of the normal oral flora, and forms sulphur granules with draining sinuses at the jaw; it is treated with penicillin.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (partially acid-fast filaments — Nocardia, 3X), 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (Actinomyces — oropharynx, 3X), 2020 INI-CET (acid-fast organisms)

subject: Microbiology
stem: In the NALC–NaOH method of processing sputum for mycobacterial culture, the role of NaOH is to
options: Liquefy mucus by breaking disulphide bonds
Decontaminate by killing normal flora, while tubercle bacilli survive because of their waxy wall
explanation:
N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NALC) is the mucolytic. The 2024 assertion–reason question swapped these two roles, so its assertion was true and its reason false.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (assertion — NALC and NaOH processing)

subject: Microbiology
stem: The cartridge-based NAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) detects M. tuberculosis and, at the same time,
options: Rifampicin resistance through mutations in the 81-bp core region of rpoB
explanation:
Rifampicin resistance is a good marker of MDR-TB. Line probe assays detect isoniazid (katG, inhA) and second-line resistance. Urine LAM is a point-of-care test for advanced HIV.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (GeneXpert — TB and drug resistance), 2015 AIIMS (urine LAM)
exam: 2017 AIIMS (GeneXpert — TB and drug resistance), 2015 AIIMS

subject: Microbiology
stem: Under the WHO 2021 definitions, extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) is MDR/RR-TB that is also resistant to
options: Any fluoroquinolone plus at least one of bedaquiline or linezolid
explanation:
MDR-TB is resistance to at least rifampicin and isoniazid. Pre-XDR is MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance. The older definition involving injectables has been dropped. Culturing XDR strains requires BSL-3.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Hard` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG (MDR-TB — R and H), 2022 INI-CET (XDR-TB needs BSL-3)
exam: 2019 NEET-PG (MDR-TB — R and H), 2022 INI-CET (XDR-TB needs

subject: Microbiology
stem: In lepromatous leprosy, bacilli are best shown on a slit-skin smear stained with
explanation:
*M. leprae* is less acid-fast than *M. tuberculosis* and cannot be grown in artificial media; it grows in mouse footpads and armadillos. The bacteriological index (BI) and morphological index (MI) are reported.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (acid-fast organisms including M. leprae)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A teenager has fever, purpuric rash and shock. CSF grows Gram-negative diplococci. The feature that separates this organism from N. gonorrhoeae is
options: Fermentation of maltose as well as glucose
explanation:
*N. meningitidis* ferments glucose and maltose; *N. gonorrhoeae* ferments glucose only. Its lipo-oligosaccharide (LOS) endotoxin drives purpura fulminans and Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (meningococcal meningitis — ferments glucose and maltose, 3X), 2021 INI-CET (LOS)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A 20-year-old has a third episode of meningococcal meningitis. The most likely underlying defect is a deficiency of
options: Late complement components C5–C9 (membrane attack complex)
explanation:
Neisseria are especially sensitive to MAC-mediated lysis. Eculizumab (anti-C5) carries the same risk, so patients are vaccinated. The MenACWY vaccines do **not** cover serogroup B.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 NEET-PG (meningococcus with MAC deficiency), 2017 AIIMS (MCV-4 not protective against B)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A man has purulent urethral discharge with Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Because of widespread resistance, the current first-line treatment is
options: Single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone (with azithromycin or doxycycline for possible chlamydia)
explanation:
Gonococci have become resistant to penicillin (PPNG), tetracycline and fluoroquinolones in turn. Culture uses Thayer–Martin (VCN) selective medium.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (penicillin-resistant gonococcus — ceftriaxone), 2023 INI-CET (drug resistance common in gonorrhoea), 2021 NEET-PG (Thayer–Martin, ceftriaxone)

subject: Microbiology
stem: An organism grows on blood agar only as tiny colonies next to a Staphylococcus aureus streak, and needs both X factor (haemin) and V factor (NAD). It is
explanation:
*S. aureus* releases V factor and lyses red cells to release X factor (satellitism). *H. parainfluenzae* needs only V factor; *H. ducreyi* needs X factor. Many *H. influenzae* strains make β-lactamase, so third-generation cephalosporins are used for meningitis. *(The 2019 NEET-PG stem labels this pattern "H. ducreyi meningitis"; satellitism and meningitis indicate H. influenzae.)*
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (satellitism — H. influenzae), 2016 AIIMS (H. influenzae media), 2014 AIIMS (cefotaxime — β-lactamase)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each genital ulcer disease with its features.

| Disease | Features |
|---|---|
| 1. Chancroid | a. Painless, indurated, clean-based single ulcer |
| 2. Primary syphilis | b. Painless, beefy-red ulcer that bleeds on touch; Donovan bodies |
| 3. Donovanosis | c. Painful, soft, ragged ulcer; "school of fish" pattern on Gram stain |
| 4. Lymphogranuloma venereum | d. Small transient ulcer followed by inguinal buboes with the "groove sign" |
explanation:
The organisms are *H. ducreyi*, *T. pallidum*, *Klebsiella granulomatis* (safety-pin Donovan bodies) and *C. trachomatis* serovars L1–L3.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (school of fish — chancroid), 2023 INI-CET (match — donovanosis, pinta), 2018 AIIMS (Donovan bodies), 2016 AIIMS (LGV incubation)

subject: Microbiology
stem: After treatment of secondary syphilis, the response to therapy is best monitored with
explanation:
Non-treponemal titres should fall at least four-fold after treatment. Treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS) usually stay positive for life, so they confirm diagnosis but not cure. Neurosyphilis is diagnosed by CSF VDRL. Syphilis can be transmitted by all blood components.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (palms and soles rash — serology), 2023 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (CSF VDRL), 2017 AIIMS (screening in pregnancy — VDRL/RPR), 2023 INI-CET (syphilis in blood components)
exam: 2024 INI-CET (palms and soles rash — serology), 2023 NEET-PG

subject: Microbiology
stem: A sewage worker has fever, conjunctival suffusion, calf tenderness and jaundice. The gold-standard serological test is
explanation:
Leptospirosis spreads through rodent urine. The organism grows in EMJH medium and is seen by dark-field microscopy (hooked ends, endoflagella). Weil disease adds jaundice and renal failure.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 INI-CET / 2014 AIIMS (EMJH medium, 3X), 2022 NEET-PG / 2018 AIIMS (MAT), 2020 INI-CET (rodent urine), 2018 NEET-PG (leptospirosis case)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A farmer has fever, a black necrotic eschar in the groin and lymphadenopathy. The Weil–Felix test agglutinates Proteus OX-K only. The vector is
explanation:
The organism is *Orientia tsutsugamushi* (scrub typhus), and the drug of choice is doxycycline. OX-19 reacts in epidemic and murine typhus. Weil–Felix is a heterophile test; IgM ELISA is preferred today.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2022 INI-CET (scrub typhus vector — trombiculid mite), 2021 INI-CET (eschar — scrub typhus), 2020 INI-CET (match — Weil–Felix test)

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each rickettsial disease with its vector.

| Disease | Vector |
|---|---|
| 1. Epidemic typhus (R. prowazekii) | a. Hard tick |
| 2. Endemic (murine) typhus (R. typhi) | b. Inhaled aerosol; no arthropod vector, no rash |
| 3. Rocky Mountain spotted fever | c. Rat flea |
| 4. Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) | d. Human body louse |
explanation:
In epidemic typhus the rash spreads from the trunk outwards and spares the palms and soles. RMSF starts at the wrists and ankles and involves the palms and soles. Coxiella is very resistant and forms "doughnut" granulomas.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2018 NEET-PG (body lice — R. prowazekii), 2014 AIIMS (obligate intracellular — Coxiella)

subject: Microbiology
stem: Clusters of bacteria (morulae) are seen inside circulating neutrophils of a patient with fever after a tick bite. The organism is
explanation:
*Ehrlichia chaffeensis* forms morulae in **monocytes**. Both are obligate intracellular bacteria treated with doxycycline.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2021 INI-CET (inclusion body in neutrophils — Anaplasma), 2014 AIIMS (obligate intracellular — Ehrlichia)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A dairy farmer has undulant fever, sweating and arthralgia. The standard agglutination test is negative at low dilutions but positive at higher ones. Handling this culture needs
options: BSL-3, because Brucella is a leading cause of laboratory-acquired infection
explanation:
Brucellosis is acquired from unpasteurised milk and contact with animals. Prozone is common in serology, and blood or bone marrow culture is slow (Castañeda biphasic medium).
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG (brucellosis — prozone), 2022 INI-CET (BSL-3)

subject: Microbiology
stem: In cholera, the toxin that loosens tight junctions and increases paracellular leak is
options: Zonula occludens toxin (Zot), which acts on occludins
explanation:
Cholera toxin (B subunit binds GM1, A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gs) raises cAMP and opens CFTR, causing rice-water stools. Zot adds a paracellular leak. TCBS gives yellow colonies.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2024 INI-CET (cholera — tight junction), 2022 INI-CET (occludins), 2014 AIIMS (zona occludens), 2019 NEET-PG (GM1 receptor)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A man with cirrhosis develops septic shock with haemorrhagic bullae 36 hours after eating raw oysters. The organism is
explanation:
This is a halophilic vibrio that causes fulminant sepsis in people with liver disease or iron overload, and wound infection after coral or seawater cuts. *V. parahaemolyticus* causes seafood gastroenteritis and is Kanagawa-positive (β-haemolysis on Wagatsuma agar).
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2017 AIIMS (coral cuts — V. vulnificus; halophilic vibrios), 2024 INI-CET / 2023 NEET-PG (Kanagawa — V. parahaemolyticus)
exam: 2017 AIIMS (coral cuts — V. vulnificus; halophilic vibrios),

subject: Microbiology
stem:
Match each E. coli pathotype with its mechanism.

| Pathotype | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| 1. ETEC | a. "Stacked-brick" aggregative adherence |
| 2. EPEC | b. Shiga toxin; does not ferment sorbitol; causes HUS |
| 3. EHEC O157:H7 | c. Heat-labile and heat-stable toxins; travellers' diarrhoea |
| 4. EAEC | d. Attaching-and-effacing lesions (intimin); infant diarrhoea |
explanation:
EHEC is isolated on sorbitol MacConkey agar (colourless colonies). EIEC invades the mucosa and causes shigella-like dysentery. "H" in O157:H7 refers to the flagellar antigen.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Hard` • Based on: 2020 INI-CET (match — ETEC, EIEC, EPEC, EAEC), 2024 INI-CET (EHEC — HUS), 2021 NEET-PG (sorbitol MacConkey), 2016 AIIMS (EPEC effacement), 2023 NEET-PG (H antigen)
exam: 2020 INI-CET (match — ETEC, EIEC, EPEC, EAEC), 2024 INI-CET

subject: Microbiology
stem: The enteric pathogen with the LOWEST infective dose (10–100 organisms), which allows person-to-person spread in crèches, is
explanation:
Shigella resists stomach acid. Cholera and non-typhoidal salmonella need doses of about 10⁶ or more. Shigella causes small-volume, frequent stools with pus and blood. Selenite F broth and XLD/DCA agar are used for isolation.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `New-adjacent` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2019 NEET-PG (Selenite F — shigellosis), 2017 AIIMS (shigella-like dysentery — EIEC)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A traveller has had fever for 3 weeks and has already taken antibiotics. The most sensitive specimen for culturing Salmonella Typhi is
explanation:
Marrow culture stays positive even after antibiotics. Blood culture is the test of choice in week 1, Widal from week 2, and stool or urine culture in weeks 3–4. Chronic carriers harbour the organism in the gallbladder.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2023 NEET-PG (typhoid — blood culture), 2020 INI-CET (match — Widal in week 2)

subject: Microbiology
stem: A burns patient's wound grows an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus with a blue-green pigment and a grape-like odour. The pigment is
explanation:
*Pseudomonas aeruginosa* is a strict aerobe that also causes ecthyma gangrenosum, otitis externa and VAP. Its exotoxin A ADP-ribosylates EF-2, like diphtheria toxin.
> `BACTERIOLOGY` • `Reworded` • `Moderate` • Based on: 2020 NEET-PG (burns, obligate aerobe, oxidase positive — Pseudomonas)
